A park where it is always windy
89345.e: In a wind farm several wind turbines stand together. In Switzerland there are wind farms in the Jura and at the Nufenen Pass, for example.
89345.m: A wind farm is made up of several wind turbines.

89346.q: What happens to a wind turbine in a very strong storm?
a: It is switched off to avoid damage
It turns as fast as it can
It is folded down to the ground
89346.e: Above a certain wind speed the rotor blades are turned out of the wind. This protects the turbine from overload.
89346.m: In a storm wind turbines are switched off for protection.

89347.q: Which form of the wind's energy does a wind turbine use?
89347.e: Moving air has kinetic energy. The rotor takes some of it and turns it into rotation, from which electricity is produced.
89347.m: Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of the air.

89348.q: Which gas is the main part of biogas?
89348.e: Biogas is usually about half to two thirds methane. The rest is mainly carbon dioxide.
89348.m: The main burnable part of biogas is methane.

89349.q: What is biogas often produced from on farms?
89349.e: Slurry and manure contain a lot of organic material. Bacteria break it down into biogas in closed tanks.
89349.m: Biogas can be made from slurry and manure.

89350.q: Under what conditions do bacteria break down the biomass in a biogas plant?
89350.e: The fermentation in the digester takes place with no air. Only then do the bacteria produce methane.
89350.m: Biogas forms when bacteria break down biomass without oxygen.

89351.q: What is the tank called in which fermentation takes place in a biogas plant?
89351.e: In the digester the biomass is kept warm and stirred. There the bacteria break down the material and form gas.
89351.m: Fermentation in a biogas plant takes place in the digester.

89352.q: What does a combined heat and power plant running on biogas produce?
89352.e: An engine burns the biogas and so produces electricity. The waste heat from the engine is also used for heating.
89352.m: A combined heat and power plant supplies electricity and heat at the same time.

89353.q: What is often done with the leftovers from a farm biogas plant?
a: They are burnt in the fireplace
89353.e: The leftovers still contain many nutrients. They are spread on fields and used as fertiliser.
89353.m: Leftovers from biogas plants are used as fertiliser.

89354.q: What is biogas called that has been cleaned and can be fed into the natural gas grid?
89354.e: For the gas grid the carbon dioxide is removed. What is left is almost pure methane, called biomethane.

89355.q: In which plants is sewage gas, a form of biogas, produced?
89355.e: The sludge from the waste water is fermented in digestion towers. This produces sewage gas, which is often used for electricity and heat.
89355.m: Sewage plants make biogas from sewage sludge.

89356.q: Where does an air-to-water heat pump get its heat from?
89356.e: The heat pump draws heat from the outside air, even at temperatures below zero. This heat is raised to a higher temperature and used for heating.
89356.m: An air-to-water heat pump uses the heat in the outside air.

89357.q: Which household appliance is a heat pump technically closely related to?
89357.e: A fridge pumps heat from its inside to the outside. A heat pump does the same, only it brings the heat from outside into the house.
89357.m: A heat pump works like a fridge in reverse.

89358.q: A heat pump makes about 4 kilowatt hours of heat from 1 kilowatt hour of electricity. Where does the rest come from?
a: From the surroundings, for example the air or ground
From the refrigerant, which gets used up
From the water in the heating
89358.e: The heat pump takes most of the heat from the environment. The electricity only drives the compressor.
89358.m: A heat pump gets most of its heat from the environment.

89359.q: What is the borehole called that a heat pump uses to get heat from underground?
89359.e: For a ground probe, a pipe is often sunk well over 100 metres deep into the ground. A liquid in it takes up the heat of the ground.
89359.m: A ground probe gets heat from underground.

89360.q: What energy does a heat pump need to run?
89360.e: The heat pump needs electricity to drive its pump for the refrigerant. But most of the heating warmth comes from the environment.

89361.q: Which substance circulates in a heat pump and evaporates even at low temperatures?
89361.e: The refrigerant takes up heat from the environment in the evaporator and turns into a gas. Then it is brought to a higher temperature and gives its heat to the heating.
89361.m: In a heat pump a refrigerant carries the heat.

89362.q: Which part of a heat pump compresses the gaseous refrigerant and so raises its temperature?
89362.e: When you squeeze a gas together, it gets warm. The compressor uses this to raise the temperature for the heating.
89362.m: In a heat pump the compressor raises the refrigerant's temperature.

89363.q: Why are heat pumps considered better for the climate than oil heating?
a: They burn no heating oil and use heat from the environment
They need no energy at all
They cool the house in winter
89363.e: Burning oil for heating produces a lot of carbon dioxide. A heat pump uses heat from the environment and electricity, most of which is produced with low CO2 in Switzerland.
89363.m: Heat pumps heat without burning heating oil.

a: A digital electricity meter that sends usage data automatically
A measuring tape for power lines
89364.e: A smart meter measures electricity use continuously and sends the data automatically to the grid operator. In Switzerland the old meters are gradually being replaced by these smart meters.
89364.m: A smart meter is an intelligent, digital electricity meter.

89365.q: What voltage does a normal socket in Switzerland supply?
89365.e: At the end of the power grid, an alternating voltage of 230 volts reaches the household. Before that, the high voltage is lowered step by step in transformers.

89366.q: What is meant by a blackout?
a: A widespread power cut lasting a long time
89366.e: In a blackout the electricity fails over a large area, often for hours. Transport, communication and the water supply are affected too.
89366.m: A blackout is a widespread power cut.

89367.q: Why is electricity sent over long distances at very high voltage?
a: Because then the losses in the lines are smaller
Because then the electricity arrives faster
Because high voltage is cheaper to measure
Because then birds do not land
89367.e: At high voltage, less current flows for the same power. That means the lines heat up less and less energy is lost.
89367.m: High voltage reduces losses when transporting electricity.

89368.q: Which device in the power grid changes the voltage, for example from high voltage to 230 volts?
89368.e: Transformers are made of coils on an iron core. Depending on the number of turns, they raise or lower the voltage.
89368.m: Transformers raise or lower the voltage in the power grid.

89369.q: What does Swissgrid's transmission network carry across Switzerland?
89369.e: Swissgrid runs Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid. It connects the big power stations with the regions and the neighbouring countries.
89369.m: Swissgrid runs the Swiss extra-high-voltage grid.

89370.q: Why is the Swiss power grid connected to the grids of neighbouring countries?
a: So that countries can exchange electricity and help each other out
So that the electricity becomes coloured
So that no power stations are needed any more
So that the electricity flows more slowly
89370.e: Through these connections Switzerland can import and export electricity. If a power station fails somewhere, the other grids help out.
89370.m: The Swiss power grid is connected to the whole of Europe.

89371.q: What must be true in the power grid at every moment so that the frequency stays stable?
a: Production and consumption must be equal
All power stations must run at the same time
Consumption must be twice as big as production
Electricity may only flow at night
89371.e: If more is used than produced, the frequency drops; in the opposite case it rises. That is why power stations are constantly adjusted.
89371.m: In the power grid, production and consumption must always be in balance.

89372.q: Who decided on the new Energy Act in Switzerland in 2017?
89372.e: On 21 May 2017 around 58 per cent of voters said yes to the new Energy Act. This started the implementation of the Energy Strategy 2050.
89372.m: In 2017 the people said yes to the Energy Strategy 2050.

89373.q: What can you do in everyday life to help with the goals of the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: Switch off the light when you leave the room
Turn the heating up high with the window open
Leave the TV on all the time
Always take the car for short trips
89373.e: The Energy Strategy 2050 wants less energy to be wasted. Every light switched off and every trip on foot saves energy.
89373.m: Saving energy helps the Energy Strategy 2050.

89374.q: What are the three main goals of the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: Save energy, expand renewable energy, gradually replace nuclear power
Burn more coal, import more oil, export more electricity
Empty all reservoirs, take down wind turbines, make petrol cheaper
Use only nuclear power and ban solar panels
89374.e: The strategy relies on more energy efficiency and expanding hydropower, solar, wind and biomass. This is meant to replace the electricity from the nuclear power stations that are shut down.
89374.m: The Energy Strategy 2050 relies on efficiency and renewable energy.

89375.q: Which federal office is mainly responsible for implementing the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE)
The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)
89375.e: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy is part of the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC). It looks after energy policy and publishes the energy statistics.
89375.m: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy implements the Energy Strategy 2050.

89376.q: What did the Federal Council decide in 2011 after the nuclear accident at Fukushima in Japan?
a: A gradual exit from nuclear power
To build many new nuclear power stations
89376.e: After the accident at Fukushima, the Federal Council under Energy Minister Doris Leuthard decided not to build any new nuclear power stations. This led to the Energy Strategy 2050.
89376.m: After Fukushima, Switzerland decided to exit nuclear power.

89377.q: What is the law for a secure electricity supply from renewable energy that the people accepted in June 2024 called?
89377.e: On 9 June 2024 around 69 per cent of voters accepted the so-called Electricity Act. It is meant to speed up the expansion of hydro, solar and wind power.
89377.m: The Electricity Act accepted in 2024 promotes the expansion of renewable energy.

89378.q: Which climate goal for 2050 did the voters accept in 2023 with the Climate and Innovation Act?
a: Twice as much heating oil as today
89378.e: On 18 June 2023 the people accepted the Climate and Innovation Act. By 2050 Switzerland is to emit no more greenhouse gases overall.
89378.m: Switzerland aims to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

a: Getting the same benefit with less energy
Using as much energy as possible
89379.e: An efficient appliance needs less energy for the same result, for example an LED lamp instead of a light bulb. Efficiency is a pillar of the Energy Strategy 2050.
89379.m: Energy efficiency means achieving the same with less energy.

89380.q: Roughly how much electricity was used in Switzerland in 2024 (final consumption)?
89380.e: According to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, electricity consumption in 2024 was 57.5 terawatt hours. One terawatt hour is a billion kilowatt hours.
89380.m: In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 terawatt hours of electricity.

89381.q: In which unit is electricity use shown on the electricity bill?
89381.e: The kilowatt hour measures energy. It shows how much electricity was used over a certain time.
89381.m: Electricity use is measured in kilowatt hours.

89382.q: A 2000-watt kettle runs for 3 hours in total. How much energy does it use?
89382.e: 2000 watts are 2 kilowatts. 2 kW times 3 h makes 6 kWh.
89382.m: Energy is calculated as power times time.

89383.q: One kilowatt hour costs 30 centimes. How much do 6 kWh cost?
89383.e: 6 times 30 centimes makes 180 centimes. That is 1.80 francs.
89383.m: Electricity costs are usage times the price per kilowatt hour.

89384.q: In which season is electricity use in Switzerland highest?
89384.e: In winter more light and heating energy is needed, for example for heat pumps. At the same time rivers and solar systems supply less electricity.
89384.m: Switzerland uses the most electricity in winter.

89385.q: What does the energy label on a fridge show?
a: How economical the appliance is with energy
89385.e: The energy label puts appliances into classes from A to G. Class A stands for the most economical appliances.
89385.m: The energy label shows how economical an appliance is.

89386.q: What is the electricity use of an appliance called that seems to be switched off but is still plugged in?
89386.e: Many appliances wait on standby for a signal from the remote control and use a little electricity all the time for this. A switchable power strip helps you save.
89386.m: Appliances on standby use electricity too.

89387.q: Why does an LED lamp use less electricity than a light bulb of the same brightness?
a: It turns more energy into light and less into heat
It only shines half as long
It needs no electricity at all
It is smaller and therefore more economical
89387.e: A light bulb turns most of the electricity into heat. LED lamps produce much more light per watt.
89387.m: LED lamps are more economical because they lose less energy as heat.

a: Heat produced centrally and delivered to many buildings through pipes
Heat from the sun in space
Heat from an electric heater in the living room
89388.e: A heating plant or a facility with waste heat heats water. This flows through well-insulated pipes to the connected houses.
89388.m: District heating is produced centrally and distributed through pipes.

89389.q: Which plants supply a large part of the district heating in many Swiss cities?
89389.e: Burning rubbish produces a lot of heat. Waste incineration plants use it for electricity and district heating.
89389.m: Waste incineration plants supply lots of district heating.

89390.q: In what form is the heat carried in most district heating networks?
a: As hot water in insulated pipes
As hot air in ventilation shafts
89390.e: Hot water or steam flows to the houses in a supply pipe. The cooled water returns to the plant in a return pipe.
89390.m: District heating mostly flows as hot water through insulated pipes.

89391.q: What advantage does a house connected to district heating have over a house with its own oil heating?
a: It needs no boiler and no oil tank of its own
It needs no radiators at all
The flat automatically stays cool in summer
It no longer has a water connection
89391.e: Instead of a boiler there is only a small transfer station in the basement. An oil tank and chimney are no longer needed.
89391.m: With district heating a house needs no boiler of its own.

89392.q: What is the part called that passes the heat from the district heating network to the house's own heating without the water mixing?
89392.e: In the heat exchanger, the water from the network and the house's heating water flow separately side by side. The heat passes through thin metal walls.
89392.m: A heat exchanger passes on heat without the liquids mixing.

89393.q: What can the waste heat from a power station usefully be used for?
89393.e: Power stations produce a lot of heat that would otherwise be lost. Through a district heating network it can heat nearby houses, for example at the Beznau nuclear power station.
89393.m: Waste heat from power stations can heat houses.

89394.q: Which fuel is used in many rural heating networks in Switzerland?
89394.e: Wood chips from Swiss forests are burnt in central heating plants. The heat is then distributed to the connected buildings.
89394.m: Many heating networks use wood chips from the region.

a: Heat produced as a by-product of a process
Heat that is turned off at night
Heat that you buy in a shop
89395.e: Waste heat is produced in factories or data centres, for example. Instead of letting it escape unused, it can be used through district heating networks.
89395.m: Waste heat is heat produced as a by-product that can be put to use.

89496.q: Which data does the Swiss Data Protection Act protect?
89496.e: The Data Protection Act sets out how information relating to a specific or identifiable person is handled. This includes things like name, address or photos.
89496.m: The Data Protection Act protects information about people.

89497.q: Under the Swiss Data Protection Act, what must a company do if it collects data about you?
a: Report the data to your school
89497.e: Companies have a duty to inform. They must say which data they collect and what they use it for.
89497.m: Anyone who collects personal data must inform the people concerned.

89498.q: What is the job of the FDPIC in Switzerland?
89498.e: FDPIC stands for Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner. It checks whether authorities and companies comply with the Data Protection Act and advises the public.
89498.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

89499.q: Which of these details counts as particularly sensitive under the Data Protection Act?
89499.e: Particularly sensitive data includes data about health, religion, political views, as well as genetic and biometric data. Stricter rules apply to it.
89499.m: Health data is particularly sensitive personal data.

89500.q: Under the Data Protection Act, what can you ask of a company that stores data about you?
a: Information about which data it has on you
A payment for every detail stored
The deletion of all data of all customers
89500.e: Everyone has a right of access. The company must say which data it processes about that person and why.
89500.m: You may ask which data a company has stored about you.

89501.q: What does it usually cost to ask a company which data it has about you?
a: Nothing, the information is usually free
A fee for each detail stored
You have to buy a yearly subscription
89501.e: The right of access is meant to be open to everyone. That is why the information is free in principle and usually has to be given within 30 days.
89501.m: Information about your own data is usually free.

89502.q: What can happen if someone deliberately breaks the Swiss Data Protection Act?
a: They can get a large fine
They only have to change their password
89502.e: For deliberate breaches there are fines of up to 250,000 francs. It is mainly the responsible people who are fined.
89502.m: Breaking data protection rules can be expensive.

89503.q: What does “privacy by default” mean in the Data Protection Act?
a: The most privacy-friendly setting is switched on from the start
All data is public by default
You have to choose a new password every year
Apps may only be used in Switzerland
89503.e: Default settings must be chosen so that only as little data as necessary is processed. Anyone who wants to share more has to set this up themselves.
89503.m: An app's basic settings should give away as little data as possible.

89504.q: What must a company do if personal data is stolen from it and this creates a high risk for the people concerned?
a: Report the incident to the FDPIC
Only inform the police in another country
89504.e: If there is a data security breach likely to cause a high risk, it must be reported to the FDPIC. The FDPIC should be informed as quickly as possible.
89504.m: A company must report serious data breaches to the FDPIC.

89505.q: Which English word does “phishing” come from?
89505.e: The fraudsters “fish” for passwords. The “ph” instead of “f” is a nod to earlier hacker spellings.
89505.m: In phishing, fraudsters fish for passwords.

89506.q: An email seems to come from your bank and asks for your password. What is correct?
a: Genuine banks never ask for passwords by email
You reply straight away with the password
You send only half of the password
You forward the email to all your friends
89506.e: Banks and other genuine companies never ask for passwords by email, text message or telephone. A request like this is almost always an attempt at fraud.
89506.m: No genuine company asks for your password by email.

89507.q: What is the best way to check where a link in a suspicious email really leads?
a: Hover the mouse over it without clicking and look at the address
89507.e: When you hover over it, the email program shows the real destination address. If it differs from the official address, be careful.
89507.m: Before clicking, you check where a link really leads.

89508.q: A phishing email knows your name and your school. Why is it particularly dangerous?
a: It can set the computer on fire
It definitely comes from the school
89508.e: Fraudsters collect information about their victim beforehand. A personal message seems believable, so it is easier to fall for it. This is called spear phishing.
89508.m: Personal phishing emails are especially hard to spot.

89509.q: Which federal office in Switzerland can you report cyber attacks such as phishing to (as of 2026)?
a: The Federal Office for Cyber Security
The Federal Office of Public Health
89509.e: The Federal Office for Cyber Security (NCSC) receives reports of cyber incidents. It grew out of the National Cyber Security Centre at the beginning of 2024.
89509.m: In Switzerland you can report cyber incidents to the Federal Office for Cyber Security.

89510.q: What is the general term for harmful programs?
89510.e: Malware is short for “malicious software”, meaning harmful software. Viruses, worms and Trojans all belong to it.
89510.m: Malware is the umbrella term for harmful programs.

89511.q: What is a harmful program called that spreads by itself over networks without attaching itself to a file?
89511.e: A computer worm uses networks and security gaps to copy itself from computer to computer. A virus, on the other hand, needs a host file.
89511.m: A worm spreads by itself over networks.

a: It secretly spies on data and behaviour
89512.e: Spyware collects information without the user knowing, such as websites visited or login details, and sends it to third parties.

89513.e: A keylogger stores every key press. This lets attackers read passwords and messages.
89513.m: A keylogger records every key press.

89514.q: What is a network of many infected computers controlled remotely by an attacker called?
89514.e: The owners of the devices often notice nothing. Botnets are used, for example, for spam or for overload attacks on websites.
89514.m: A botnet consists of many remotely controlled, infected devices.

89515.q: Which kind of harmful program mainly shows unwanted advertising?
89515.e: Adware (from “advertising”) shows advert windows without being asked. It is often installed together with free programs.
89515.m: Adware floods the device with advertising.

89516.q: How does harmful software most often get onto smartphones?
a: Through apps from unsafe sources outside the official app stores
By charging with your own charger
89516.e: Apps from unknown sources are not checked and can contain harmful code. Official stores check apps, though not perfectly.
89516.m: You should only install apps from official stores.

89517.q: Why is a harmful program like a rootkit particularly hard to detect?
a: It hides deep in the operating system
It is always marked in red
It shows itself as an advert every day
89517.e: A rootkit changes parts of the operating system so that harmful programs stay invisible. That is why even antivirus programs find it hard to detect.
89517.m: A rootkit hides harmful software deep in the system.

89518.q: What does a computer virus need in order to spread?
a: A host file or a program to attach itself to
89518.e: Like a biological virus, a computer virus needs a host. It copies itself into other files and becomes active when they are opened.
89518.m: A computer virus needs a host file.

89519.q: Why is a computer virus called that?
a: Because it multiplies like a biological virus and infects other files
Because it only appears when you are ill
Because it comes from a laboratory
Because it gives the computer a cold
89519.e: The name describes its behaviour: the program copies itself and “infects” other programs. The term became well known in the 1980s.
89519.m: A computer virus infects other files like a real virus.

89520.q: What is the protective program called that searches files for known viruses?
89520.e: An antivirus program compares files with the identifying features of known harmful programs and watches for suspicious behaviour.
89520.m: An antivirus program finds and removes harmful software.

89521.q: Why does an antivirus program need to be updated regularly?
a: Because new viruses are appearing all the time
Because otherwise it gets too loud
Because otherwise there are no more emails
89521.e: The program mainly recognises pests whose features (signatures) it knows. Without new signatures, new viruses go undetected.
89521.m: Virus protection only works with up-to-date signatures.

89522.q: Why should you not enable macros in Word or Excel files from strangers?
a: They use too much printer ink
89522.e: Macros are small programs inside documents. Attackers often hide viruses in them, which start working when enabled.
89522.m: You should not enable macros in documents from strangers.

89523.q: What was the name of the computer worm from 2000 that spread by email as a love letter?
89523.e: The attachment was called LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU. Anyone who opened it sent the pest on to all their contacts; millions of computers were affected.
89523.m: The ILOVEYOU pest spread as a love letter in 2000.

89524.q: How did the first PC viruses in the 1980s mainly spread?
89524.e: At that time most computers were not connected to the internet. Viruses such as Brain from 1986 travelled on floppy disks from computer to computer.
89524.m: The first PC viruses spread on floppy disks.

89525.q: What should you do if an antivirus program raises the alarm on the school computer?
a: Tell the teacher or the IT support
Send the suspicious file to friends
89525.e: Experts can check whether the file is really dangerous and remove it. Trying things out yourself can make the damage worse.
89525.m: If there is a virus alarm, you get help from experts.

89526.q: What is a Trojan in computing?
a: A program that looks useful but secretly does damage
89526.e: A Trojan disguises itself, for example, as a free game or a utility. In the background, however, it carries out harmful functions.
89526.m: A Trojan disguises itself as a useful program.

89527.q: Which legend is the Trojan named after?
a: The wooden horse in the battle for Troy
The building of the Tower of Babel
The wanderings in the Minotaur's labyrinth
89527.e: In the Greek legend, warriors hid inside a wooden horse that the Trojans themselves pulled into their city. In the same way, the computer Trojan gets into the system unnoticed.
89527.m: The Trojan is named after the wooden horse of Troy.

89528.q: What makes a Trojan different from a computer virus?
a: A Trojan usually does not copy itself
A Trojan does not need an operating system
89528.e: A virus copies itself into other files. A Trojan, on the other hand, is installed by the victim themselves, because they think it is useful.
89528.m: A Trojan is usually installed by the victim themselves.

89529.q: What can a Trojan with a backdoor allow an attacker to do?
89529.e: A backdoor opens a secret way in. The attacker can then steal files, start programs or switch on the webcam.
89529.m: Through a backdoor an attacker can control the computer remotely.

89530.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from Trojans?
a: Only download programs from trustworthy sources
Install as many free programs as possible
Save all files on the desktop
89530.e: Trojans often hide in cracked games or dodgy downloads. Official websites and app stores are much safer.
89530.m: Only download software from trustworthy sources.

89531.q: What do Trojans most often disguise themselves as?
89531.e: Free offers tempt people to install a file without checking it. Illegal copies of paid games in particular often contain harmful code.
89531.m: Free offers from dodgy sources often contain Trojans.

89532.q: What is a Trojan called that secretly downloads more harmful programs from the internet?
89532.e: A downloader is small and inconspicuous at first. After installation it fetches more pests such as spyware or ransomware onto the device.
89532.m: A downloader Trojan fetches more pests.

89533.q: What is a Trojan called that specifically targets login details for online banking?
89533.e: Banking Trojans intercept login details or change payment orders without anyone noticing. Swiss bank customers have also been targets of such attacks.
89533.m: Banking Trojans are after the money in bank accounts.

a: It encrypts data and demands a ransom
89534.e: A ransom is money demanded to release something. The victims are supposed to pay to be able to read their data again.
89534.m: Ransomware demands a ransom for encrypted data.

89535.q: In what form do ransomware blackmailers usually demand the ransom?
a: In cash at the bank counter
89535.e: Cryptocurrencies are hard to trace. That is why attackers usually demand payment in Bitcoin or similar currencies.

89536.q: What do experts and authorities recommend if you become a victim of ransomware?
a: Do not pay the ransom and report the incident
89536.e: There is no guarantee that the data will come back after paying. Payments also fund further attacks.
89536.m: With ransomware you should not pay but report the attack.

89537.q: What happened in May 2017 in the attack with the ransomware “WannaCry”?
a: Hundreds of thousands of computers were encrypted, including in hospitals
The whole internet was switched off for a week
All mobile phones were repaired for free
Only a single computer was affected
89537.e: WannaCry used a security gap in Windows and spread by itself. Computers in over 150 countries were affected, including hospitals in Great Britain.
89537.m: WannaCry was one of the biggest ransomware attacks in 2017.

89538.q: What should you do if you notice that ransomware is encrypting files right now?
a: Disconnect the device from the network immediately
89538.e: If the device is disconnected from the network, the harmful software cannot spread to other devices on the network. After that you get expert help.
89538.m: If ransomware strikes, you disconnect the device from the network immediately.

89539.q: What is the blackmail called in which attackers encrypt data and also threaten to publish it?
89539.e: The attackers copy the data before encrypting it. This is meant to push even people who have a backup into paying.
89539.m: In double extortion, attackers also threaten to publish the data.

89540.q: Which organisations often become victims of ransomware because they urgently depend on their data?
89540.e: When hospitals or administrations can no longer work, the pressure to pay is very high. Municipalities and companies in Switzerland have also been affected.
89540.m: Ransomware often hits organisations that cannot work without their data.

89541.q: How does ransomware often get onto a computer?
89541.e: Many attacks start with an email whose attachment looks like a bill. If you open it, the harmful software starts.
89541.m: You do not open unexpected email attachments.

a: You log in with two different kinds of proof
You need two passwords that are the same
Two people have to log in together
You log in twice a day
89542.e: As well as the password, you need a second proof of a different kind, such as a code on your mobile phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough.
89542.m: Two-factor authentication requires two different kinds of proof.

89543.q: Which category of factors does a password belong to?
89543.e: A password is something you know. A mobile phone that a code is sent to, on the other hand, belongs to the category of possession.
89543.m: A password is a factor from the knowledge category.

89544.q: Which category of factors does a fingerprint belong to?
89544.e: Biometric features such as a fingerprint or a face are firmly linked to the person.
89544.m: A fingerprint is a biometric feature.

89545.q: Which combination is genuine two-factor authentication?
a: Password and a code from an app on your phone
89545.e: Password, date of birth and username all belong to the knowledge category. Only a factor from another category, such as the phone as possession, makes it two factors.
89545.m: The two factors must come from different categories.

89546.q: How long is a code from an authenticator app typically valid?
89546.e: Such one-time codes are calculated from a secret key and the current time. They usually change every 30 seconds.
89546.m: Codes from authenticator apps expire after a short time.

89547.q: What does the abbreviation 2FA stand for?
89547.e: 2FA is the common short form for two-factor authentication.
89547.m: The abbreviation 2FA stands for two-factor authentication.

89548.q: You get a 2FA code by text message, although you did not want to log in at all. What does this probably mean?
a: Someone knows your password and is trying to log in
89548.e: The code is only sent after the correct password has been entered. You should not give the code to anyone and should change your password immediately.
89548.m: An unexpected login code is a sign of a stolen password.

89549.q: What are the recovery codes for that you get when setting up 2FA?
a: For logging in if you lose your phone
89549.e: Without the second factor you would otherwise no longer get into your account. You keep the codes in a safe place, separate from your phone.
89549.m: Recovery codes save your access if your phone is missing.

89550.q: What is a small device for the USB port that serves as a second factor called?
89550.e: A security key belongs to the possession category. It confirms the login at the press of a button and is well protected against phishing.
89550.m: A security key is a device that serves as a second factor.

89551.q: What does a password manager do?
a: It stores many passwords encrypted in one place
It gives passwords away to friends
It deletes all passwords every day
It makes all passwords the same
89551.e: The password manager is like a digital safe. You can use a different, strong password for every account without having to remember them all.
89551.m: A password manager is a safe for passwords.

89552.q: What is the one password that opens a password manager called?
89552.e: The master password protects all the other stored passwords. It must be especially strong and must never be forgotten.
89552.m: The master password opens the password manager.

89553.q: Why should you not use the same password for all accounts?
a: If it is stolen once, all accounts are in danger
Because it would get too long
Because websites technically do not allow it
89553.e: Attackers try stolen passwords on many services. With different passwords the damage stays limited to one account.
89553.m: Every account needs its own password.

89554.q: What help do many password managers offer when creating new accounts?
a: They write the password on a piece of paper
They always use your date of birth
89554.e: The built-in password generator mixes capital and small letters, digits and special characters. Passwords like these are almost impossible to guess.
89554.m: A password generator creates strong random passwords.

89555.q: How does a password manager help against phishing sites?
a: It only fills in passwords automatically on the real web address
89555.e: The manager remembers the address a password belongs to. On a fake site with a different address it does not offer it.
89555.m: If the password manager fills nothing in, the site may be fake.

89556.q: How are the passwords stored in a good password manager?
a: On a note in your desk
89556.e: Without the master password the stored data is unreadable. Even if someone steals the file, they cannot do much with it.
89556.m: A password manager stores passwords encrypted.

89557.q: What is especially important with a password manager?
a: Choosing a strong master password and also protecting it with 2FA
Keeping the master password as short as possible
Telling all your friends the master password
Sticking the master password on the screen
89557.e: Anyone who knows the master password has access to all accounts. A long sentence as a password and a second factor make the safe secure.
89557.m: The master password needs to be especially well protected.

89558.q: What minimum password length do experts recommend for important accounts (as of 2026)?
89558.e: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords. The Federal Office for Cyber Security recommends at least 12 characters.
89558.m: Long passwords are much harder to crack than short ones.

a: It controls which data may go into and out of a network
89559.e: A firewall checks data traffic according to set rules. Unwanted connections are blocked.
89559.m: A firewall filters data traffic according to rules.

89560.q: What does the word “firewall” literally mean?
89560.e: Just as a fireproof wall stops a fire, the firewall is meant to stop attacks from the internet.
89560.m: A firewall works like a fireproof wall for computers.

89561.q: Where at home is there often a firewall that protects the whole home network?
89561.e: The router connects the home network to the internet. Many routers have a built-in firewall that rejects unwanted connections from outside.
89561.m: The router often protects the home network with a firewall.

89562.q: What is a firewall called that runs directly on your own computer?
89562.e: A personal firewall is a program on the device itself. It can even allow or block internet access for individual programs.
89562.m: A personal firewall protects a single computer.

89563.q: How does a firewall decide whether to allow a connection?
a: By set rules, for example about addresses and ports
By the colour of the screen
By the time of the last update
By the name of the user at the screen
89563.e: The rules set which senders, receivers and ports are allowed. Everything else is rejected.
89563.m: A firewall works with rules for addresses and ports.

89564.q: Does a firewall alone protect you from all dangers on the internet?
a: No, it is only part of the protection
No, it has no effect at all
89564.e: A firewall does not stop, for example, a phishing email that you open yourself. Updates, virus protection and care are just as important.
89564.m: A firewall does not replace care and updates.

89565.q: What is a port in connection with a firewall?
a: A number that identifies a particular service on a device
89565.e: A computer uses port numbers to tell different services apart, such as websites or email. The firewall can open or close individual ports.
89565.m: Ports are numbers for different network services.

89566.q: Why should you not simply switch off the firewall on your computer?
a: Because the computer can then be attacked more easily
Because the screen would go black
Because the keyboard would stop working
89566.e: Without a firewall, attackers can reach open services on the computer directly. This is especially dangerous on public Wi-Fi networks.
89566.m: It is best to leave the firewall switched on at all times.

89567.q: What is a cookie on the internet?
a: A small text file that a website stores in the browser
A harmful program that deletes files
89567.e: Cookies store, for example, that you are logged in or what is in your shopping basket. On your next visit the browser sends them back to the website.
89567.m: A cookie is a small file that lets a website remember you.

89568.q: Why are cookies useful in an online shop?
a: So that the shopping basket is kept as you click on
So that the shop delivers faster
So that the computer starts faster
89568.e: Without cookies, the website would forget what you had chosen with every new click. The cookie remembers the shopping basket.
89568.m: Cookies remember things like the contents of your shopping basket.

89569.q: What are cookies called that do not come from the website you are visiting but from another company, for example for advertising?
89569.e: Third-party cookies come, for example, from advertising networks that are built into many sites. This allows browsing behaviour to be tracked across many websites.
89569.m: Third-party cookies are often used to track browsing behaviour.

89570.q: What happens to a session cookie?
a: It is deleted when you close the browser
It is sent to all your contacts
89570.e: Session cookies only apply for one visit. Persistent cookies, on the other hand, have an expiry date that can be far in the future.
89570.m: A session cookie disappears when you close the browser.

89571.q: What can you do to get rid of stored cookies?
a: Delete them in the browser settings
89571.e: In every browser you can delete cookies one by one or all at once. Afterwards, though, you have to log in again on websites.
89571.m: Cookies can be deleted in the browser settings.

89572.q: What does a cookie banner on a website ask you?
a: Whether you agree to certain cookies
89572.e: Many websites ask for permission before they set cookies for statistics or advertising. You can often allow only the necessary cookies.
89572.m: With cookie banners you can often allow only necessary cookies.

a: In the browser on your own device
89573.e: A website puts cookies in the browser on your computer or phone. On your next visit the browser sends them back to the website.
89573.m: Cookies are kept in the browser on your own device.

89574.q: Can cookies themselves run programs on your computer like a virus?
a: No, they only contain stored text data
Yes, they format the hard drive
89574.e: Cookies are pure data and not executable code. The main problem is that they can be used to track browsing behaviour.
89574.m: Cookies are not programs but stored data.

a: The traces you leave on the internet
The size of your shoes in an app
A step counter on your wrist
89575.e: It includes posts, photos, comments, searches and websites you have visited. Much of it stays stored for a long time.
89575.m: Everything you do online leaves traces.

89576.q: What is part of your active digital footprint?
a: A photo that you post yourself on social media
Data that a website secretly collects about you
The location your phone reports in the background
The IP address that a server stores
89576.e: You leave active traces on purpose, for example through posts, comments or reviews.
89576.m: What you post yourself is part of your active digital footprint.

89577.q: What is part of your passive digital footprint?
a: Data that websites automatically collect about you while you browse
89577.e: Websites and apps store, for example, which pages you visit and for how long. This often happens without you noticing.
89577.m: Passive traces are created without you consciously sharing anything.

89578.q: Why should you think carefully before posting a photo?
a: Because pictures can be copied and hardly ever disappear completely
Because photos on the internet are deleted automatically after an hour
Because only adults can see photos
89578.e: Others can save pictures, forward them or take screenshots. Even if you delete the original, copies can still exist.
89578.m: Once something is on the internet, it can hardly be fully taken back.

89579.q: Which hidden information can a mobile phone photo contain that gives something away about you?
a: The place it was taken as GPS coordinates
The height of the person taking the photo
89579.e: The metadata (EXIF) of a photo can include the date, time and GPS location. You can switch off the camera's location function.
89579.m: Photos can secretly reveal where they were taken.

89580.q: Who sometimes looks at your digital footprint when you apply for something?
a: No one, it is technically impossible
89580.e: Some companies search for applicants' names on the internet. Embarrassing or hurtful posts can make a bad impression.
89580.m: Future apprenticeship companies can also see your online traces.

89581.q: What helps keep your own digital footprint small?
a: Checking privacy settings in apps and sharing little personal information
Installing as many apps as possible
Giving your date of birth everywhere
89581.e: In the settings you can decide who sees posts and which data an app gets. Less shared information means fewer traces.
89581.m: Good privacy settings make your digital footprint smaller.

89582.q: How can you easily check what can be found about you publicly on the internet?
a: Type your own name into a search engine
89582.e: A search for your own name shows which pictures, profiles or posts can be found publicly. This is also called “egosurfing”.
89582.m: If you search for your name, you see part of your digital footprint.

89583.q: What is advertising called that is chosen for you based on your previous traces on the internet?
89583.e: An interest profile is built from pages visited, searches and clicks. You are then shown advertising that matches it.
89583.m: Your digital footprint decides which adverts you see.

89584.q: Why are software updates important for security?
89584.e: With updates, manufacturers fix errors that attackers could exploit. Anyone who does not update stays open to attack.

89585.q: What is a small update that fixes a particular error called?
89585.e: A patch is a piece of material used to mend a hole. A software patch mends a hole in the program, so to speak.
89585.m: A patch mends an error in a program.

89586.q: What is a security gap called that attackers exploit before the manufacturer knows about it or has a patch?
89586.e: The manufacturer had “zero days” to close the gap. Gaps like this are especially dangerous and valuable to attackers.
89586.m: A zero-day vulnerability is not yet closed when attackers use it.

89587.q: Which setting helps you not to miss important updates?
a: Never connecting the device to the internet
89587.e: Automatic updates are installed as soon as they are available. This way the device is quickly protected again.
89587.m: Automatic updates keep devices up to date without any effort.

89588.q: Microsoft usually releases security updates on a fixed day each month. Why?
a: So that companies can prepare for installing them
Because computers only have power on that day
To make things easier for attackers
Because otherwise updates would cost nothing
89588.e: This fixed date is called “Patch Tuesday” and is usually the second Tuesday of the month. This lets companies plan when to update their computers.
89588.m: Microsoft usually delivers security updates on the second Tuesday of the month.

89589.q: What does it mean when an operating system no longer gets “support”?
a: It no longer gets security updates
It is automatically replaced for free
It can no longer show photos
89589.e: After support ends, newly discovered gaps are no longer closed. Systems like this should be replaced or upgraded.
89589.m: Without support there are no more security updates.

89590.q: Where should you get updates for programs from?
a: Directly from the manufacturer or through the built-in update function
Through a link in an unknown email
From a random website with adverts
From a USB stick you found
89590.e: Fake update messages are a popular trick for spreading harmful software. Only official update routes are safe.
89590.m: Real updates come directly from the manufacturer.

89591.q: Since October 2025 Windows 10 no longer gets free security updates. What does this mean?
a: Newly discovered security gaps stay open
The computer no longer switches on
89591.e: After support ends, Microsoft no longer closes new gaps for free. A system like this should be upgraded or replaced.
89591.m: Regular support for Windows 10 ended in October 2025.

89592.e: Hay is grass and herbs that have been mown and dried in the sun. Dry hay keeps for a long time.

89593.q: Why must hay not go into the barn wet?
89593.e: Wet hay starts to go mouldy and gets warm. In the worst case it can even catch fire by itself.
89593.m: Hay must be dry so that it does not go mouldy.

89594.q: What weather does the farmer need for making hay?
89594.e: The mown grass has to dry in the sun for a few days. Rain would stop it drying.

89595.q: Which animals eat lots of hay in winter?
89595.e: In winter hardly any grass grows outside. That is why cows, horses, sheep and goats get hay as food.

89596.q: Why is mown grass turned over in the meadow?
89596.e: When it is turned, the damp underside comes up into the sun and wind. This way the grass dries evenly.

89597.q: Where is hay stored on the farm?
89597.e: The hayloft is in the barn, usually above the cowshed. The hay stays dry there.
89597.m: Hay is stored dry in the hayloft.

89598.q: What are round, pressed bundles of hay called?
89598.e: A baler rolls the hay up into big round bales. This makes it easy to transport and store.
89598.m: Round bundles of hay are called round bales.

89599.e: Straw is the dry stalks of cereals such as wheat or barley after threshing. Hay, on the other hand, comes from the meadow.
89599.m: Straw comes from cereals, hay from the meadow.

89600.q: In Switzerland, what is the haymaking season called?
89600.e: The Heuet is the hay harvest in early summer. The Wümmet, on the other hand, is the grape harvest in autumn.
89600.m: In Switzerland the hay harvest is called the Heuet.

89601.e: After the first mowing, the grass grows again. If it is mown and dried a second time, it is called Emd.
89601.m: Emd is hay from the second cut.

89602.q: What is second-cut hay (Emd) like compared with the first hay?
89602.e: At the second cut the grass has more leaves and fewer hard stalks. That is why second-cut hay is finer.
89602.m: Second-cut hay is finer than the first hay.

a: In summer after the first cut
In spring before the first cut
In January when it is frosty
89603.e: First comes the hay harvest in early summer. When the grass has grown again, the second cut is made in summer.
89603.m: The second cut follows the first hay harvest in summer.

89604.q: What does the farmer use second-cut hay (Emd) for?
89604.e: Second-cut hay is dried grass from the second cut. In winter cows, goats and sheep eat it in the shed.
89604.m: Second-cut hay is winter food for the animals.

89605.q: Why can a meadow be mown several times a year?
a: Because it is sown again each time
89605.e: After cutting, grass grows back from the bottom. That is why there are more cuts after the first hay.

89606.q: In which country do people often call second-cut hay “Emd”?
89606.e: The word Emd is used mainly in Switzerland and in the south of the German-speaking area.
89606.m: In Switzerland second-cut hay is called Emd.

89607.q: Which meadow flower has white petals and a yellow centre?
89607.e: The ox-eye daisy flowers in many meadows in early summer. It looks like a big daisy.
89607.m: The ox-eye daisy is white with a yellow centre.

89608.q: Which yellow meadow flower later turns into a dandelion clock?
89608.e: After its yellow flower, the dandelion forms a white ball of seeds with little parachutes. The wind carries them away.
89608.m: The dandelion turns into a dandelion clock.

89609.q: Which animals collect nectar and pollen in a flower meadow?
89609.e: Bees fly from flower to flower. Honeybees make honey from the nectar.
89609.m: Bees collect nectar in the flower meadow.

89610.q: Which blue meadow flower looks like a little bell?
89610.e: The bellflower has blue or purple flowers. Their shape looks like a bell.
89610.m: The bellflower is shaped like a bell.

89611.q: Which meadow plant has round flower heads and three little leaves?
89611.e: Clover usually has three little leaves on one stalk. Its flowers are little balls, often red or white.

89612.q: What do butterflies find in a flower meadow?
89612.e: Butterflies suck nectar from the flowers with their long proboscis. That is why they need meadows with lots of flowers.

89613.q: When do most meadow flowers bloom?
89613.e: In spring and summer it is warm and bright. That is when most flowers bloom in the meadows.
89613.m: Meadow flowers bloom mainly in spring and summer.

89614.q: Which meadow flower with blue-violet flowers is related to a kitchen herb?
89614.e: Meadow clary belongs to the same plant genus as the sage in the herb garden. It has blue-violet flowers.
89614.m: Meadow clary is related to kitchen sage.

89615.q: What does a rich, fertilised meadow get a lot of?
89615.e: A rich meadow is fertilised with manure and slurry. That is why the soil has lots of nutrients.
89615.m: A rich meadow is heavily fertilised.

89616.q: What is the liquid fertiliser from the cowshed called?
89616.e: Slurry is a mixture of the animals' dung, urine and water. The farmer spreads it on the meadows as fertiliser.
89616.m: Slurry is liquid fertiliser from the shed.

89617.q: Does a lot of grass or a little grass grow in a rich, fertilised meadow?
89617.e: Because the soil has lots of nutrients, the grass grows quickly and thickly.
89617.m: Lots of grass grows in a rich meadow.

89618.q: How often can a rich, fertilised meadow be mown in a year?
89618.e: On a fertilised meadow the grass grows back quickly. That is why it can be mown several times a year.
89618.m: A rich meadow is mown several times a year.

89619.q: Which yellow flower often grows in huge numbers in fertilised meadows?
89619.e: The dandelion likes soil with lots of nutrients. In spring some rich meadows are completely yellow with it.
89619.m: Lots of dandelions show a fertilised meadow.

89620.q: How many different kinds of flowers are there usually in a rich, fertilised meadow?
89620.e: In fertilised meadows a few strong plants grow very quickly. They crowd out many other flowers.
89620.m: Rather few kinds of flowers grow in rich meadows.

89621.q: Where does the manure used to fertilise a meadow come from?
89621.e: Manure is a mixture of animal dung and straw. It comes from the shed and makes the soil fertile.
89621.m: Manure comes from the animal shed.

89622.q: Where in Switzerland are there especially many rich, fertilised meadows?
89622.e: On the Swiss Plateau the land is flat and fertile. There are many farms with fertilised meadows there.
89622.m: There are many rich meadows on the Swiss Plateau.

89623.q: Which plant with white umbrella-shaped flower heads often grows in heavily fertilised meadows?
89623.e: Cow parsley has lots of small white flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters. It likes to grow where lots of fertiliser is used.
89623.m: Lots of cow parsley shows lots of fertiliser.

89624.q: How much fertiliser does a poor, unfertilised meadow get?
89624.e: A poor meadow is hardly fertilised or not at all. That is why the soil has few nutrients.
89624.m: A poor meadow gets little fertiliser.

89625.q: How often is a poor, unfertilised meadow usually mown?
89625.e: On a poor meadow the grass grows slowly. It is usually mown only once or twice a year.
89625.m: A poor meadow is rarely mown.

89626.q: What is there especially lots of in a poor, unfertilised meadow?
89626.e: Because no grass takes over everything, lots of different flowers have room. That is why poor meadows are very colourful.
89626.m: Poor meadows are rich in kinds of flowers.

89627.q: Where do you often find poor, unfertilised meadows?
89627.e: Steep, dry slopes are hard to fertilise and farm. That is why poor meadows have often survived there.
89627.m: Poor meadows are often on sunny slopes.

89628.q: Which rare flowers sometimes grow in poor, unfertilised meadows?
89628.e: Wild orchids grow in Switzerland. Many of them need poor meadows and are protected.
89628.m: Wild orchids grow in poor meadows.

89629.q: Why does the grass in a poor, unfertilised meadow stay rather short?
a: The farmer cuts it every day
89629.e: Plants need nutrients to grow. If the soil is poor, the grass grows slowly and stays short.
89629.m: Poor soil makes the grass grow slowly.

89630.q: Which animals do you often hear chirping in a warm, dry meadow in summer?
89630.e: Lots of grasshoppers and crickets live in sunny dry meadows. On warm days you can hear their chirping everywhere.
89630.m: Lots of grasshoppers chirp in dry meadows.

89631.q: Why does Switzerland protect many dry meadows?
a: Many rare plants and animals live there
89631.e: Many dry meadows have disappeared. Switzerland protects the most important ones so that rare plants and animals can go on living there.
89631.m: Dry meadows are a habitat for rare species.

89632.q: What is a pasture on a farm?
a: A meadow that no one ever walks on
89632.e: On a pasture the animals eat the grass straight from the ground. In German the word for pasture, Weide, also means a willow tree.
89632.m: On a pasture animals eat the grass.

89633.q: Which animals do you often see in a pasture in Switzerland?
89633.e: Cows, sheep, goats and horses eat grass. That is why they are let out onto the pasture.
89633.m: Cows and sheep graze in the pasture.

89634.q: What is a pasture fence for?
a: So that the animals do not run away
So that the grass grows faster
89634.e: The fence keeps the animals in the pasture. So they do not run onto the road or into the next field.
89634.m: The pasture fence keeps the animals in.

89635.q: What flows through many pasture fences so that the animals keep their distance?
89635.e: With an electric fence the animals feel a short, mild shock when they touch it. After that they avoid the fence.
89635.m: An electric fence gives a mild shock.

89636.q: What happens to the grass on a pasture?
89636.e: With a pasture the farmer does not have to mow the grass. The animals fetch their food themselves.
89636.m: On the pasture the animals graze the grass themselves.

89637.q: What is a fenced pasture for horses called?
89637.e: A paddock is a fenced piece of pasture. Horses can move around freely there.

89638.q: What do cows leave on the pasture that fertilises the ground?
89638.e: Cowpats are the dung of cows. It contains nutrients and so fertilises the pasture.

89639.q: Which word fits: The cows ... in the pasture?
89639.e: When animals eat grass in a pasture, we say that they graze.

89640.q: What do we call animals like cows that bring their food back up and chew it again?
89640.e: Cows, sheep and goats chew the grass roughly at first. Later they bring it back up from the stomach and chew it again.

89641.q: In which season are the cows up on the alpine pasture?
89641.e: In summer fresh grass grows on the alpine pastures in the mountains. In winter they are covered in snow.
89641.m: In summer the cows are on the alpine pasture.

89642.q: In Switzerland, what is the procession called when the cows go up to the alpine pasture in early summer?
89642.e: At the Alpaufzug, farmers walk with their cows up to the alpine pastures. The animals stay there for the summer.
89642.m: At the Alpaufzug the cows go up to the alp.

89643.q: In Switzerland, what is the festival called when the cows come down from the alpine pasture in autumn?
89643.e: In autumn it gets cold in the mountains. At the Alpabzug the cows return to the valley, festively decorated.
89643.m: At the Alpabzug the cows come down to the valley.

89644.q: What do cows often wear on their heads when they come down from the alpine pasture?
89644.e: The cows are decorated with flowers and ribbons. This shows that the summer on the alp went well.
89644.m: Cows wear flower decorations when they come down from the alp.

89645.q: What is made from the milk up on the alpine pasture?
89645.e: The cows' milk is made into cheese right there on the alp. This cheese is called alpine cheese.
89645.m: Alpine milk is made into alpine cheese.

89646.q: What is the man who makes cheese on the alpine pasture called in Switzerland?
89646.e: The Senn, an alpine dairyman, works on the alp in summer. He milks the cows and makes cheese from the milk.
89646.m: The Senn makes cheese on the alp.

89647.q: Why do cows on the alpine pasture often wear bells?
a: So that people can find them
So that they can see better
89647.e: Alpine pastures are big and sometimes foggy. From the sound of the bells you can hear where the cows are.
89647.m: Cowbells help people find the cows.

89648.e: Alpine pastures are high up in the mountains above the villages. Only in summer is there enough grass there.
89648.m: Alpine pastures are in the mountains.

89649.q: Where do the alpine herders live in summer on the alpine pasture?
89649.e: On the alp there are simple huts made of wood or stone. The herders live there and often make the cheese there too.
89649.m: The alpine herders live in an alpine hut.

a: Because of the water in the stalk
Because of the soil on the roots
89650.e: The leaves contain a green pigment called chlorophyll. With it the plant makes food from sunlight.

89651.q: What is the stem of a grass called?
89651.e: The stem of a grass is called a stalk or culm. It is usually hollow inside.
89651.m: The stem of grass is called a stalk.

89652.q: What are people with hay fever allergic to?
89652.e: Despite its name, hay fever usually comes from pollen, for example from grasses. Your nose runs and your eyes itch.
89652.m: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen.

89653.q: What is short mown grass in the garden called?
89653.e: A lawn is an area of grass that is mown often. You can play and lie on it.
89653.m: Short grass in the garden is called a lawn.

89654.q: Which grass provides the grains for polenta?
89654.e: Maize is also a grass. Polenta is cooked from its ground grains.

89655.q: How do grasshoppers often get around?
89655.e: Grasshoppers have long, strong back legs. With them they can jump very far.
89655.m: Grasshoppers jump with their back legs.

89656.q: How does a grasshopper make its chirping sound?
a: It rubs parts of its body together
It blows into a blade of grass
89656.e: Grasshoppers rub, for example, a leg against a wing or two wings together. That is how the chirping is made.

89657.q: What colours are many grasshoppers so that you can hardly see them in the grass?
89657.e: Green and brown grasshoppers match grass and soil well. This way they are well camouflaged from enemies.
89657.m: Green grasshoppers are well camouflaged in the grass.

89658.q: Where does the great green bush-cricket have its ears?
89658.e: The great green bush-cricket is a kind of grasshopper. Its hearing organs are on its front legs.
89658.m: The great green bush-cricket hears with its front legs.

89659.q: In which season do you hear grasshoppers chirping the most?
89659.e: Grasshoppers are grown up and active in summer. On warm days they chirp in the meadows.

89661.q: Which bird likes to eat grasshoppers?
89661.e: Storks look for food in meadows. They eat frogs, mice, worms and grasshoppers too.
89661.m: The stork likes to eat grasshoppers.

89662.q: What very long things does the great green bush-cricket have on its head?
89662.e: The great green bush-cricket has antennae that are longer than its body. It uses them to feel and smell.
89662.m: The great green bush-cricket has very long antennae.

89663.q: Where does the mole usually live?
a: In the roof of a house
89663.e: The mole lives almost all the time in its tunnels under the ground. It only rarely comes out.

89664.q: What does the mole like to eat most?
89664.e: The mole does not eat plants. It catches earthworms and insect larvae in its tunnels.

89665.q: What does the mole dig with?
89665.e: Its front paws are as wide as shovels and have strong claws. With them it pushes the soil away.
89665.m: The mole digs with its shovel-like paws.

89666.q: How well can the mole see?
89666.e: It is dark underground. The mole's eyes are tiny, but it can smell and feel very well.

89667.q: What does the mole's fur look like?
89667.e: The short black fur is as soft as velvet. It can be stroked in any direction, so the mole can move forwards and backwards through its tunnels.
89667.m: The mole has velvety black fur.

89668.e: When the mole digs, there is soil left over. It pushes it up out of the ground.
89668.m: A molehill is made of dug-out soil.

a: Yes, but only when it snows
89669.e: The mole does not hibernate. In winter it digs deeper, because that is where the worms live.
89669.m: The mole is awake in winter too.

89670.q: Why do farmers not like lots of molehills in the meadow?
a: Soil gets into the animal feed
89670.e: When the grass is mown and made into hay, the soil from the hills gets mixed in. Dirty feed is bad for the animals.
89670.m: Soil from molehills makes the feed dirty.

89671.q: What does the farmer usually mow large meadows with today?
89671.e: A mower is fitted to the tractor. It cuts a wide strip of grass in a short time.
89671.m: Large meadows are mown with the tractor.

89672.q: Which machine is often used for mowing on steep slopes?
89672.e: A motor mower is small and light and is guided by hand. On a slope it does not tip over as easily as a big tractor.
89672.m: On steep slopes people mow with a motor mower.

89673.q: Which young wild animals often hide in the long grass in early summer?
89673.e: Roe deer mothers leave their fawns in the long grass. When there is danger, the fawns do not run away but press themselves to the ground.
89673.m: Fawns hide in the long grass.

89674.q: What do people use today to look for hidden fawns before mowing?
89674.e: Drones with a thermal camera can see the warm animals in the grass. This way they can be taken to safety before mowing.
89674.m: Drones help to save fawns before mowing.

89675.q: Why is a flower meadow only mown after the flowers have bloomed?
a: So that the flowers can make seeds
So that the grass is wet
So that the cows can sleep
89675.e: The flowers need time to make seeds after flowering. New flowers grow from the seeds the next year.
89675.m: Late mowing lets the flowers make seeds.

89676.q: What does the farmer do with mown grass to turn it into hay?
a: He lets it dry in the sun
He washes it in the stream
He buries it in the ground
89676.e: The mown grass lies in the sun for a few days and is turned. When it is completely dry, it is called hay.

89677.q: Which machine mows the lawn in the garden?
89677.e: The lawnmower cuts the grass short. This keeps the lawn nice and low.
89677.m: You mow the lawn with a lawnmower.

89678.e: With a scythe you cut grass by hand. In the past all meadows were mown like this.
89678.m: The scythe is a tool for mowing.

89679.q: What does the blade of a scythe look like?
89679.e: The blade of the scythe is long, thin and slightly curved. When you swing it, it cuts the grass just above the ground.
89679.m: The scythe has a long, curved blade.

89680.q: What is used to sharpen the blade of the scythe while mowing?
89680.e: The mower keeps running the whetstone over the edge. This keeps the scythe sharp.
89680.m: The scythe is sharpened with a whetstone.

89681.q: What do you do with a scythe?
89681.e: You cut grass with the sharp blade of the scythe. For chopping wood you need an axe, and for digging a spade.
89681.m: You cut grass with a scythe.

89682.q: Where is the scythe still used today?
89682.e: Where no machine can go, for example in very steep places or along streams, people still mow with a scythe.
89682.m: In steep places people still mow with a scythe.

89683.q: What is the long handle of a scythe usually made of?
89683.e: The long handle of the scythe is usually made of wood. It has two grips for the hands.
89683.m: The handle of the scythe is made of wood.

89684.q: How do you hold the scythe when mowing?
a: With both hands on two grips
With one hand on the blade
With one hand right at the top of the handle
Over your shoulder with a rope
89684.e: The scythe has two grips on its handle. You hold it with both hands and swing it evenly.
89684.m: You hold the scythe with both hands.

89685.q: Which tool has a short, very curved blade and only a small handle?
89685.e: The sickle is smaller than the scythe. You hold it in one hand and use it to cut small tufts of grass or cereal.
89685.m: The sickle is the scythe's little sister.

89686.q: What are the thicker places on a grass stalk called?
89686.e: A grass stalk is divided into sections. Between them there are small thickenings called nodes.
89686.m: The thick places on a grass stalk are called nodes.

89687.q: Which grass often grows in wet fields in Asia?
89687.e: Rice is a cereal and belongs to the grasses. It often grows in fields that are under water.
89687.m: Rice is a grass that likes standing in water.

89688.q: Which shiny yellow meadow flower do cows leave alone because it is poisonous?
89688.e: The buttercup has shiny yellow flowers. When fresh it is poisonous, which is why cows leave it standing in the pasture.

89689.q: About how long is a mole without its tail?
89689.e: A mole is about 11 to 16 centimetres long. On top of that there is a short tail of 2 to 4 centimetres.
89689.m: A mole is about 15 centimetres long.

89690.q: What are the big bales of grass wrapped in plastic film in the field called?
89690.e: The grass is only dried briefly and then wrapped airtight in film. This way it keeps for a long time and is food for the cows in winter.
89690.m: Grass wrapped in film is called silage bales.

89691.q: What do you learn from a weather forecast?
a: What the weather will be like
89691.e: In the weather forecast, experts predict what the weather will be like over the next few days. That way you can prepare for it.
89691.m: The weather forecast predicts the coming weather.

89692.e: Precipitation is water that falls from the clouds to the ground. It can be liquid or frozen.
89692.m: Rain, snow and hail are precipitation.

89693.e: Meteorologists study the weather. They predict whether it will rain or the sun will shine.

89694.q: At which chance of rain had you better take an umbrella?
89694.e: The chance of rain tells you how likely it is to rain. At 90 per cent, it will very probably rain.
89694.m: When the chance of rain is high, you take an umbrella.

89695.q: What is the warm, dry wind that blows down from the Alps in Switzerland called?
89695.e: The Föhn is a warm wind that blows down the north or south side of the Alps. It is often very strong.
89695.m: The Föhn is a warm wind from the Alps.

89696.q: What does a picture of a sun and a cloud mean in the weather forecast?
89696.e: Small pictures called weather symbols show the weather. A sun with a cloud means partly sunny.
89696.m: A sun with a cloud means partly sunny.

89697.q: What does a rain gauge measure?
89697.e: A rain gauge collects rainwater in a container. That way you know how much it has rained.
89697.m: A rain gauge measures the amount of rain.

89698.q: In which unit is the amount of rain often given?
89698.e: You measure how high the water stands in the rain gauge. This height is given in millimetres.

89699.q: How much water is 1 millimetre of rain on one square metre?
89699.e: One square metre times one millimetre of height makes exactly one litre of water.
89699.m: One millimetre of rain is one litre per square metre.

89700.q: Where is the best place to set up a rain gauge?
a: Under the roof of the house
89700.e: The rain must be able to fall freely into the rain gauge. Trees and roofs would keep water out.
89700.m: A rain gauge needs an open spot.

89701.q: What does a simple rain gauge have at the top?
89701.e: The rain falls in through the opening at the top. The funnel guides it into the measuring container.
89701.m: The rain falls in through a funnel at the top.

89702.q: How do you read the amount of rain on a simple rain gauge?
a: On a scale on the container
By the smell of the water
By the colour of the water
By the weight of the lid
89702.e: Lines with numbers are printed on the container. You look to see which line the water reaches.
89702.m: You read the amount of rain on the scale.

89703.q: Why do you empty the rain gauge after reading it?
89703.e: If the old water stays in, you count it twice next time. That is why it is emptied after every reading.
89703.m: The rain gauge is emptied after reading.

a: The direction and strength of the wind
89704.e: The windsock turns with the wind and fills up. That way you can see where the wind is coming from and how strong it is.
89704.m: A windsock shows wind direction and wind strength.

89705.q: What colours does a windsock often have?
89705.e: A windsock usually has red and white or orange and white stripes. That makes it easy to see from far away.
89705.m: Windsocks are often striped red and white.

89706.q: What does it mean when a windsock hangs down limply?
a: There is a very strong storm
It is about to get dark
89706.e: Without wind, the fabric tube does not fill with air. So it just hangs down from the pole.
89706.m: A limp windsock shows there is no wind.

89707.q: What does it mean when a windsock sticks out completely horizontally?
89707.e: The stronger the wind blows, the more it fills the windsock. In a strong wind, it sticks out completely straight.
89707.m: A horizontal windsock shows a strong wind.

89708.q: Why do windsocks hang on some motorway bridges?
a: To show where petrol stations are
89708.e: On bridges, strong crosswinds can push cars and lorries to the side. The windsock warns drivers.
89708.m: Windsocks on bridges warn of crosswinds.

a: A fabric tube, wider at the front than at the back
89709.e: A windsock is a tube made of fabric. The opening at the front is wide, and it gets narrower towards the back.
89709.m: A windsock is a fabric tube.

89710.q: Where does a weathercock often sit?
89710.e: Weathercocks sit high up on towers and roofs. The wind can reach them easily there.
89710.m: The weathercock sits high up on the tower.

89711.q: Which animal does a weathercock show?
89711.e: The name says it all: a weathercock is a metal figure in the shape of a cockerel.
89711.m: A weathercock looks like a cockerel.

89712.q: What is the general name for a device like the weathercock?
89712.e: A weather vane turns in the wind and shows its direction. The weathercock is a weather vane in the shape of a cockerel.
89712.m: The weathercock is a weather vane.

89713.q: What do the letters N, E, S and W under a weathercock stand for?
89713.e: N means north, E east, S south and W west. That way you can tell which direction the wind is blowing from.
89713.m: N, E, S and W are the points of the compass.

89714.q: Which direction does the E under the weathercock stand for?
89714.e: E stands for east. The sun rises in the east.

89715.e: The wind pushes against the large surface of the cockerel. So it turns until it is lined up with the wind.

89716.q: What happens to the liquid in a thermometer when it gets warmer?
89716.e: Warmth makes the liquid expand a little. That is why it rises in the thin tube.
89716.m: When it is warm, the liquid in the thermometer rises.

89717.q: Where do you measure the air temperature correctly?
89717.e: In the sun, the thermometer itself heats up and shows too high a value. That is why air temperature is measured in the shade.
89717.m: Air temperature is measured in the shade.

89718.q: In the morning it is 4 degrees, at midday 12 degrees. By how many degrees has it got warmer?
89718.e: You work out 12 minus 4 equals 8. So it has got 8 degrees warmer.
89718.m: You find the difference by subtracting.

89719.q: What are thick, white clouds that look like cotton wool called?
89719.e: Cumulus clouds have a flat base and a tall, rounded top. They look like balls of cotton wool.
89719.m: Cumulus clouds look like cotton wool.

89720.q: What are thin, wispy clouds high up in the sky called?
89720.e: Cirrus clouds float very high up and are made of ice crystals. They look like delicate feathers.
89720.m: Cirrus clouds are thin and high.

89721.q: What are clouds that cover the sky like a grey blanket called?
89721.e: Stratus clouds form an even grey layer. The sun often cannot be seen then.
89721.m: Stratus clouds cover the sky like a blanket.

89722.q: What do dark grey clouds often mean?
89722.e: Thick clouds hold a lot of water and let little light through. That is why they look dark and often bring rain.

89723.q: What often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days in winter?
89723.e: In winter, cold air stays trapped over the Plateau. Above it a grey blanket of fog forms, called high fog.
89723.m: In winter, high fog often lies over the Plateau.

89724.q: What are the white streaks behind aeroplanes in the sky called?
89724.e: The exhaust from the engines contains water vapour. In the cold air high up, it freezes into tiny ice crystals.

89725.q: What happens when the droplets in a cloud become too heavy?
89725.e: The tiny droplets bump into each other and grow bigger. When they are too heavy, they fall down as rain.
89725.m: Heavy drops fall out of the cloud as rain.

89726.q: What do you hear after a flash of lightning?
89726.e: Lightning heats the air extremely quickly. The air expands, and there is a crack and a rumble.

89727.q: Why do you only hear the thunder after the lightning?
a: The thunder comes from the ground
89727.e: The light from the lightning reaches us almost at once. Sound is much slower and takes longer.

89728.q: You count 6 seconds between lightning and thunder. Roughly how far away is the storm?
89728.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. You work out 6 divided by 3 equals 2, so about 2 kilometres.
89728.m: Seconds divided by three gives you roughly the kilometres.

89729.q: Where are you safe during a thunderstorm?
89729.e: A house with lightning protection keeps you safe. Lone trees, hills and water are dangerous in a thunderstorm.
89729.m: In a thunderstorm, you go into a house.

89730.q: What does a lightning conductor on a house do?
a: It carries the lightning into the ground
89730.e: A lightning conductor is a metal rod with a wire. It carries the electricity from the lightning safely into the ground.
89730.m: A lightning conductor protects the house from lightning.

89731.q: What should you do if a thunderstorm comes while you are swimming in a lake?
a: Get out of the water at once
89731.e: Water conducts electricity. That is why you must get out of the water at once in a thunderstorm and find shelter.
89731.m: In a thunderstorm, you leave the water at once.

89732.q: Which clouds does hail fall from?
89732.e: Hail forms in large, tall thunderclouds. They have strong updraughts and a lot of ice.

89733.e: Hailstones fall fast and are hard. They dent cars, smash roof tiles and ruin fruit and vegetables.

89734.q: What do farmers use to protect their fruit trees from hail?
89734.e: Nets are stretched over the fruit trees. They catch the hailstones before they hit the fruit.

89735.q: How big can hailstones sometimes get?
a: As big as a golf ball
89735.e: Hailstones are usually as small as peas. But in very strong thunderstorms they can be as big as golf balls or even bigger.
89735.m: Hailstones can be the size of golf balls.

89736.q: What happens to a hailstone in a thundercloud?
a: It is whirled upwards and grows
It always stays just as small
89736.e: Strong winds carry the ice grain upwards again and again. Each time, new water freezes onto it and it gets bigger.
89736.m: Hailstones grow as they go up and down in the cloud.
