89737.q: What are small, soft ice pellets that often fall in spring called?
89737.e: Graupel are small white pellets made of ice and snow. They are softer than hail.
89737.m: Graupel are small, soft ice pellets.

89738.q: What should you do when it is hailing hard outside?
a: Run into the middle of a field
89738.e: Large hailstones can hurt you. That is why you quickly find shelter under a roof.
89738.m: In a hailstorm, you find shelter under a roof.

89739.q: How many arms does a snow crystal usually have?
89739.e: Snow crystals almost always grow with six arms. This is because of the way ice is built.
89739.m: A snow crystal has six arms.

89740.q: Are two snow crystals exactly the same?
89740.e: Each crystal grows along its own path through the cloud. That is why almost every one looks a little different.
89740.m: Almost every snow crystal is unique.

a: It reflects a lot of light
89741.e: The many tiny ice crystals reflect the light in all directions. That is why snow looks white.
89741.m: Snow reflects light and looks white.

89742.q: When does precipitation fall as snow?
89742.e: If the air is cold enough all the way to the ground, the ice crystals do not melt. Then snow falls instead of rain.
89742.m: Snow falls when it is cold enough.

89743.q: What is very loose, dry snow called?
89743.e: Powder snow falls when it is very cold. It is light and puffs up like dust when you step in it.
89743.m: Powder snow is loose and dry.

89744.q: Which snow is best for building a snowman?
89744.e: Wet snow sticks together well. That is why you can roll balls out of it.

89745.q: Where is the sun when you see a rainbow?
89745.e: You only see a rainbow when the sun is shining from behind you and rain is falling in front of you.
89745.m: When you see a rainbow, the sun is behind you.

89746.q: Which colour is on the very inside of a rainbow?
89746.e: In the main rainbow, violet is on the inner edge. The other colours lie in between.
89746.m: Violet is on the inside of the rainbow.

89747.q: How many colours are usually counted in a rainbow?
89747.e: Usually seven colours are counted, including indigo, a dark blue violet. In fact, though, the colours blend smoothly into one another.
89747.m: Usually seven rainbow colours are counted.

89748.q: Which colour lies between yellow and blue in a rainbow?
89748.e: The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. So green lies between yellow and blue.
89748.m: Green lies between yellow and blue.

89749.q: How are the colours arranged in a second, fainter rainbow?
89749.e: In a secondary rainbow, the light is reflected twice inside the drops. That is why the order of the colours is reversed.
89749.m: In a secondary rainbow, the colours are reversed.

89750.q: How can you make a small rainbow yourself?
89750.e: A garden hose or a spray bottle makes lots of droplets. If the sun is behind you, you will see a rainbow in them.
89750.m: Water droplets and sunshine make a rainbow.

89751.q: What does MeteoSwiss do every day?
89751.e: Experts at MeteoSwiss analyse measurements. From them they make forecasts for the weather over the next few days.

89752.q: What does MeteoSwiss warn the public about?
89752.e: When there are storms, heavy rain, thunderstorms or heatwaves, MeteoSwiss issues warnings. That way people can protect themselves.

89753.q: How many danger levels do weather warnings have in Switzerland?
89753.e: The warnings have levels 1 to 5. The higher the level, the greater the danger.

89754.q: What does danger level 5 mean in weather warnings?
89754.e: Level 1 means no or low danger. Level 5 is the highest level and means very great danger.

89755.q: What does MeteoSwiss send up into the sky to measure the air high above?
89755.e: MeteoSwiss regularly sends up weather balloons. They carry small measuring instruments and measure the air high above Switzerland.
89755.m: Weather balloons measure the air high up.

89756.q: What does a weather radar measure?
a: Where it is raining or snowing
89756.e: A weather radar sends out signals that bounce back from raindrops and snowflakes. That way you can see where it is wet right now.
89756.m: Weather radar shows where it is raining.

89757.q: Where does MeteoSwiss get many of its measurements from?
89757.e: There are weather stations all over Switzerland. They measure things like temperature, wind and rain.

89758.q: What is a weather balloon filled with?
a: A gas that is lighter than air
89758.e: The balloon contains a light gas such as helium or hydrogen. That is why it rises up.
89758.m: A weather balloon is filled with a light gas.

89759.q: What hangs underneath a weather balloon?
89759.e: A small measuring instrument called a radiosonde hangs from the balloon. It measures the weather high up.
89759.m: A measuring instrument hangs from a weather balloon.

89760.q: What happens to a weather balloon high up?
a: It stays still in the air
89760.e: High up, the air is very thin. The balloon keeps expanding until it bursts.
89760.m: The weather balloon bursts high up.

89761.q: Roughly how high do the weather balloons from Payerne rise?
89761.e: The balloons rise about 30 kilometres high, some even higher. That is much higher than aeroplanes fly.
89761.m: Weather balloons rise higher than aeroplanes.

89762.q: What does the sonde on a weather balloon measure?
a: Only the colour of the clouds
89762.e: As it rises, the sonde keeps measuring the temperature, the humidity and the wind. That way the air is known at every height.
89762.m: The sonde measures temperature, humidity and wind.

89763.q: How does the sonde send its measurements to the ground?
89763.e: The sonde sends its data by radio to a ground station. That is why it is called a radiosonde.
89763.m: The radiosonde radios its data to the ground.

89764.q: What slows the sonde down once the balloon has burst?
89764.e: After the balloon bursts, the sonde falls back down. A parachute makes sure it sinks slowly.
89764.m: A parachute slows down the falling sonde.

89765.q: How often a day does a weather balloon go up in Payerne?
89765.e: In Payerne a weather balloon is launched twice a day, at fixed times that are the same all over the world. That way the measurements can be compared with other countries.
89765.m: In Payerne a weather balloon goes up twice a day.

89766.q: Which thermometer shows the highest and lowest temperature of a day?
89766.e: This thermometer remembers the warmest and the coldest value. That way you can see in the morning how cold it was during the night.
89766.m: A maximum and minimum thermometer remembers the extreme values.

89767.q: Which thermometer do you use to check whether a child has a temperature?
89767.e: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature very precisely. It also shows tenths of a degree.
89767.m: You check for a fever with a clinical thermometer.

89768.q: In the evening it is 3 degrees. During the night it gets 5 degrees colder. How cold is it then?
89768.e: You work out 3 minus 5 equals minus 2. It is then 2 degrees below zero, so minus 2 degrees.
89768.m: Below zero, you carry on counting with minus degrees.

89769.q: At what height above the ground does a weather station measure the air temperature?
89769.e: Weather stations measure the air temperature about 2 metres above the ground. That way measurements can be compared everywhere.
89769.m: Air temperature is measured about two metres above the ground.

89770.q: What are small white clouds in groups that look like a flock of sheep called?
89770.e: Lots of small, roundish clouds lie side by side in the sky. They look like a flock of sheep.
89770.m: Altocumulus clouds look like a flock of sheep.

89771.q: Through which sheet of muscle between the chest and the belly does the food pipe pass?
89771.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the belly. The food pipe goes through an opening in the diaphragm to the stomach.
89771.m: The food pipe passes through the diaphragm.

89772.q: What does the food pipe look like?
89772.e: The food pipe is a long, soft tube. It connects the throat with the stomach.
89772.m: The food pipe is a soft tube.

89773.q: What pushes food down the food pipe?
89773.e: The muscles of the food pipe squeeze together like a wave. That way they push each mouthful down bit by bit.
89773.m: Muscles in the food pipe push food down.

89774.q: Does food still reach your stomach if you swallow while doing a handstand?
a: No, it stays in your throat
89774.e: The food pipe does not only work with gravity. Its muscles push food into the stomach even when you are upside down.
89774.m: The food pipe pushes food into the stomach even upside down.

89775.q: Roughly how long is an adult's food pipe?
89775.e: In adults the food pipe is about 25 centimetres long. That is roughly as long as a school ruler.
89775.m: An adult's food pipe is about 25 centimetres long.

89776.q: Which tube lies in the neck directly in front of the food pipe?
89776.e: There are two tubes in the neck, one behind the other. At the front is the windpipe for air, behind it the food pipe for food.
89776.m: The windpipe lies in front of the food pipe in the neck.

89777.q: What is the burning feeling called when stomach juice rises into the food pipe?
89777.e: Sometimes sour stomach juice flows back into the food pipe. This burns behind the breastbone and is called heartburn.
89777.m: Sour stomach juice in the food pipe causes heartburn.

89778.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to get from the mouth to the stomach?
89778.e: The mouthful slides quickly down the food pipe. After a few seconds, about ten at most, it is already in the stomach.
89778.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach in a few seconds.

89779.e: Saliva comes from the salivary glands. They are in front of the ears, under the tongue and under the jaw.

89780.q: Why do we need saliva when we eat?
89780.e: Saliva makes food soft and slippery. That makes each mouthful easier to swallow.

89781.q: What is saliva mostly made of?
89781.e: Saliva is almost all water. Only a few other substances are dissolved in it.

89782.q: Roughly how much saliva does an adult make in a day?
89782.e: An adult makes about half a litre to one and a half litres of saliva a day. Most of it is swallowed without noticing.
89782.m: We make about a litre of saliva every day.

89783.q: Why does bread taste sweeter if you chew it for a long time?
89783.e: Saliva contains a substance that breaks down the starch in bread into sugar. That is why bread chewed for a long time tastes slightly sweet.
89783.m: Saliva starts digesting food in the mouth.

89784.q: What often happens in your mouth when you smell tasty food?
89784.e: Just the smell of food tells the salivary glands to get to work. People then say: “It makes my mouth water.”
89784.m: The smell of food makes saliva flow.

89785.q: How does saliva help our teeth?
a: It rinses away bits of food
89785.e: Saliva rinses small bits of food off the teeth. It also helps protect the teeth from acid.
89785.m: Saliva rinses and protects the teeth.

89786.q: When does the body make especially little saliva?
89786.e: At night the salivary glands make only a little saliva. That is why your mouth is often dry in the morning.
89786.m: The body makes little saliva during sleep.

89787.q: What is saliva also called in everyday language?
89787.e: In everyday life saliva is also called spit. The word comes from “to spit”.

89788.q: Which teeth do you use to bite a piece off an apple?
89788.e: The incisors at the front are flat and sharp. You use them to bite pieces off.

89789.q: Which teeth do you use to grind up food?
89789.e: The molars at the back of the mouth are broad. They grind food like a mill.

89790.q: Which part of the body pushes food between the teeth while you chew?
89790.e: The tongue is a strong muscle. It keeps turning the food and pushing it back between the teeth.
89790.m: The tongue pushes food to the teeth.

89791.q: Which bone moves up and down when you chew?
89791.e: When you chew, only the lower jaw moves. The upper jaw is fixed firmly to the skull.
89791.m: The lower jaw moves when you chew.

89792.q: Which part of the jaw moves up and down when you chew?
89792.e: When you chew, only the lower jaw moves. Strong muscles in the cheek pull it up powerfully.
89792.m: The lower jaw moves when you chew.

89793.q: What shouldn't you do while chewing with a full mouth?
89793.e: If you talk with your mouth full, it is easier to choke. It is also rude.
89793.m: Don't talk with your mouth full.

89794.q: What do food and saliva become when you chew?
89794.e: The teeth break the food into small pieces and the saliva makes it wet. This turns it into a soft mush that is easy to swallow.
89794.m: Chewing turns food into a soft mush.

89795.q: What do you notice more easily if you eat slowly and chew well?
89795.e: The feeling “I'm full” comes a little late. If you eat slowly, you notice it in time and don't eat too much.
89795.m: If you eat slowly, you notice better when you are full.

89796.q: What helps if a dry mouthful is hard to swallow?
89796.e: Water makes the mouthful moist and slippery. Then it slides down the throat more easily.
89796.m: A sip of water helps you swallow.

89797.q: What do you usually do when food goes down the wrong way?
89797.e: When something gets into the windpipe, the body coughs hard. That pushes the food back out.
89797.m: Coughing gets food that went down the wrong way back out.

89798.q: Can you swallow and breathe in at the same time?
89798.e: When you swallow, the windpipe is closed for a moment. That is why your breathing stops briefly.
89798.m: Breathing pauses briefly when you swallow.

89799.q: Which part of the body pushes a mouthful back into the throat when you swallow?
89799.e: The tongue presses the mouthful against the roof of the mouth and pushes it backwards. Then swallowing begins.
89799.m: The tongue pushes the mouthful back for swallowing.

89800.q: What do we say when food gets into the windpipe while swallowing?
a: It went down the wrong way
89800.e: People say: “It went down the wrong way.” The body then tries to get the food out of the windpipe quickly.
89800.m: When food gets into the windpipe, it has gone down the wrong way.

89801.q: What should small children not put in their mouths because they could swallow it?
89801.e: Small hard things like marbles can get stuck in the throat. That is why they don't belong in the mouth.
89801.m: Small toys don't belong in the mouth.

89802.q: Do you swallow even when you are not eating?
89802.e: We swallow our saliva again and again all day long. It usually happens all by itself.
89802.m: We keep swallowing saliva even without food.

89803.q: What can you see bobbing in the neck when someone swallows?
89803.e: When you swallow, the voice box is pulled up for a moment. In many people you can see this clearly in the neck.
89803.m: The voice box moves up when you swallow.

89804.q: What can give you tummy ache?
89804.e: If you eat too much, your stomach is very full. That can press and hurt.
89804.m: Eating too much can give you tummy ache.

89805.q: What often helps with a mild tummy ache?
89805.e: Warmth relaxes the tummy. A hot-water bottle or a warm cushion often helps with a mild tummy ache.
89805.m: Warmth is good for the tummy.

89806.q: What do people often drink when they have tummy ache?
89806.e: Fennel tea and camomile tea are mild and warm. Many people drink them when their tummy hurts.
89806.m: Fennel tea is a popular tea for tummy ache.

89807.q: Who should you tell if your tummy hurts badly?
89807.e: With a bad tummy ache, an adult should help. If needed, you go to the doctor.
89807.m: With a bad tummy ache, get an adult.

89808.q: What is it called when you can't go to the toilet for a long time and your tummy feels tight?
89808.e: With constipation, poo stays in the gut too long and becomes hard. That can give you tummy ache.
89808.m: Constipation can give you tummy ache.

89809.q: What helps keep poo nice and soft?
89809.e: Water, vegetables and fruit keep poo soft. Exercise helps the gut as well.
89809.m: Drinking plenty and eating vegetables keeps poo soft.

89810.q: On which side does the tummy usually hurt with appendicitis?
89810.e: The appendix is in the lower right of the belly. When it is inflamed, it usually hurts there, and you must see a doctor.
89810.m: With appendicitis, the lower right of the belly usually hurts.

89811.q: What can also give you tummy ache without you being ill?
89811.e: Fear or excitement, for example before a test, can also make your tummy feel tight. The tummy and feelings are connected.
89811.m: Worries can also give you tummy ache.

89812.q: Where does food go after the stomach?
89812.e: From the stomach the mushy food goes into the gut. There it is digested further.
89812.m: After the stomach comes the gut.

89813.q: What is the first, long and thin part of the gut called?
89813.e: First comes the small intestine. It is much longer than the large intestine, but narrower.
89813.m: The small intestine comes straight after the stomach.

89814.q: Is an adult's gut longer or shorter than the person is tall?
89814.e: The gut is several metres long. It lies neatly folded up in the belly.
89814.m: The gut is several metres long and lies folded in the belly.

89815.q: What does the small intestine take from food into the blood?
89815.e: In the small intestine the nutrients from food pass into the blood. That way they reach every part of the body.
89815.m: The small intestine passes nutrients into the blood.

89816.q: What does the large intestine mainly take back from the mushy food?
89816.e: In the large intestine a lot of water is taken out of the mushy food. That makes it firmer.
89816.m: The large intestine takes water from the mushy food.

89817.q: Which tiny helpers live in huge numbers in the gut?
89817.e: Countless useful bacteria live in the gut. They help with digestion and protect against illness.
89817.m: Useful bacteria help with digestion in the gut.

89818.q: Which foods with lots of fibre are good for the gut?
89818.e: Fibre is found in wholegrain foods, vegetables and fruit. It keeps the gut moving.
89818.m: Fibre from wholegrain foods and vegetables is good for the gut.

89819.q: What is left over from food and leaves the gut in the toilet?
89819.e: What the body cannot use comes out as poo. It is also called stool or faeces.
89819.m: Undigested leftovers leave the body as poo.

89820.q: What does the small intestine have inside so that it can take in lots of nutrients?
89820.e: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered in tiny finger-like villi, like a towel. That makes it very large so it can take in a lot.
89820.m: Tiny villi in the small intestine take in the nutrients.

89821.q: What is a fart made of?
89821.e: A fart is gas from the gut. It escapes through your bottom.
89821.m: A fart is gas from the gut.

89822.q: Roughly how often does a healthy person fart in a day?
89822.e: Doctors think about 20 to 25 farts a day are normal. Many of them you hardly notice.
89822.m: People fart many times every day.

89823.q: After which food do you often fart more?
89823.e: Beans contain substances that only the gut bacteria can break down. This makes a lot of gas.
89823.m: Beans often cause lots of farts.

89824.e: Farting is part of digestion. It is completely normal and healthy.

89825.q: Why do some farts smell bad?
89825.e: Some gases in a fart contain sulphur. They smell like rotten eggs.

89826.q: What do you swallow when you eat in a hurry that can later come out as a fart?
89826.e: If you eat or drink fast, you swallow a lot of air. Some of it travels all the way to the gut.
89826.m: Eating in a hurry puts air in your tummy.

89827.q: What is polite if you accidentally fart when other people are around?
a: Blame the person next to you
89827.e: A fart can happen to anyone. A quick “excuse me” is polite.
89827.m: After a fart it is polite to say excuse me.

89829.q: Where does the air come from when you burp?
89829.e: When you burp, air escapes from the stomach. It comes out of the mouth, often with a noise.
89829.m: A burp is air from the stomach.

89830.q: After which drink do you often have to burp?
89830.e: Fizzy drinks bring gas into the stomach. The gas wants to get out again, so you have to burp.

89832.q: What do you politely hold in front of your mouth when you have to burp?
89832.e: In Switzerland, burping loudly at the table is thought to be rude. You put your hand in front of your mouth and say excuse me.
89832.m: When you burp, hold your hand in front of your mouth.

89833.q: What is another word for burping?
89833.e: Burping is also called belching. Air from the stomach is pushed upwards.

89834.q: How should you drink so that you burp less?
89834.e: If you drink slowly, you swallow less air. Then less air has to come back out of the stomach.

89835.q: Which animals give off the gas methane when they burp?
89835.e: Cows have a special stomach in which bacteria digest the grass. This makes methane, which cows mainly burp out.
89835.m: Cows burp out the gas methane.

89836.q: Through which tube does the air come up when you burp?
89836.e: The air from the stomach takes the same path as food, only backwards. It rises through the food pipe into the mouth.
89836.m: The air of a burp rises through the food pipe.

89837.q: What do you always do after going to the toilet?
89837.e: After the toilet you wash your hands with soap. That removes germs.
89837.m: After the toilet, wash your hands with soap.

89838.q: What is the toilet often called for short in Switzerland?
89838.e: In Switzerland people usually say WC. It comes from the English “water closet”.
89838.m: In Switzerland people often say WC.

89839.q: What do you press after using the toilet so that the water washes everything away?
89839.e: When you flush, water flows through the toilet. It washes everything into the drain.
89839.m: After using the toilet you press the flush.

89840.q: What can you put down the toilet?
89840.e: Toilet paper dissolves in water. Wet wipes and other rubbish block the pipes and belong in the bin.
89840.m: Only toilet paper goes down the toilet.

89841.q: Where does the waste water from the toilet go in Switzerland?
89841.e: The waste water flows through pipes to the sewage treatment plant, called ARA in Switzerland. There it is cleaned before it goes back into rivers and lakes.
89841.m: Waste water is cleaned at the sewage treatment plant.

89842.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
89842.e: For clean hands, you rub them with soap for about 20 to 30 seconds. That is about as long as singing a short song twice.
89842.m: Wash your hands with soap for about 20 to 30 seconds.

89843.q: What is best to do with the toilet lid before flushing?
89843.e: With the lid closed, less water splashes around when you flush. That is cleaner.

89844.q: Should you wait if you urgently need the toilet?
a: Yes, until you can't feel it any more
89844.e: If you often wait too long, it confuses the body and you can get tummy ache. That is why you go to the toilet soon when you need to.
89844.m: When you need to go, go to the toilet soon.

89845.q: What do you dry your hands with after washing them?
89845.e: A clean towel or paper towel dries the hands. Dry hands spread fewer germs.
89845.m: Dry your hands well after washing them.

89846.q: What colour is urine usually if you drink enough?
89846.e: If you drink enough, your urine is usually light, pale yellow. If it is dark yellow, you should drink more.
89846.m: Pale urine shows you have drunk enough.

89847.q: Can you drink tap water in Switzerland?
89847.e: Tap water in Switzerland is clean drinking water. It is checked regularly.
89847.m: You can drink Swiss tap water.

89848.q: When does the body need especially plenty to drink?
a: On hot days and during sport
89848.e: When it is hot or you do sport, you sweat. You have to drink to replace the lost water.
89848.m: In hot weather and during sport you need to drink more.

89849.q: Roughly how long can a person survive without water?
89849.e: Without drinking, a person survives only a few days. Without food they can last much longer.
89849.m: Without water you only survive a few days.

89850.q: Is more or less than half of the human body made of water?
89850.e: More than half of the human body is water. In children the share is a little higher than in older people.
89850.m: More than half of our body is water.

89851.q: How does the body lose water?
89851.e: The body loses water when we sweat, breathe and go to the toilet. That is why you have to drink every day.
89851.m: We lose water by sweating, breathing and going to the toilet.

89852.q: Why are sweet drinks not good for quenching thirst?
a: They contain a lot of sugar
89852.e: Sweet drinks contain a lot of sugar. It harms the teeth, and water quenches thirst better.
89852.m: Sweet drinks contain lots of sugar and harm the teeth.

89853.q: What can happen if you drink too little?
89853.e: If you drink too little, you get tired and can get a headache. Thinking also becomes harder.
89853.m: Drinking too little makes you tired and gives you headaches.

89854.q: What does the body need food for?
89854.e: Food gives the body energy to play, learn and grow. When energy runs low, we get hungry.

89855.q: What is the small mid-morning snack called in Switzerland?
89855.e: The Znüni is eaten in the morning, at about nine o'clock. An apple or some bread makes a good Znüni.
89855.m: The Znüni is eaten in the morning.

89856.q: What is the afternoon snack called in Switzerland?
89856.e: The Zvieri is eaten in the afternoon, at about four o'clock. The name means “at four o'clock”.
89856.m: The Zvieri is the afternoon snack.

89857.q: What is the first meal of the morning called?
89857.e: Breakfast is the first meal of the day. In Switzerland it is also called Zmorge.
89857.m: The first meal of the day is breakfast.

89858.q: How do you feel when you have eaten enough?
89858.e: When the stomach is full enough, the body says: full. That is the best time to stop eating.
89858.m: When you have eaten enough, you are full.

89859.q: What is often harder when you are very hungry?
89859.e: With an empty tummy the brain is short of energy. That is why you find it harder to concentrate and often get grumpy more quickly.
89859.m: When you are hungry it is harder to concentrate.

89860.q: Which part of the body tells us that we are hungry?
89860.e: The stomach and the blood send signals to the brain. The brain then makes us feel hungry.
89860.m: The brain makes us feel hungry.

89861.q: Which snack keeps you full for longer?
89861.e: Wholemeal bread and cheese give energy for a long time. Sweets only fill you up briefly, then hunger soon comes back.
89861.m: Wholemeal bread keeps you full longer than sweets.

89862.q: What do you often hear when you are hungry?
89862.e: When you are hungry, your tummy often rumbles so others can hear it. People say: “My stomach is rumbling.”
89862.m: When you are hungry, your stomach often rumbles.

89863.q: What makes the noise when your stomach rumbles?
a: Air and juices being pushed along
A little animal in your tummy
89863.e: The stomach and gut move using muscles. This pushes air and liquid around, which bubbles and rumbles.
89863.m: Air and liquid moving around make your stomach rumble.

89864.q: What are the noises from the tummy also called?
89864.e: The bubbling sounds don't only come from the stomach but mainly from the gut too. That is why they are also called bowel sounds.
89864.m: Tummy noises are also called bowel sounds.

a: Yes, you must go to hospital
89865.e: A rumbling stomach is a normal sound of digestion. It happens to everyone.
89865.m: A rumbling stomach is completely normal.

89866.q: What usually helps when your stomach rumbles with hunger?
89866.e: When your stomach rumbles with hunger, a meal or a mid-morning snack helps. Then it usually goes quieter.
89866.m: Eating something calms a rumbling stomach.

89867.q: Can your tummy rumble after eating too?
89867.e: The stomach and gut also move while digesting. That is why it can bubble after eating too.
89867.m: Your tummy can rumble while digesting too.

89868.q: What does a rumbling stomach often sound like?
89868.e: A rumbling stomach sounds like a deep grumbling or gurgling. Sometimes it is so loud that others can hear it too.
89868.m: A rumbling stomach sounds like a grumble.

89869.q: What can a doctor use to hear the noises in the tummy well?
89869.e: With a stethoscope the doctor listens to the tummy. That way they can tell whether the stomach and gut are working well.
89869.m: A stethoscope lets you hear tummy noises.

89871.q: How does sound normally reach our ears?
89871.e: The vibrations are passed on from air particle to air particle. That is how they reach our ears.
89871.m: Sound travels through the air to our ears.

89873.e: In solids such as stone or metal, sound is much faster than in water or air. In steel it is more than ten times as fast as in air.

89874.q: Why can you sometimes hear the neighbours through the wall?
a: Sound only travels through open windows
The wall throws the sound back
89874.e: Sound can also travel through solids such as walls and floors. That is why you often hear loud music in the next room.

89875.q: Can sound travel through water too?
a: Yes, even faster than through air
89875.e: In water, sound is about four times as fast as in air. That is why you can hear an engine well under water, for example.

89876.q: How does something vibrate that makes a high note?
89876.e: Fast vibrations make high notes, slow vibrations low notes. A short, tight string vibrates fast and sounds high.

89877.q: Which pets can hear sounds that are too high for us?
89877.e: Dogs hear much higher sounds than people. That is why there are dog whistles we can hardly hear.
89877.m: Dogs hear sounds that are too high for us.

89878.q: Can you sometimes feel sound too?
a: Yes, loud bass in your tummy
89878.e: Very loud, deep sounds make the body vibrate too. That is why you sometimes feel loud bass in your tummy.
89878.m: You can feel loud deep sounds in your body.

89879.e: An echo happens when sound bounces back off a wall or a mountain. Then you hear the call a second time.
89879.m: An echo is sound that is thrown back.

89880.q: Where in Switzerland can you often hear a good echo?
a: In front of a rock face in the mountains
In the middle of a flat meadow
In a room full of cushions
89880.e: Rock faces throw sound back well. That is why you often hear a clear echo in the mountains.
89880.m: In the mountains, rock faces throw back the echo.

89881.q: Why does the echo come a little later than your own call?
a: The sound needs time for the journey
The wind holds the call up
89881.e: The sound has to travel to the wall and back again. This journey takes a little time.
89881.m: The echo needs time to get there and back.

89882.q: Which animals find their way in the dark using echoes?
89882.e: Bats make high calls and listen to the echo. That way they notice where obstacles and insects are.
89882.m: Bats find their way with echoes.

89883.q: Which sea animals also use echoes to find their way?
89883.e: Dolphins send out clicking sounds and listen to their echo. That way they find fish even in murky water.
89883.m: Dolphins use echoes to find their way.

89884.q: In which room is there more echo?
a: In a room with carpet and curtains
In a wardrobe full of clothes
In a tent full of cushions
89884.e: Smooth, bare walls throw sound back strongly. Soft things in the room, on the other hand, muffle it.

89885.q: What absorbs a lot of sound in a room so that there is less echo?
89885.e: Soft materials absorb the sound and hardly throw it back. Hard, smooth surfaces, on the other hand, throw it back.

89886.q: What is the device called that ships use to measure water depth by echo?
89886.e: The echo sounder sends sound down to the bottom. From the time it takes for the echo to come back, it works out the depth.
89886.m: An echo sounder measures water depth with sound.

89887.q: Do you hear a clearly separate echo from a nearby wall or from a wall far away?
89887.e: If the wall is very close, the sound comes back so fast that it merges with the call. Only from about 17 metres away do you hear the echo separately.
89887.m: A clear echo needs a wall far away.

89888.e: A pneumatic drill on a building site is very loud. Whispering and rustling leaves are quiet.
89888.m: A pneumatic drill is very loud.

89889.q: How does a sound change as you move away from it?
89889.e: The further you are from a sound source, the quieter you hear it. The sound spreads out on the way.
89889.m: With distance, a sound gets quieter.

89890.q: What can very loud music do to your ears?
89890.e: Very loud noises can damage your hearing for good. That is why you should not turn headphones up too loud.
89890.m: Music that is too loud harms your hearing.

89891.q: How do you hit a drum to make it sound louder?
89891.e: A hard hit makes the skin vibrate more strongly. Big vibrations sound loud.

89892.q: Where in Switzerland should you be especially quiet?
89892.e: In a library, many people want to read and study in peace. That is why you speak quietly there.
89892.m: You are quiet in the library.

89893.q: What is louder than a normal conversation?
89893.e: A normal conversation is about 60 decibels. A rock concert is much louder and can reach over 100 decibels.
89893.m: A rock concert is much louder than a conversation.

89894.q: What do you call unpleasant, disturbing sound?
89894.e: Noise is sound that disturbs or can make you ill. That is why there are noise barriers along motorways, for example.

89895.q: What is the outer part of the ear that you can see called?
89895.e: The outer ear catches sound like a funnel. It guides it into the ear canal.

89896.q: Which thin membrane in the ear vibrates when sound arrives?
89896.e: At the end of the ear canal is the eardrum. Sound makes it vibrate, like the skin of a drum.
89896.m: The eardrum vibrates with the sound.

89897.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body, found in the ear, called?
89897.e: The stirrup in the middle ear is only about 3 millimetres long. It is the smallest bone in the body.
89897.m: The stirrup in the ear is the smallest bone.

89898.q: Which three tiny bones are in the middle ear?
89898.e: The three ear bones are named after their shapes: hammer, anvil and stirrup. They pass the vibrations on.
89898.m: Hammer, anvil and stirrup pass the sound on.

89899.q: Which part of the inner ear looks like a snail shell?
89899.e: The cochlea in the inner ear is coiled like a snail shell. There the vibrations are turned into signals for the brain.
89899.m: The cochlea in the inner ear turns sound into signals.

89900.q: Apart from hearing, what does the inner ear help with?
89900.e: The organ of balance is also in the inner ear. It notices whether we are turning or tilted.
89900.m: The inner ear also helps with balance.

89901.q: Why is it good to have two ears?
a: You can hear where a sound comes from
You hear twice as many colours
89901.e: A sound usually reaches one ear a little earlier and louder. That way the brain notices which direction it comes from.
89901.m: With two ears you can hear the direction of a sound.

89902.q: What should you not push deep into your ear?
89902.e: Cotton buds can push earwax deeper or injure the eardrum. You only clean the outer ear.
89902.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear.

89903.e: Earwax traps dust and dirt. It protects the ear canal and moves outwards by itself.

89904.q: What vibrates on a drum when you hit it?
a: The air in the next room
89904.e: The tight skin of the drum vibrates after the hit. We hear this vibration as a sound.
89904.m: On a drum, the skin vibrates.

89905.e: A big skin vibrates more slowly than a small one. Slow vibrations sound low.

89906.q: What do you usually hit a drum with?
89906.e: Drums are played with drumsticks, beaters or the hands. This makes the skin start to vibrate.
89906.m: Drums are played with sticks or beaters.

89907.q: What drumming music is the city of Basel famous for?
89907.e: At the Basel carnival, many drummers and pipers march through the city. Since 2017, the Basel carnival has been part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage.
89907.m: Basel is famous for drumming at the carnival.

89908.q: What is a person who plays the drum in a Swiss band often also called?
89908.e: In Switzerland, drummers are often called tambours. The word comes from French.
89908.m: In Switzerland, a drummer is often called a tambour.

89909.q: What is the large kettledrum in the orchestra called?
89909.e: The timpani have a large kettle-shaped body with a skin over it. They can be tuned to different notes.

89910.q: What happens to the sound when you tighten the drumskin?
89910.e: A tight skin vibrates faster. Fast vibrations sound higher.

89911.q: How can you see that a drumskin is vibrating?
a: Grains of rice jump on it
It gets as warm as an oven
89911.e: If you put a few grains of rice on the skin and hit next to them, they jump. That way you can see the vibration.
89911.m: Jumping rice grains show the skin vibrating.

89912.q: What do you need a tuning fork for?
89912.e: A tuning fork always gives exactly the same note. Musicians tune their instruments to it.
89912.m: You tune instruments with a tuning fork.

89913.q: How many prongs does a tuning fork have?
89913.e: A tuning fork has two prongs, like a U with a handle. The two prongs vibrate towards and away from each other.
89913.m: A tuning fork has two prongs.

89914.q: Which note does a standard tuning fork give?
89914.e: Most tuning forks give concert pitch A. It vibrates 440 times per second.
89914.m: A tuning fork usually gives concert pitch A.

89915.q: What happens if you hold a sounding tuning fork in water?
89915.e: The prongs vibrate back and forth very fast. In water you can see this, because it splashes.
89915.m: A sounding tuning fork makes water splash.

89916.q: How do you make a tuning fork sound?
a: You put it in the light
89916.e: You tap the prongs lightly against something soft, for example your knee. Then they start to vibrate.
89916.m: A tuning fork sounds when you tap it.

89917.q: What happens to the sound if you stand a sounding tuning fork on a table by its handle?
89917.e: The table vibrates too and passes the sound on to much more air. That is why the note sounds louder.
89917.m: A table makes the tuning fork's note louder.

89918.q: How do you stop the sound of a tuning fork?
89918.e: With your fingers you stop the vibrating prongs. Without vibration there is no more sound.
89918.m: Touching the prongs stops the sound.

89919.q: Where do you hold a tuning fork when you tap it?
a: You do not, it lies down
89919.e: You hold the tuning fork by the handle. That way the prongs can vibrate freely.
89919.m: Hold a tuning fork by the handle.

89920.q: What do you need for a tin can telephone?
a: A mobile phone and a tin
89920.e: A tin can telephone is made of two tins or cups joined by a long string. You do not need a cable.
89920.m: A tin can telephone needs two tins and a string.

89921.q: How must the string of a tin can telephone be?
89921.e: Only a tight string passes the vibrations on well. A loose string damps them.
89921.m: On a tin can telephone, the string must be tight.

89922.q: What does the sound travel through to the other cup on a tin can telephone?
89922.e: The vibrations of the voice travel along the tight string to the other cup.
89922.m: On a tin can telephone, the sound travels through the string.

89923.q: What vibrates on a tin can telephone when you speak into it?
89923.e: Your voice makes the bottom of the tin vibrate. At the other end, the bottom of the second tin vibrates too.
89923.m: On a tin can telephone, the bottom of the tin vibrates.

89924.q: What happens if someone holds the string of the tin can telephone in the middle?
89924.e: The hand stops the vibrations of the string. Then hardly any sound reaches the other end.
89924.m: Holding the string stops the sound.

89925.q: What can you use instead of tins for a string telephone?
89925.e: Yoghurt pots have a firm bottom that vibrates well. Soft things such as cotton wool or fabric swallow the sound.
89925.m: You can build a string telephone with yoghurt pots too.

89926.q: What do you do with the second tin when the other person is speaking?
a: You hold it to your ear
You put it in the fridge
89926.e: With a tin can telephone, one person speaks into the tin and the other holds their tin to their ear. Then you swap.
89926.m: When listening, you hold the tin to your ear.

89927.q: Does a tin can telephone need electricity?
89927.e: The tin can telephone works only with vibrations. It needs no electricity.
89927.m: A tin can telephone works without electricity.

89928.q: What does not vibrate when you whisper, unlike when you speak normally?
89928.e: When you speak normally, the vocal folds in the larynx vibrate. When you whisper, they stay still and you only hear the sound of air.
89928.m: When whispering, the vocal folds do not vibrate.

89929.q: What is the game called where a word is passed on in a whisper?
89929.e: In “Telephone”, everyone whispers the word into their neighbour's ear. At the end, something quite different often comes out.
89929.m: In Telephone, you pass a word on in a whisper.

89930.e: When someone is asleep, you do not want to wake them. That is why you whisper.
89930.m: You whisper so others are not disturbed.

89931.q: How loud is whispering compared with normal speaking?
89931.e: When you whisper, only air without voice comes out of your mouth. That is why it is much quieter than normal speaking.

89932.q: What do you often hold round your mouth when whispering so only one person hears?
89932.e: A hand round your mouth directs the sound straight into the other person's ear. So the others hear less.
89932.m: With a hand at your mouth, you whisper more precisely.

89933.q: Which sounds can you hear well when someone whispers?
89933.e: Hissing sounds like “s” and “sh” are made with air alone. That is why you can hear them well even in a whisper.
89933.m: You can hear hissing sounds well even in a whisper.

89934.q: What is a teacher usually doing when they say “Shh”?
89934.e: “Shh” is a quiet hissing sound. It means: please be quiet.

89935.q: Can you hear a whisper well from a long way away?
a: Yes, as far as the next village
89935.e: Whispering is very quiet and gets weaker quickly with distance. That is why you only hear it from close by.
89935.m: You only hear whispering from close by.

89936.q: Why do people wear ear protection?
a: To protect the ears from noise
89936.e: Ear protection makes loud noises quieter. That way your hearing is not damaged.
89936.m: Ear protection protects the ears from noise.

89937.q: Which ear protection do you put straight into your ears?
89937.e: Earplugs are small, soft plugs. You put them into the ear canal.

89938.q: Where do workers often wear ear protection?
89938.e: On a building site, machines such as drills and pneumatic drills are very loud. That is why the workers wear ear protection.
89938.m: On loud building sites, people wear ear protection.

89939.q: When is ear protection a good idea for children?
89939.e: Fireworks, for example on 1 August, can bang very loudly. Ear protection protects sensitive ears.
89939.m: At loud fireworks, ear protection protects the ears.

89940.q: What do ear defenders look like?
89940.e: Ear defenders have two padded cups on a headband. They cover the whole ears.
89940.m: Ear defenders look like big headphones.

89941.q: Do damaged hearing cells in the ear grow back by themselves?
89941.e: The fine hearing cells in the inner ear do not grow back. That is why it is important to protect your hearing.
89941.m: Damaged hearing cells do not grow back.

89942.q: At carnival, a Guggenmusik band is playing very loudly. What protects your ears?
89942.e: Close to loudspeakers or Guggenmusik bands it is very loud. Earplugs make the noise quieter and protect your ears.

89943.q: What is a sign that it was too loud?
89943.e: After very loud noise, your ears sometimes beep or ring. This is a warning sign for your hearing.
89943.m: A ringing in the ears warns of too much noise.

89944.q: In a thunderstorm, what reaches us first?
89944.e: Light is much faster than sound. That is why you see the lightning before you hear the thunder.
89944.m: In a thunderstorm, you see the lightning before the thunder.

89945.q: What makes the loud thunder in a thunderstorm?
a: The lightning heats the air very quickly
Two clouds bump into each other
The wind whistles over the mountains
89945.e: Lightning heats the air extremely strongly in a flash. The air suddenly expands, and that makes the loud bang.
89945.m: Thunder happens because lightning heats the air.

89946.q: About how far away is a thunderstorm if you count 3 seconds between lightning and thunder?
89946.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. So at 3 seconds, the storm is about 1 kilometre away.
89946.m: Three seconds between lightning and thunder is about one kilometre.

89947.q: About how far away is a thunderstorm if you count 9 seconds?
89947.e: You divide the seconds by 3. 9 divided by 3 is 3, so the storm is about 3 kilometres away.
89947.m: Divide the seconds by three to get the kilometres.

89948.q: What does it mean when lightning and thunder come almost at the same time?
89948.e: The shorter the time between lightning and thunder, the closer the storm. Then you should be safely indoors.
89948.m: If lightning and thunder come together, the storm is close.

89949.q: Why does thunder often rumble and roll for a long time?
a: The sound from near and far arrives at different times
The wind blows the thunder further
The rain makes the thunder longer
89949.e: A flash of lightning is very long. The sound from near and far parts arrives at different times, and mountains throw it back.
89949.m: Thunder rolls because its sound travels for different lengths of time.

89950.q: Where is the best place to go when there is thunder?
a: Into a lake for a swim
89950.e: In a thunderstorm, you are safest in a house or a car. Lone trees, summits and water are dangerous.
89950.m: When it thunders, go into a house.

89951.q: In a thunderstorm, what do you really need to take shelter from, the thunder or the lightning?
89951.e: Thunder is only loud; it does not hurt. The lightning is what is dangerous.
89951.m: The lightning is dangerous, not the thunder.

89952.q: About how long should you stay indoors after the last thunder?
89952.e: Even a storm that is moving away can still send lightning. That is why you wait about half an hour after the last thunder.
89952.m: After the last thunder, wait about half an hour.

89953.q: What do you need a megaphone for?
89953.e: A megaphone makes your voice louder. So even people far away can hear what you are saying.
89953.m: A megaphone makes your voice louder.

89954.e: A megaphone is wide at the front and narrow at the back, like a funnel. You speak into the narrow end.
89954.m: A megaphone is shaped like a funnel.

89955.q: In German, a megaphone is jokingly called “Flüstertüte”. What does that mean?
89955.e: As a joke, the megaphone is called a “whisper bag” in German. Yet it actually makes the voice louder.
89955.m: In German, a megaphone is jokingly called a whisper bag.

89956.e: The fire brigade and police use megaphones to tell lots of people outdoors something. Coaches and tour guides use them too.
89956.m: The fire brigade and police often use a megaphone.

89957.q: What do electric megaphones need to work?
89957.e: Electric megaphones have a loudspeaker. It gets its electricity from batteries.

89958.q: How can you make a simple megaphone with your hands?
a: Hold your hands like a funnel round your mouth
Put your hands over your ears
Put your hands in your pockets
89958.e: If you hold your hands like a funnel round your mouth, your call is focused. So it can be heard further away.
89958.m: With your hands round your mouth, your call carries further.

89959.q: What can you use to make a simple megaphone yourself?
89959.e: A piece of card rolled into a funnel focuses the sound. That makes your voice louder.
89959.m: A card funnel is a simple megaphone.

89960.q: In which direction is a megaphone especially loud?
89960.e: The funnel focuses the sound forwards. Behind the megaphone it is quieter.
89960.m: A megaphone is loudest towards the front.

89961.q: What material is an alphorn usually made of?
89961.e: An alphorn is usually made of wood, often spruce. In the past, people used a tree that had grown crooked on a slope.
89961.m: An alphorn is usually made of wood.

89962.q: Which country is the alphorn especially known for?
89962.e: The alphorn is a symbol of Swiss folk music. You hear it at festivals and in the mountains.
89962.m: The alphorn is typical of Switzerland.

89963.q: How many finger holes or keys does an alphorn have?
89963.e: An alphorn has no holes, keys or valves. It is simply a long, open tube with a mouthpiece.
89963.m: An alphorn has no finger holes.

89964.q: What does the alphorn player use to make the different notes?
89964.e: The player blows into the mouthpiece and tightens the lips by different amounts. This makes higher or lower notes.
89964.m: On the alphorn, you make the notes with your lips.

89965.q: What did herders use the alphorn for in the past?
89965.e: The sound of the alphorn can be heard a long way off. Herders used it to give signals across the Alps.
89965.m: In the past, herders gave signals with the alphorn.

89966.q: Why can you hear the alphorn so far away?
a: It has a loud, carrying sound
89966.e: The long tube makes a strong, deep sound. It carries far over valleys and mountains.
89966.m: The alphorn's strong sound carries far.

89967.q: What shape is the end of an alphorn?
89967.e: The lower end of the alphorn is curved upwards and wide open. This shape comes from the tree that grew crooked.
89967.m: The end of the alphorn curves upwards.

89968.q: What did Copernicus put at the centre of his model of the universe?
89968.e: Copernicus explained that the Earth and the other planets go round the Sun. This view of the world is called heliocentric.
89968.m: With Copernicus, the Sun is at the centre.

89969.q: Roughly when did Nicolaus Copernicus live?
89969.e: Copernicus lived from 1473 to 1543. His main work came out in the year he died.

89971.q: What shape did the planets' orbits still have in Copernicus's model?
89971.e: Copernicus held on to perfect circular orbits and so still needed small extra circles.
89971.m: Copernicus still had the planets move in circles.

89972.q: How did Copernicus explain why the Sun and the stars rise and set every day?
a: The Earth turns on its axis.
The sky turns round the Earth.
The Sun circles the Earth every day.
89972.e: According to Copernicus, the Earth turns once a day on its axis. This makes the whole sky seem to move.
89972.m: The Earth's daily turning makes the sky seem to circle.

89973.q: In which country did Copernicus study, among other places in Bologna and Padua?
89973.e: After his studies in Kraków, Copernicus went to Italy, where he studied church law and medicine.
89973.m: Copernicus studied in Italy for several years.

89974.q: Which chemical element is named after Nicolaus Copernicus?
89974.e: The artificially made element 112 was named copernicium in 2010 in honour of Copernicus.
89974.m: The element copernicium bears the name of Copernicus.

89975.q: Which view of the universe was accepted in Europe before Copernicus?
a: The Earth is at the centre
The Sun is at the centre
The Moon is at the centre
The Earth is a disc on a whale
89975.e: For a long time people believed that the Sun, the Moon and the planets circle the Earth. Copernicus put the Sun in the centre instead.
89975.m: Before Copernicus, the Earth was at the centre of the view of the universe.

89976.q: Which observation of Venus supported the heliocentric model for Galileo?
a: Venus shows phases like the Moon.
Venus always looks the same size.
89976.e: Galileo saw that Venus shows full and thin phases. This is easiest to explain if it orbits the Sun.
89976.m: The phases of Venus supported the heliocentric model.

89977.q: What did Galileo realise when he looked at the Milky Way through his telescope?
a: It is made up of countless stars.
It is a cloud of water vapour.
It is a reflection of the Earth.
It is made of glowing gas.
89977.e: With his telescope, Galileo resolved the milky band into a great many individual faint stars.
89977.m: The Milky Way is made up of countless stars.

89978.q: What did Galileo discover on the surface of the Moon with his telescope?
89978.e: Galileo saw light and shadow on the Moon and concluded that there were mountains and craters. So the Moon was not a perfectly smooth ball.
89978.m: Galileo was one of the first to see mountains and craters on the Moon.

89979.q: To what punishment was Galileo sentenced by the Inquisition in 1633?
89979.e: Galileo had to renounce the heliocentric model and spent the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence.
89979.m: After his trial, Galileo lived under house arrest.

89980.q: What did Galileo find out about free fall?
a: Without air, all objects fall equally fast.
Objects fall at a constant speed.
89980.e: Galileo realised that without air resistance all objects speed up at the same rate, no matter how heavy they are.
89980.m: Without air resistance, all objects fall equally fast.

89981.q: How does the Catholic Church view the trial of Galileo today?
a: It has admitted the verdict was a mistake
It still thinks the verdict was right
It has made Galileo a saint
It has never mentioned the trial
89981.e: In 1992 Pope John Paul II declared publicly that the Church had wronged Galileo.
89981.m: In 1992 the Church admitted that the verdict against Galileo was wrong.

89982.q: Which famous sentence is attributed to Galileo, although he probably never said it?
89982.e: The sentence “Eppur si muove” is said to have been spoken after the trial, but it was only recorded long after Galileo’s death.
89982.m: The sentence “And yet it moves” is probably a legend.

89983.q: According to Kepler’s first law, what shape of path do the planets move on?
89983.e: Kepler found that planetary orbits are slightly stretched ellipses and not perfect circles.

89984.q: According to Kepler’s first law, where is the Sun?
a: At one focus of the ellipse
Exactly in the middle of the ellipse
On the edge of the ellipse
89984.e: An ellipse has two foci. The Sun is at one of them, not at the centre.
89984.m: The Sun is at one focus of a planet’s orbit.

89985.q: What does Kepler’s second law mean for the speed of a planet?
a: It is faster near the Sun.
It is faster far from the Sun.
It always has the same speed.
89985.e: The line joining the Sun and the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. So near the Sun the planet must move faster.
89985.m: A planet moves fastest near the Sun.

89987.q: Kepler mainly studied the observations of which planet to find his laws?
89987.e: Kepler spent years calculating with Tycho Brahe’s precise data on Mars. The orbit of Mars is clearly elliptical, which led him to the solution.
89987.m: The orbit of Mars revealed the elliptical shape to Kepler.

89988.q: Around what time did Johannes Kepler live?
89988.e: Kepler lived from 1571 to 1630. The telescope was also invented during this time.

89989.q: Kepler published planetary tables in 1627. What were they used for?
a: To predict the positions of the planets
89989.e: With the Rudolphine Tables you could calculate where a planet would be in the sky on a particular day. They were much more accurate than older tables.
89989.m: Kepler’s tables predicted the positions of the planets accurately.

89990.q: Against which accusation did Kepler successfully defend his mother in a long trial?
89990.e: From 1615, Katharina Kepler was accused of witchcraft. Johannes Kepler took on her defence, and she was released in 1621.
89990.m: Kepler saved his mother from being convicted of witchcraft.

89991.q: What is the telescope described by Kepler made of?
89991.e: The Keplerian telescope uses two converging lenses. It shows the image upside down, but has a wider field of view.
89991.m: The Keplerian telescope works with two converging lenses.

89992.q: Which country did the astronomer Tycho Brahe come from?
89992.e: Tycho Brahe was born in 1546 in Scania, which then belonged to Denmark, and he was a Danish nobleman.
89992.m: Tycho Brahe was a Danish astronomer.

89993.q: What was the name of the observatory that Tycho Brahe built on the island of Hven?
89993.e: The Danish king gave Tycho the island of Hven. There he built the Uraniborg observatory, named after Urania, the muse of astronomy.
89993.m: Tycho Brahe did his research in his Uraniborg observatory.

89994.q: Which event in the sky did Tycho Brahe observe in the constellation Cassiopeia in 1572?
89994.e: In 1572 Tycho saw a very bright star that suddenly appeared, known today as a supernova. He showed that even the sky of fixed stars can change.
89994.m: Tycho Brahe observed a supernova in 1572.

89995.q: What did Tycho Brahe lose in a duel as a student?
89995.e: In a sword duel in 1566, part of his nose was cut off. Afterwards he wore a replacement nose made of metal.
89995.m: After a duel, Tycho Brahe wore a metal nose.

89996.q: What was Tycho Brahe’s model of the universe like?
a: The planets circle the Sun, and the Sun circles the Earth.
All the planets and the Sun circle the Moon.
The Earth and all the planets circle the Sun.
The Sun stands still, and the Earth circles Mars.
89996.e: Tycho combined the models: the Earth stays still at the centre, the Sun circles it, and the other planets circle the Sun.
89996.m: Tycho Brahe designed a mixed model between the two views of the universe.

89997.q: What did Tycho Brahe use to make his very precise measurements?
a: Large angle-measuring instruments without a telescope
89997.e: The telescope did not yet exist during Tycho’s lifetime. He measured with huge quadrants and sextants more precisely than anyone before him.
89997.m: Tycho Brahe measured amazingly precisely without a telescope.

89998.q: Which famous astronomer later used Tycho Brahe’s precise measurements?
89998.e: Kepler worked with Tycho Brahe at the end of Tycho’s life and inherited his data. With it he found out that the planets orbit the Sun on ellipses.
89998.m: Using Tycho’s data, Kepler discovered the laws of planetary orbits.

89999.q: What did Tycho Brahe show with his measurements of the great comet of 1577?
a: The comet was farther away than the Moon.
The comet was in the Earth’s atmosphere.
The comet was made of fire.
89999.e: Tycho could not measure any shift of the comet against the stars. So it had to be far beyond the Moon and not in the air.
89999.m: Comets travel through space far beyond the Moon.

90000.q: In which city did the scholar Claudius Ptolemy work?
90000.e: Ptolemy lived and did research in Alexandria in Egypt, one of the great centres of knowledge in ancient times.
90000.m: Ptolemy did his research in Alexandria.

90001.q: In which century did Claudius Ptolemy live?
90001.e: Ptolemy lived from about AD 100 to 170, so in the 2nd century.
90001.m: Ptolemy lived in the 2nd century AD.

90002.q: What was at the centre of Claudius Ptolemy’s view of the universe?
90002.e: Ptolemy described a view of the universe in which the Sun, the Moon and the planets circle the Earth. It is called the geocentric model.
90002.m: For Ptolemy, the Earth was at the centre.

90003.q: Who put the Sun in the centre in the 16th century, replacing Ptolemy’s view of the universe?
90003.e: Copernicus described a view of the universe in which the Earth and the other planets circle the Sun. It gradually became accepted.
90003.m: Copernicus replaced Ptolemy’s view of the universe with one that has the Sun at the centre.

90004.q: How did Ptolemy explain the looping movements of the planets?
a: With small circles on large circles
With elliptical orbits around the Sun
90004.e: Ptolemy had each planet move on a small circle, the epicycle, whose centre travelled on a large circle around the Earth.
90004.m: Ptolemy explained planetary loops with epicycles.

90005.q: Ptolemy already described many constellations such as Orion and Hercules. Where do their names come from?
90005.e: In the 2nd century, Ptolemy collected the constellations of the Greeks. Many of them are named after heroes and animals from Greek myths.
90005.m: Many constellation names come from Greek myths.

90006.q: In which other field did Ptolemy write a famous work listing locations?
90006.e: In his “Geographia”, Ptolemy collected the coordinates of about 8,000 places. The work shaped map-making until modern times.
90006.m: Ptolemy was also an important geographer.

90007.q: Roughly how long was Ptolemy’s view of the universe the accepted one in Europe?
90007.e: From the 2nd century until the time of Copernicus and Kepler in the 16th and 17th centuries, scholars relied on Ptolemy, so for about 1,400 years.
90007.m: Ptolemy’s model lasted for more than a thousand years.

90008.q: What is at the centre of the universe in the geocentric model?
90008.e: In the geocentric model the Earth rests at the centre, and all the heavenly bodies move around it.
90008.m: In the geocentric model the Earth is at the centre.

90009.q: Which Greek philosopher supported the geocentric model and so shaped people’s thinking for a long time?
90009.e: In the 4th century BC, Aristotle taught that a motionless Earth lies at the centre. In the Middle Ages his teaching was seen as a great authority.
90009.m: Aristotle put the Earth at the centre of the world.

90010.q: Which everyday observation seemed to confirm the geocentric model?
a: The Sun seems to travel across the sky.
90010.e: Every day the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west, while you yourself feel no movement.
90010.m: The apparent path of the Sun made the Earth seem to stand still.

90011.q: In the ancient geocentric model, what were the heavenly bodies thought to be attached to?
90011.e: People imagined crystal-clear spheres, one inside another, that turned around the Earth and carried the heavenly bodies with them.
90011.m: In the old view of the universe, the heavenly bodies sat on spheres.

90012.q: In the geocentric model, which heavenly body was closest to the Earth?
90012.e: The innermost sphere carried the Moon. Above it came Mercury, Venus, the Sun and the outer planets.
90012.m: In the old model the Moon was on the innermost sphere.

90013.q: Which planetary movement was hard to explain in the geocentric model?
90013.e: Planets such as Mars sometimes move backwards and form loops. This could not be described with simple circles around the Earth.
90013.m: Planetary loops caused problems for the geocentric model.

90014.q: What formed the outermost shell of the universe in the geocentric model?
90014.e: Beyond the sphere of Saturn lay the sphere of the fixed stars. All the stars were thought to be the same distance from the Earth.
90014.m: The sphere of fixed stars closed off the old universe on the outside.

90015.q: What does the Greek word “ge” in the term “geocentric” mean?
90015.e: “Ge” is the Greek word for earth, as in geography or geology.
90015.m: Geocentric means that the Earth is at the centre.

90016.q: What does the Greek word “helios” in the term “heliocentric” mean?
90016.e: Helios is the Greek word for sun. So heliocentric means “with the Sun at the centre”.
90016.m: Heliocentric means that the Sun is at the centre.

90017.q: How does the heliocentric model explain the loops that Mars makes in the sky?
a: The Earth overtakes Mars on its inner orbit.
Mars circles a moon of its own.
90017.e: The Earth is faster than Mars. When it overtakes Mars, Mars seems to move backwards for a few weeks.
90017.m: Planetary loops happen because the Earth overtakes other planets.

90018.q: Which astronomer put the Sun at the centre of the universe in his book in 1543?
90018.e: Nicolaus Copernicus described how the Earth and the planets circle the Sun. His book appeared in 1543, the year he died.
90018.m: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre.

90019.q: What happened to Copernicus’s main work in 1616?
a: It was put on the Index of banned books.
It was taught in all schools.
It was given an award by the Pope.
90019.e: In 1616 the Catholic Church put the book on the Index. It could only be read in a corrected form.
90019.m: In 1616 the Church banned Copernicus’s book for the time being.

90020.q: What did Copernicus claim in his main work?
a: The Earth is a flat disc
90020.e: Copernicus described a view of the universe with the Sun at the centre. In it the Earth spins on its own axis and goes around the Sun once a year.
90020.m: According to Copernicus, the Earth circles the Sun.

90021.q: Which physicist explained with his law of gravitation why the planets circle the Sun?
90021.e: In 1687 Newton showed that the same gravity that makes an apple fall also keeps the planets in their orbits.
90021.m: The Sun’s gravity keeps the planets in their orbits.

90022.q: Why do you never see Mercury and Venus high in the sky at midnight?
a: Their orbits lie inside the Earth’s orbit.
They are too far away at night.
They only shine during the day.
The Moon hides them at night.
90022.e: Mercury and Venus orbit closer to the Sun than the Earth does. Seen from here, they are therefore always near the Sun in the sky.
90022.m: You can only see the inner planets in the morning or the evening.

90023.q: What is meant by the “Copernican revolution”?
a: The change to a view of the universe with the Sun at the centre
The turning of the Earth’s axis every 26,000 years
The reversal of the Moon’s orbit
The change from the Julian calendar
90023.e: With Copernicus began the shift from an Earth-centred to a Sun-centred view of the universe. Today the term is used generally for a complete change in thinking.
90023.m: The Copernican revolution fundamentally changed the picture of the universe.

90024.q: Which country did Giordano Bruno come from?
90024.e: Giordano Bruno was born in 1548 in Nola near Naples. Later he travelled through many countries in Europe.

90025.q: What was Giordano Bruno as a young man?
90025.e: Bruno joined the Dominican order in Naples. Because of his unusual views, he later left the monastery.
90025.m: Giordano Bruno was first a monk.

90026.q: What did Giordano Bruno teach about the size of the universe?
90026.e: Bruno imagined the universe without a boundary and without a fixed centre, with countless worlds.
90026.m: For Bruno, the universe was infinite.

90027.q: What were the stars in the night sky for Giordano Bruno?
a: Distant suns that might have their own planets
Holes in a dome of the sky
90027.e: Bruno suspected that the stars are suns like ours and are orbited by their own worlds. Today we actually know of many exoplanets.
90027.m: Bruno thought the stars were distant suns.

90028.q: Why did the Inquisition condemn Giordano Bruno?
90028.e: Among other things, Bruno taught an infinite universe with many worlds. The Church saw this as false teaching and had him executed in Rome in 1600.
90028.m: Giordano Bruno was condemned because of his teachings.

90029.q: What does the monument to Giordano Bruno in Rome stand for today?
90029.e: Since 1889 the monument has stood in the Campo de’ Fiori, where Bruno was executed. It stands for the right to think freely.
90029.m: The Bruno monument in Rome stands for freedom of thought.

90030.q: Giordano Bruno lived briefly in Geneva in 1579. How did things go for him there?
a: He got into a dispute and was arrested
He was celebrated as a hero
90030.e: In Geneva Bruno joined the Calvinists. After writing a pamphlet against a professor, he was arrested and expelled.
90030.m: In Geneva too, Bruno got into conflict with the Church.

90031.q: How did Giordano Bruno’s life end?
a: He was burned at the stake
He was banished to a distant country
He died peacefully as a rich man
90031.e: After a long trial by the Inquisition, Bruno was burned at the stake in Rome in February 1600.
90031.m: Giordano Bruno was burned in Rome in 1600.

90032.q: What did Aristarchus of Samos already suggest in ancient times?
90032.e: Aristarchus was one of the first to put the Sun in the centre and have the Earth circle it. But hardly anyone agreed with him.
90032.m: Already in ancient times, Aristarchus thought of a view of the universe with the Sun at the centre.

90033.q: Which ancient culture did the scholar Aristarchus of Samos come from?
90033.e: Samos is a Greek island. Aristarchus lived there around 300 BC, about 1,800 years before Copernicus.
90033.m: Aristarchus was a Greek from ancient times.

90034.q: What conclusion did Aristarchus come to about the size of the Sun?
a: It is much bigger than the Earth.
It is smaller than the Moon.
It is the same size as the Earth.
It is as big as a mountain.
90034.e: From his measurements, Aristarchus concluded that the Sun is many times bigger than the Earth. That is why he thought it logical that the Earth circles the Sun.
90034.m: Aristarchus realised that the Sun is much bigger than the Earth.

90035.q: At which phase of the Moon did Aristarchus measure the angle between the Moon and the Sun?
90035.e: At half moon, the Earth, the Moon and the Sun form a right-angled triangle. From the angle he could estimate the ratio of the distances.
90035.m: At half moon, the Earth, the Moon and the Sun form a right-angled triangle.

90036.q: What did Aristarchus of Samos try to work out with geometry, as one of the first to do so?
a: How far the Sun and the Moon are from the Earth
90036.e: Aristarchus measured angles in the sky and estimated the distances of the Sun and the Moon from them. His numbers were still inaccurate, but his method was right.
90036.m: Aristarchus used geometry to estimate the distances of the Sun and the Moon.

90037.q: What was at the centre of Aristarchus’s model of the universe?
90037.e: More than 2,000 years ago, Aristarchus already thought that the Earth circles the Sun. Most scholars did not believe him at the time.
90037.m: Aristarchus put the Sun at the centre.

90038.q: Which event in the sky did Aristarchus use to estimate the size of the Moon?
90038.e: During a lunar eclipse the Moon passes through the Earth’s shadow. From how long it took, Aristarchus worked out the size of the Moon compared with the Earth.
90038.m: The Earth’s shadow during a lunar eclipse helps to measure the Moon.

90039.q: Why did many scholars in ancient times reject Aristarchus’s model of the universe?
a: No shift of the stars could be seen.
The Sun was too small for it.
The Moon would have had to fall down.
90039.e: If the Earth goes around the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over the year. This shift is so tiny that it could not be seen at the time.
90039.m: Without a measurable shift of the stars, people did not believe the Earth moved.

90040.q: Which country did the astronomer Edwin Hubble come from?
90040.e: Edwin Hubble was born in 1889 in the US state of Missouri and worked in the USA throughout his career as a researcher.
90040.m: Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer.

90041.q: What did Edwin Hubble prove about the Andromeda Nebula in 1924?
a: It is a separate galaxy outside the Milky Way.
It is a gas cloud in the Milky Way.
90041.e: Hubble measured the distance to the Andromeda Nebula and found that it lies far outside our Milky Way. This made it clear that there are many galaxies.
90041.m: Hubble showed that there are galaxies outside the Milky Way.

90042.q: What is the name of our own galaxy, which Hubble showed is not the only one?
90042.e: Before Hubble, many people thought the Milky Way was the whole universe. Hubble showed that there are countless other galaxies.
90042.m: The Milky Way is just one of countless galaxies.

90043.q: What did Edwin Hubble use to make his most important discoveries?
a: A large reflecting telescope on a mountain
90043.e: Hubble worked at the Mount Wilson Observatory in California. Its telescope had a 2.5-metre mirror and was the largest in the world at the time.
90043.m: Hubble observed with a huge reflecting telescope.

90044.q: By which feature did Edwin Hubble classify galaxies?
90044.e: Hubble distinguished, for example, between elliptical galaxies and spiral galaxies. His scheme looks like a tuning fork lying on its side.
90044.m: Hubble sorted galaxies by their shape.

90045.q: What do you call a galaxy whose arms wind around the centre like a whirlpool?
90045.e: Spiral galaxies have bright arms that wind around a bright centre. Our Milky Way is also a spiral galaxy.

90046.q: Hubble found that almost all galaxies are moving away from us. What does this mean?
a: The Earth is pushing the galaxies away
90046.e: The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away. This shows that the whole universe is expanding.
90046.m: Hubble’s observations show that the universe is expanding.

90047.q: What can you conclude from the fact that the universe is expanding?
a: In the past, everything was much closer together
The universe is getting hotter and hotter
The stars are getting bigger and bigger
The Earth is getting heavier and heavier
90047.e: If everything is moving apart, it must once have been much closer together. This led to the idea of the Big Bang.
90047.m: The expansion of the universe led to the idea of the Big Bang.

90048.q: Why does the telescope named after Edwin Hubble orbit in space instead of standing on a mountain?
a: The Earth’s atmosphere does not get in the way there
In space it is closer to the stars
It is not allowed on mountains
90048.e: Air shimmers and swallows part of the light. That is why the Hubble Space Telescope delivers especially sharp images. The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier helped to repair it.
90048.m: Without air in the way, the Hubble telescope sees especially sharply.

90049.q: In which country did the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky do research for most of his life?
90049.e: From 1925 Zwicky worked at the California Institute of Technology in California. There he searched the sky with large telescopes.
90049.m: Fritz Zwicky did most of his research in the USA.

90050.q: What is Fritz Zwicky from Glarus known for?
a: He invented the Swiss Army knife
He was the first to climb the Matterhorn
90050.e: Fritz Zwicky was a citizen of Mollis in the canton of Glarus. He became famous as an astronomer and discovered many exploding stars.
90050.m: Fritz Zwicky from Glarus was a famous astronomer.

90051.q: Fritz Zwicky studied physics at ETH. In which city is ETH?
90051.e: Zwicky studied at ETH Zurich from 1917 to 1925. He also wrote his doctoral thesis there.
90051.m: Fritz Zwicky studied at ETH Zurich.

90052.q: What term did Zwicky use for the invisible mass he suspected in galaxy clusters?
90052.e: In 1933 Zwicky wrote about “dark matter”, because the visible galaxies did not have enough mass to hold the cluster together.
90052.m: Fritz Zwicky coined the term dark matter.

90053.q: According to the idea of Zwicky and Walter Baade, which star remnants are formed in a supernova?
90053.e: In 1934 Zwicky and Baade suggested that an extremely dense neutron star is left behind after a supernova.
90053.m: A supernova can produce a neutron star.

90054.q: Fritz Zwicky discovered more than a hundred supernovae. What is a supernova?
a: The huge explosion of a star
A constellation in the southern sky
90054.e: In a supernova a star explodes and for a short time shines brighter than a whole galaxy. Zwicky found more of them than any other astronomer of his time.
90054.m: A supernova is the explosion of a star.

90055.q: Fritz Zwicky invented the “morphological box”. What does this method help with?
90055.e: You break a problem down into features and combine their possibilities. This produces many new ideas. The method is still used in engineering and design today.
90055.m: Fritz Zwicky’s morphological box helps you find new ideas.

90056.q: What did Fritz Zwicky predict about whole galaxies in 1937?
a: They can bend light like a lens.
They all circle the Milky Way.
90056.e: Zwicky suggested that the gravity of a galaxy can focus the light of objects behind it. Such gravitational lenses were actually discovered later.
90056.m: Galaxies can act as gravitational lenses.

90057.q: What did the Swiss astronomer Rudolf Wolf regularly count on the Sun?
90057.e: Rudolf Wolf from Fällanden near Zurich observed the dark spots on the Sun and counted them carefully.

90058.q: Which observatory did Rudolf Wolf found and run as its first director?
90058.e: Wolf founded the Swiss Federal Observatory in Zurich and ran it from 1864 until his death in 1893.
90058.m: Rudolf Wolf was the first director of the Swiss Federal Observatory.

90059.q: Which number for solar activity bears Rudolf Wolf’s name?
90059.e: In 1849 Wolf developed a measure for sunspots, the Wolf number or relative sunspot number. It is still kept up today.
90059.m: The Wolf number measures sunspot activity.

90060.q: According to Rudolf Wolf: relative number equals 10 times the number of sunspot groups plus the number of individual spots. What is it for 3 groups with 12 spots in total?
90060.e: You calculate 10 times 3, which makes 30, and add the 12 spots, so 30 plus 12 equals 42.
90060.m: In the relative number, sunspot groups count ten times.

90061.q: What period did Rudolf Wolf find for the rise and fall in sunspots?
90061.e: Wolf studied old observations and worked out that the sunspot cycle lasts about 11 years.
90061.m: The number of sunspots rises and falls over about eleven years.

90062.q: In 1852, which phenomenon on Earth did Rudolf Wolf link to sunspots?
a: Changes in the Earth’s magnetic field
90062.e: At the same time as other researchers, Wolf realised that the Earth’s magnetic field changes in step with the sunspots.
90062.m: Solar activity affects the Earth’s magnetic field.

90063.q: At which university in Zurich was Rudolf Wolf a professor of astronomy?
90063.e: Rudolf Wolf taught at ETH Zurich, where he also ran the Swiss Federal Observatory and the library.
90063.m: Rudolf Wolf was a professor at ETH Zurich.

90064.q: In which other field was Rudolf Wolf a Swiss pioneer?
90064.e: Wolf chaired the Swiss Meteorological Commission and was the first director of the Central Meteorological Institute.
90064.m: Rudolf Wolf helped to build up Switzerland’s weather service.

90065.q: Roughly what is the average air pressure at sea level?
90065.e: Standard pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals. The actual value varies with the weather.
90065.m: At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.

90066.q: In which unit do weather services such as MeteoSwiss usually give air pressure?
90066.e: One hectopascal equals 100 pascals. People used to say millibars instead; the number is the same.
90066.m: Air pressure is given in hectopascals.

90067.q: Near the ground, by roughly how much does air pressure fall for every 8 metres of height?
90067.e: At low altitudes, air pressure falls by about 1 hectopascal for roughly every 8 metres you climb. Higher up, the decrease becomes slower.
90067.m: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

90068.q: At what height is air pressure about half as great as at sea level?
90068.e: At about 5.5 kilometres up, only half of the air’s mass is above you. That is why the pressure there is about half as great.
90068.m: At 5500 metres, the air pressure is only half as great.
