90354.q: What did the first stage of Rail 2000 bring passengers in 2004?
90354.e: With the timetable change in December 2004, more trains ran and many connections became faster. It was one of the biggest timetable changes in Switzerland.
90354.m: Rail 2000 brought more trains and faster connections.

90355.q: Since Rail 2000, roughly how long do the fastest trains take from Bern to Zurich?
90355.e: The journey time fell from 69 to 58 and later to 56 minutes. This was made possible mainly by the new line across the Central Plateau.
90355.m: Since Rail 2000 the journey from Bern to Zurich takes under an hour.

90356.q: Which principle describes the aim of Rail 2000?
a: As fast as necessary, not as fast as possible
Each train runs only once a day
90356.e: The trains were not meant to set records, but to reach the hubs on time. That way the connections fit together everywhere.
90356.m: With Rail 2000, good connections count for more than top speed.

90357.q: Why does the train driver see the signals on a screen in the cab at 200 km/h?
a: Because at that speed signals beside the track can hardly be seen in time
Because signals beside the track are banned
Because a screen is cheaper than a lamp
Because the train never runs at night
90357.e: At high speed the signals beside the track fly past too fast. That is why the ETCS system shows the driver all the information directly in the cab.
90357.m: At high speed ETCS shows the signals in the cab.

90358.q: Why should the journey time between two big hubs be just under an hour with Rail 2000?
a: So that the trains make the connections at both hubs
So that the staff can take a break
So that no goods trains can run
90358.e: At the hubs the trains meet on the hour. If the journey time between them is just under an hour, changing trains works at both stations.
90358.m: Journey times under Rail 2000 are matched to the hubs.

a: A description of an algorithm in simple, semi-formal language
A real programming language for robots
90459.e: Pseudocode describes the steps of an algorithm in a similar way to a program, but without the strict rules of a programming language. It is meant for people.
90459.m: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in simple, program-like language.

90460.q: Can a computer run pseudocode directly?
a: No, it first has to be translated into a programming language
Yes, but only on a mobile phone
No, it is only printed on paper
90460.e: Pseudocode has no fixed rules that a computer could understand. That is why you first translate it, for example, into Python or Scratch.
90460.m: Pseudocode is written for people and has to be translated first for the computer.

90461.q: Why do people often write pseudocode before they program?
a: To plan the steps without worrying about the exact way of writing them
So that the program runs faster
So that nobody can read the program
90461.e: With pseudocode you can first concentrate on the idea of the algorithm. The exact rules of the programming language only come afterwards.
90461.m: With pseudocode you plan the idea first and the exact code afterwards.

90462.q: Pseudocode: x ← 5, then x ← x + 3, then OUTPUT x. What is output?
90462.e: First x gets the value 5. Then 3 is added, so x = 8.
90462.m: In an assignment, the new value is calculated from the old value and stored.

90463.q: What does the arrow ← mean in many pseudocodes, for example in “points ← 0”?
a: A value is assigned to the variable
Something is drawn to the left
90463.e: The arrow stands for an assignment: the variable “points” gets the value 0. In Python you write points = 0.
90463.m: The arrow in pseudocode stands for an assignment to a variable.

90464.q: Pseudocode: sum ← 0, then FOR i FROM 1 TO 4: sum ← sum + i, then OUTPUT sum. What is output?
90464.e: The loop adds up 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. That gives 10.
90464.m: With a counting loop you can add up many numbers one after another.

90465.q: Pseudocode: number ← 7. IF number MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT “even” ELSE OUTPUT “odd”. What is output?
90465.e: MOD 2 gives the remainder when dividing by 2. For 7 the remainder is 1, so the condition is false and the ELSE part is carried out.
90465.m: With the remainder when dividing by 2 you can tell even and odd numbers apart.

90466.q: Pseudocode: a ← 3, b ← 5, then a ← b, then b ← a. What values do a and b have at the end?
90466.e: After a ← b, a = 5 and the old value 3 is lost. Then b gets the value of a, so 5 again.
90466.m: To swap two variables you usually need a helper variable.

90467.q: Pseudocode: x ← 3. WHILE x < 20: x ← x · 2. Then OUTPUT x. What is output?
90467.e: x is doubled: 3, 6, 12, 24. At 24 the condition x < 20 is false, so the loop ends.
90467.m: A while loop checks its condition before every run.

a: To show the steps of a program clearly
90468.e: A structogram uses blocks to show which steps a program carries out in sequence, in branches and in loops. It is also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram after its inventors.
90468.m: A structogram shows the steps of a program.

90469.q: Which other diagram also shows the steps of a program graphically, but with arrows?
90469.e: Structograms and flowcharts both show the steps of programs. The flowchart connects the steps with arrows, the structogram stacks blocks.
90469.m: Structograms and flowcharts show the steps of programs.

90470.q: Which basic shapes is a structogram made of?
a: Rectangles placed one below the other
90470.e: A structogram consists of rectangular blocks. The instructions are carried out in order from top to bottom.
90470.m: A structogram consists of rectangular blocks that you read from top to bottom.

90471.q: What is there not in a structogram, unlike in a flowchart?
a: Arrows that jump back and forth anywhere
90471.e: In a structogram the order is fixed by the arrangement of the blocks. Jumps anywhere, as in a flowchart, are not possible.

90472.q: How is a branch (if, then, else) shown in a structogram?
a: With a triangle at the top and two columns for yes and no
With a circle in the middle
90472.e: At the top is the condition in a field with triangles. Below it the block divides into a yes column and a no column.
90472.m: A branch in a structogram divides into a yes column and a no column.

90473.q: How do you recognise a loop in a structogram?
a: A block encloses the repeated instructions from the left
Two blocks stand side by side
90473.e: In a loop the condition is at the top, and a wide border encloses the instructions that are repeated. This shows what belongs to the loop.
90473.m: In a structogram the loop block encloses all the repeated instructions.

90474.q: A structogram contains: number ← 4, then “repeat 3 times: number ← number + 2”, then “output number”. What is output?
90474.e: The number starts at 4 and is increased by 2 three times: 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10.
90474.m: The blocks of a structogram are worked through in order.

90475.q: What are instructions called that simply stand one below the other in a structogram and are carried out one after another?
90475.e: A sequence is a series of instructions without a condition. It is carried out exactly once from top to bottom.
90475.m: A sequence is a series of instructions that are carried out one after another.

90476.q: Why is bubble sort called that?
a: Large values rise like bubbles to the end
It was invented by Mr Bubble
90476.e: In every pass, the large values move step by step towards the end, like rising air bubbles.
90476.m: In bubble sort the large values rise like bubbles to the end of the list.

90477.q: How many comparisons does bubble sort make in one pass through a list of 6 numbers?
90477.e: Two neighbours are always compared: place 1 with 2, 2 with 3 and so on up to 5 with 6. That makes 5 comparisons.
90477.m: With n numbers, bubble sort makes n minus 1 comparisons per pass.

90478.q: When can bubble sort stop sorting early?
a: When nothing was swapped in a pass
When the first number is a 1
When the list has an even number of numbers
90478.e: If there is no swap in a whole pass, the list is already sorted. More passes are then not needed.
90478.m: If there is no swap in a pass, the list is fully sorted.

90479.q: Bubble sort sorts the list 3, 2, 1 in ascending order. How many swaps are needed in total?
90479.e: 3, 2, 1 becomes 2, 3, 1 and then 2, 1, 3. In the second pass 2, 1, 3 becomes 1, 2, 3. That makes 3 swaps.
90479.m: The more jumbled a list is, the more bubble sort has to swap.

90480.q: What is the maximum number of passes bubble sort needs for 5 numbers so that the list is definitely sorted?
90480.e: After every pass at least one more number is in the right place. With 5 numbers, 4 passes are enough, because then the last one is in the right place too.
90480.m: With n numbers, bubble sort needs at most n minus 1 passes.

90481.q: How many comparisons does bubble sort make in total for 4 numbers if it does all the passes and leaves out the finished part at the end each time?
90481.e: The first pass needs 3 comparisons, the second 2 and the third 1. Together that makes 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
90481.m: Bubble sort compares one pair fewer in every pass.

90482.q: Why is bubble sort hardly ever used for very large amounts of data?
a: It needs a great many comparisons and swaps
It only sorts in descending order
90482.e: With twice as many numbers, bubble sort needs about four times as many comparisons. For large lists there are much faster methods.
90482.m: Bubble sort is easy to understand, but too slow for large lists.

90483.q: How many swaps does bubble sort make with the already sorted list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
90483.e: All neighbours are already in the right order. That is why nothing is swapped.
90483.m: An already sorted list needs no swaps.

90484.q: What is always true of the front part of the list in insertion sort?
90484.e: Insertion sort builds up a sorted part of the list at the front step by step. Each new element is inserted there in the right place.
90484.m: In insertion sort a sorted part grows at the front of the list.

90485.q: The sorted part is 2, 5, 7. Where does insertion sort insert the number 4 next?
90485.e: 4 is greater than 2 but smaller than 5. So it belongs between 2 and 5, giving 2, 4, 5, 7.
90485.m: Insertion sort inserts every new element exactly in the right place.

90486.q: Insertion sort sorts the list 4, 3, 1, 2. What does the list look like after the first two numbers are sorted?
90486.e: The 3 is inserted before the 4. The numbers 1 and 2 have not been dealt with yet and stay where they are.
90486.m: Insertion sort deals with the numbers in order from front to back.

90487.q: For which list does insertion sort work especially fast?
a: For a list sorted in reverse
For a list with only negative numbers
For a list with very large numbers
90487.e: If the list is almost sorted, hardly any element has to be moved far. Then insertion sort needs only a few steps.
90487.m: Insertion sort is very fast with almost sorted lists.

90488.q: For which starting list does insertion sort have to work the hardest?
a: For a list sorted in reverse
For a list of identical numbers
For a list with two numbers
90488.e: If the list is sorted in reverse, every new element has to move right to the front. This needs the most comparisons and moves.
90488.m: A list sorted in reverse is the worst case for insertion sort.

90489.q: How many comparisons does insertion sort need for the already sorted list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6?
90489.e: Every element from the second onwards is compared only once with its left neighbour and then stays put. That makes 5 comparisons.
90489.m: With a sorted list, insertion sort needs only one comparison per element.

90490.q: Insertion sort works like sorting playing cards in your hand. What do you do with each new card?
a: You slot it in at the right place
You always put it right at the back
You shuffle all the cards again
You swap it with the first card
90490.e: You compare the new card with the cards already sorted and slot it in where it belongs. That is exactly how insertion sort works.
90490.m: Insertion sort sorts like arranging playing cards.

90491.q: Does insertion sort need a second list of the same size as temporary storage?
a: No, it sorts directly in the existing list
90491.e: Insertion sort moves the elements within the existing list. This is called “in-place”; it needs only very little extra memory.
90491.m: Insertion sort sorts directly in the list and so saves memory.

90492.q: Roughly what share of the list is left after each comparison in a binary search?
90492.e: Binary search compares with the middle element and then rules out one half. This halves the search area with every step.
90492.m: Binary search halves the search area with every comparison.

90493.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs in a sorted list of 1000 entries?
90493.e: You can halve 1000 at most about ten times until only one entry is left, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1024. That is why 10 comparisons are enough.
90493.m: With 10 halvings you can find one entry among 1000.

90494.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs in a sorted list of one million entries?
90494.e: 2 to the power of 20 is a little more than a million. That is why 20 halvings are enough to find any entry.
90494.m: Even with a million entries, binary search needs only about 20 comparisons.

90495.q: A sorted list becomes twice as long. How many more comparisons does binary search need at most?
90495.e: One extra comparison halves the list that is twice as long back to the old length. After that everything works as before.
90495.m: A list twice as long costs binary search only one more comparison.

90496.q: Binary search looks for 7 in the list 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 29. After how many comparisons is the 7 found?
90496.e: First it compares with the middle, 15; 7 is smaller. In the left part 3, 7, 11 the middle is 7, so it is found after the second comparison.
90496.m: Binary search always jumps to the middle of the remaining area.

90497.q: The number you are looking for is smaller than the middle element of a list sorted in ascending order. Where does binary search continue?
90497.e: In a list sorted in ascending order the smaller numbers are at the front. So the back half can be ruled out.
90497.m: If the value you want is smaller than the middle, you keep searching at the front.

90498.q: How does binary search know that the number it is looking for is not in the list?
a: The first number is a zero
The middle is always the same
90498.e: With every comparison the search area shrinks. If it is empty and the number has not been found, it is not in the list.
90498.m: An empty search area means the value is missing.

90499.q: Which element does binary search compare the value it is looking for with at each step?
a: With the middle element of the search area
With the first element of the list
With the last element of the list
90499.e: The middle element splits the area into two halves of the same size. This lets you rule out half with one comparison.
90499.m: Binary search always compares with the middle of the search area.

90500.q: Which well-known algorithm finds the shortest path from a starting point in a network with distances?
90500.e: Starting from a start node, Dijkstra's algorithm gradually examines the nearest nodes. In this way it finds the shortest paths to all destinations.
90500.m: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in a network.

90501.q: A satnav is meant to find the fastest route, not the shortest. Which number does it then need for each road?
90501.e: For the fastest route, what matters is how long each section takes. A short road with a traffic jam can be slower than a detour.
90501.m: For the fastest route you calculate with travel times.

90502.q: Where are shortest-path algorithms often used in everyday life?
a: In navigation apps and route planners
90502.e: Navigation apps represent roads as a network with lengths or travel times. In it they look for the shortest or fastest route.
90502.m: Route planners use algorithms to find the shortest route.

90503.q: Routes: A to B 4 km, B to C 3 km, A to C 9 km, C to D 2 km, B to D 8 km. How long is the shortest route from A to D?
90503.e: A, B, C, D gives 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 km. A, C, D gives 11 km and A, B, D gives 12 km.
90503.m: To find the shortest route you compare the total distances of all possible routes.

90504.q: What does the weight of an edge tell you when searching for the shortest path?
a: How long or costly that connection is
90504.e: The edge weight can be a distance, a travel time or a price. The shortest path has the smallest total of weights.
90504.m: For the shortest path, what counts is the total of the edge weights.

90505.q: Is the route with the fewest edges always the shortest route?
a: No, what matters is the total of the weights
No, the longest route is always the fastest
90505.e: A detour over several short connections can be shorter than a single long connection. It is only always true if all edges are the same length.
90505.m: Several sections together can still be shorter than a single long one.

90506.q: In a network, every connection counts the same. Which route is then the shortest?
a: The route with the fewest connections
The route with the most connections
The route that was drawn first
The route via the largest node
90506.e: If all connections are the same length, you only count the steps. The fewer connections, the shorter the route.
90506.m: If all connections are the same length, the route with the fewest steps wins.

90507.q: Routes: A to B 2 km, B to C 2 km, A to C 5 km. How long is the shortest route from A to C?
90507.e: Via B it is 2 + 2 = 4 km. The direct route, at 5 km, is longer.
90507.m: A detour can be shorter than the direct route.

90508.q: A satnav learns about a traffic jam on the planned route. What is the sensible thing for it to do?
a: It looks for a new route with a shorter travel time
It drives through the jam anyway
It no longer shows a route
It always chooses the longest route
90508.e: The jam increases the travel time on this route. The satnav recalculates the fastest route with the new values.
90508.m: If travel times change, the satnav recalculates the route.

90509.q: A railway network is shown as a graph. What are the nodes?
90509.e: Nodes are the points of a graph, here the stations. The connections between them are the edges.
90509.m: In a graph, places are the nodes and connections are the edges.

90510.q: In a graph, the people in a class are the nodes. What could the edges be?
90510.e: An edge always connects two nodes. A friendship between two people is therefore a suitable edge.
90510.m: An edge always connects two nodes with each other.

90511.q: Which kind of graph do you need for a road network with one-way streets?
90511.e: In a directed graph every edge has a direction, like an arrow. This lets you show that a road can only be driven in one direction.
90511.m: Directed graphs have edges with a fixed direction.

90512.q: What is a graph called in which every edge carries a number such as a distance?
90512.e: The numbers on the edges are called weights. They can give, for example, kilometres, minutes or costs.
90512.m: In a weighted graph every edge carries a number.

90513.q: A node is connected by edges to 4 other nodes. What degree does this node have?
90513.e: The degree of a node is the number of edges that end at it. Here there are 4.
90513.m: The degree of a node counts its edges.

90514.q: 5 people all shake hands with each other once. How many edges does the matching graph have?
90514.e: Each of the 5 people shakes hands with 4 others, which gives 5 · 4 = 20. Because every handshake was counted twice, it is 20 : 2 = 10.
90514.m: In handshake problems you may only count each handshake once.

90515.q: What is a connected graph that contains no cycles called?
90515.e: In a tree there is always exactly one path between two nodes. Folder structures on a computer, for example, have this shape.
90515.m: A tree is a connected graph without cycles.

90516.q: What does it mean that a graph is connected?
a: From every node you can get to every other node via edges
All nodes have the same number of edges
Every node is directly connected to every other
90516.e: In a connected graph there is a path between any two nodes. This path may also lead via other nodes.
90516.m: In a connected graph every node can be reached from every other.

90517.q: What does decomposition mean in problem solving?
a: Splitting a big problem into smaller sub-problems
Passing a problem on to someone else
Copying out a problem several times
90517.e: Smaller sub-problems are clearer and easier to solve. Put together, their solutions give the solution to the whole problem.
90517.m: You solve big problems by breaking them down into small sub-problems.

90518.q: You want to program a game. What is decomposition?
a: Splitting the task into parts such as character, controls and points
Writing the whole game in one step
90518.e: Instead of solving everything at once, you split the game into small parts. Each part is simpler and can be programmed and tested separately.
90518.m: Breaking a problem down into parts is called decomposition.

90519.q: Which division is a sensible decomposition for planning a class party?
a: Invitations, food, games and tidying up
90519.e: Each of these sub-tasks can be planned and done on its own. Together they make up the whole party.
90519.m: A good decomposition gives sub-tasks that you can do separately.

90520.q: How are sub-problems often put into practice when programming?
90520.e: You write a separate function for each sub-problem. The main program then calls these functions in order.
90520.m: When programming, sub-problems often become separate functions.

90521.q: What advantage is there when a team breaks a program down into sub-problems?
a: Different people can work on parts at the same time
The program no longer needs electricity
90521.e: If the parts are clearly separated, each person can work on one part. Afterwards the parts are put together and tested together.
90521.m: Decomposition lets a team work on different parts at the same time.

90522.q: What is the approach called in which you start from the whole problem and break it down into finer and finer parts?
90522.e: With top-down you start at the top with the whole and refine it step by step. With bottom-up, on the other hand, you put small parts together into something bigger.
90522.m: Top-down means working from the whole to the details.

90523.q: When do you not need to break a sub-problem down any further?
a: When you can solve it directly
When it has more than three words
When it is at the end of the list
When it is already a week old
90523.e: Decomposition stops as soon as a sub-problem is simple enough to solve directly. Breaking it down further would only create work.
90523.m: You keep breaking things down until every sub-problem can be solved directly.

90524.q: A quiz program is to be programmed. Which is a sensible sub-problem?
a: Checking the answer and counting points
90524.e: Checking the answer and counting the points is a clearly separate part of the program. The other tasks have nothing to do with the program itself.
90524.m: A sub-problem is a clearly separate part of the actual task.

90525.q: What does abstraction mean in computing?
a: Leaving out unimportant details and keeping what matters
Making a program as complicated as possible
90525.e: With abstraction you concentrate on what is important for the task. Everything else you leave out on purpose.
90525.m: Abstraction means keeping what matters and leaving out what does not.

90526.q: Which map is a good example of abstraction?
a: A bus and tram network map
An aerial photo of the whole city
A video of a tram ride
90526.e: The network map only shows stops and lines, not the exact distances or buildings. That is enough to find the right connection.
90526.m: A network map only shows what you need for the journey.

90527.q: What is a simplified picture of reality that contains only the important features called?
90527.e: A model leaves out details on purpose. This makes it easier to understand a problem or calculate it with a computer.
90527.m: A model is a simplified picture of reality.

90528.q: You are planning a bike tour with a program. Which information is most important for this?
a: Distance and climb of the route
Colour of the houses along the way
Number of windows in the station
90528.e: For a bike tour, what mainly counts is the length and steepness of the route. The program can leave out the other details.
90528.m: Good abstraction keeps only the information that is needed for the task.

90529.q: You call print() in Python without knowing how the output works inside. What is this an example of?
90529.e: The function print() hides the complicated details. You only need to know what it does, not how it does it.
90529.m: Functions hide details and are therefore a form of abstraction.

90530.q: What is the part called through which you operate a device or program without knowing its inner workings?
90530.e: An interface sets out how you use something. In a car, for example, that is the steering wheel and pedals; you do not need to understand the engine.
90530.m: Through an interface you use something without knowing its inner workings.

90531.q: A turtle program is to draw any regular polygon with n corners. By how many degrees does the turtle turn after each side?
90531.e: After all n turns, the turtle has turned all the way round once, so by 360 degrees. With 6 corners, for example, that is 360 : 6 = 60 degrees.
90531.m: A program with a parameter solves many similar tasks at once.

90532.q: A game stores only the position, health points and equipment of a character. Which way of thinking is behind this?
90532.e: The game stores only what is needed for playing. All other details are left out on purpose.
90532.m: Through abstraction, programs store only the properties they need.

90533.q: What does pattern recognition mean in computational thinking?
a: Finding similarities and repetitions in problems
90533.e: If you notice that something repeats or is similar to a known problem, you can reuse known solutions. This saves time and work.
90533.m: Pattern recognition helps you reuse known solutions.

90534.e: Each number is three times as big as the one before. 54 · 3 = 162.
90534.m: In some sequences each number is multiplied by the same factor.

90535.e: Each number is doubled and then reduced by 1: 33 · 2 = 66, and 66 minus 1 is 65. You can also see it from the gaps 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, which double.
90535.m: If you look at the gaps in a sequence, you can often see the pattern.

90536.q: How does the letter sequence A, C, E, G, ... continue?
90536.e: One letter is skipped each time. So after G comes I.
90536.m: With letters, too, you can find patterns with fixed gaps.

90537.q: For 1 square made of matches you need 4 matches, for 2 squares in a row 7, for 3 squares 10. How many matches do you need for 10 squares in a row?
90537.e: Each extra square adds 3 matches. So you need 4 + 9 · 3 = 31 matches.
90537.m: If you recognise the pattern, you can work out large cases without a drawing.

90538.q: In a program, the same two commands appear eight times in a row. How can you simplify this?
90538.e: You spot the pattern of repetition and put the two commands into a loop that runs eight times. The program becomes shorter and clearer.
90538.m: You group repeated commands together in a loop.

90539.q: How does a spam filter recognise unwanted emails?
a: By typical patterns it has learnt from many example emails
It reads every email aloud to a person
It deletes all emails with pictures
It blocks all emails at the weekend
90539.e: Spam filters compare new emails with the features of known spam emails, for example certain words or senders. If the pattern matches, the email goes into the spam folder.
90539.m: Spam filters recognise unwanted emails by typical patterns.

90540.q: Which kind of pattern recognition do many smartphones use to unlock the screen?
90540.e: The phone compares the features of the face with stored data. If the pattern matches, the screen is unlocked.
90540.m: With face recognition the phone compares facial features with stored data.

90541.e: These are the square numbers 1 · 1, 2 · 2, 3 · 3 and so on. Next comes 6 · 6 = 36.
90541.m: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself.

90542.q: What is a common cause of an unintended infinite loop?
a: The variable in the condition is never changed in the loop
The program has too many comments
The variable has a long name
90542.e: If the variable in the condition never changes, the condition stays true for ever. Then the loop keeps running without end.
90542.m: A loop only ends if its condition changes at some point.

90543.q: Pseudocode: i ← 10. WHILE i ≠ 0: i ← i − 3. Why does this loop never end?
a: The condition is false from the start
90543.e: i takes the values 10, 7, 4, 1, -2, -5 and so on. It never hits 0 exactly, so the condition always stays true.
90543.m: A condition with “not equal to” can lead to an infinite loop if the value is skipped.

90544.q: Which Scratch block is deliberately an infinite loop?
90544.e: The “forever” block repeats its contents until the program is stopped. It is often used for games and animations.
90544.m: In Scratch, “forever” creates an intended infinite loop.

90545.q: Where is an infinite loop often intended?
90545.e: Traffic light control is meant to run through the same phases again and again as long as the system is switched on. An infinite loop makes sense for this.
90545.m: Control systems that are meant to run all the time use intended infinite loops.

90546.q: Which key combination usually stops a program that has hung in a console?
90546.e: In the console, Ctrl + C sends a stop signal to the running program. This lets you stop an infinite loop.
90546.m: In the console, Ctrl + C stops a running program.

90547.q: How can you often tell that a program is stuck in an infinite loop?
a: It stops responding and never finishes
It shows the right result straight away
90547.e: The program keeps calculating without end and never gets to the next step. Often it no longer responds to input.
90547.m: A program in an infinite loop never finishes.

90548.q: Can a program reliably predict for any other program whether it will run for ever?
a: No, Alan Turing proved this in 1936
90548.e: This question is called the halting problem. Alan Turing showed that there cannot be a program that answers it correctly for all programs.
90548.m: There is no program that can tell for every program whether it runs for ever.

90549.q: Which of these loops is an infinite loop (x starts at 1)?
90549.e: If x keeps getting bigger, x > 0 stays true for ever. In the other loops the condition becomes false after a few runs.
90549.m: A loop runs for ever if the variable moves away from the stopping condition.

90550.q: When programming a game, what is the “game loop”?
a: An intended infinite loop that reads input and redraws the picture
An error that makes the game crash
90550.e: The game loop runs through again and again during the whole game. In every run it processes input, moves characters and draws the picture.
90550.m: Games run in a game loop that repeats all the time.

90551.q: What does the running time of an algorithm describe?
a: How many steps or how much time it needs
How many lines the code has
How long the computer has been running
90551.e: The running time tells you how much work an algorithm takes. What matters most is how much it grows with larger inputs.
90551.m: The running time measures how much work an algorithm needs.

90552.q: Why do people often count calculation steps rather than seconds for running time?
a: Because computers do not know about time
90552.e: The same algorithm runs in fewer seconds on a fast computer. But the number of steps stays the same and is easier to compare.
90552.m: Calculation steps make algorithms comparable regardless of the computer.

90553.q: A list becomes twice as long. How does the number of comparisons in a linear search change in the worst case?
a: It becomes four times as big
It only goes up by one
90553.e: In the worst case, linear search checks every element once. Twice as many elements means twice as many comparisons.
90553.m: With linear running time, the work grows at the same rate as the input.

90554.q: A loop runs n times, and inside it a second loop also runs n times. How often is the inner part carried out when n = 20?
90554.e: For each of the 20 outer runs, the inner loop runs 20 times. That gives 20 · 20 = 400.
90554.m: Nested loops multiply the number of runs.

90555.q: What is the case called in which an algorithm needs the most steps?
90555.e: The worst case tells you the longest an algorithm can take. That way you know what you can rely on.
90555.m: The worst case shows the greatest possible work for an algorithm.

90556.q: Why does a search program usually need more time for a longer list?
a: Because it has to check more elements
90556.e: The more elements a list has, the more steps an algorithm needs to work through it. That is why the running time grows with the size of the input.
90556.m: More data usually means more calculation steps.

90557.q: In a class of 30 people, every person is to be compared with every other person exactly once. How many comparisons is that?
90557.e: Each person is compared with 29 others, which gives 30 · 29 = 870. Because every comparison is counted twice, it is 870 : 2 = 435.
90557.m: Comparing all pairs becomes a lot of work in large groups.

90558.q: A program tries out all the possibilities of a 4-digit number code. What is the maximum number of codes it has to test?
90558.e: Each of the 4 places can be a digit from 0 to 9. That gives 10 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 10,000 possibilities.
90558.m: Every extra digit makes trying them all ten times as much work.

90559.q: What colour are the tiny female flowers of the hazel?
90559.e: The female flowers of the hazel are very small and look like buds. Fine red threads stick out at the top.
90559.m: Female hazel flowers are small and red.

90560.q: What are the long, hanging flowers of the hazel called?
90560.e: The male flowers of the hazel hang from the twigs like little yellow sausages. They are called catkins.
90560.m: The hanging flowers of the hazel are called catkins.

90561.q: In which season does the hazel flower?
90561.e: The hazel flowers very early, often from January to March. It has no leaves yet then.
90561.m: The hazel flowers as early as late winter.

90562.q: What carries hazel pollen to other flowers?
90562.e: The hazel is pollinated by the wind. The wind carries the fine yellow pollen far away.
90562.m: The wind carries the hazel's pollen.

90563.q: Which animal likes to collect hazelnuts as a store in autumn?
90563.e: Squirrels hide hazelnuts in the ground. In winter they look for their stores again.

90564.e: Hazelnuts ripen from the end of August into autumn. Then they fall from the bush.

90565.q: Which small animal is named after the hazel?
90565.e: The hazel dormouse likes to eat hazelnuts. It hibernates for a long time.
90565.m: The hazel dormouse is named after the hazel.

90566.q: What can hazel pollen cause in some people?
90566.e: Hazel pollen flies early in the year. People with an allergy get hay fever from it.
90566.m: Hazel pollen can cause hay fever.

90567.q: What surrounds the kernel of a hazelnut?
90567.e: The edible kernel of the hazelnut is inside a hard, brown shell. You crack it with a nutcracker.
90567.m: The hazelnut has a hard shell.

90568.q: What colour are the flowers of the black elder?
90568.e: The elder has lots of small, creamy white flowers. They have a strong scent.

90569.e: Ripe elderberries are almost black with a purple sheen. That is where the name black elder comes from.

90570.q: What do people in Switzerland often call the elder?
90570.e: In Switzerland the elder is often called Holder. People talk about Holderblüten, for example, meaning elderflowers.
90570.m: In Switzerland the elder is often called Holder.

a: Yes, as many as you like
Yes, but only the green ones
90571.e: Raw elderberries can cause tummy ache and sickness. Cooking makes them safe to eat.

90572.q: When does the black elder flower?
90572.e: The elder flowers in late spring and early summer. The berries are then ripe in late summer.
90572.m: The elder flowers in May and June.

90573.q: What do the flower heads of the elder look like?
90573.e: Lots of small flowers sit together in a big, flat umbrella shape. It looks like a plate.
90573.m: Elderflowers form big, flat umbrella shapes.

90574.e: Young elder twigs are filled with soft, white pith. You can easily push it out.
90574.m: Elder twigs have soft, white pith.

90575.q: Which animals like to eat elderberries?
90575.e: Many birds such as blackbirds and starlings eat the berries. They spread the seeds in their droppings.

90576.q: What can you make from cooked elderberries?
90576.e: Elderberries are cooked and made into jam, jelly or juice.
90576.m: Cooked elderberries are made into jam.

90577.q: What does the hawthorn have on its twigs?
90577.e: The hawthorn has sharp thorns. They protect it from being eaten by animals.

90578.q: What colour are the fruits of the hawthorn in autumn?
90578.e: In autumn the hawthorn has small red fruits called haws. They look like tiny apples.
90578.m: The fruits of the hawthorn are red.

90579.q: In which season does the hawthorn flower?
90579.e: The hawthorn flowers in spring, usually in May. Then the shrub is full of white flowers.

90580.q: Which animals like to visit the flowers of the hawthorn?
90580.e: Bees, flies and beetles collect nectar and pollen. As they do, they pollinate the flowers.
90580.m: Insects like to visit the hawthorn's flowers.

90581.q: What is the hawthorn traditionally used for as a medicinal plant?
90581.e: Remedies for the heart are made from the leaves and flowers of the hawthorn. It is a well-known medicinal plant.
90581.m: The hawthorn is a medicinal plant for the heart.

90582.q: Who likes to eat the fruits of the hawthorn in winter?
90582.e: The fruits stay on the shrub for a long time. Thrushes and other birds find food there in winter.
90582.m: Birds eat hawthorn fruits in winter.

90583.q: Which plant family does the hawthorn belong to?
90583.e: Like the apple and the rose, the hawthorn belongs to the rose family. Its flowers have five petals.
90583.m: The hawthorn belongs to the rose family.

90584.q: Why do birds like to build nests in the hawthorn?
a: The thorns protect them from enemies
It is as warm there as in a house
90584.e: Cats and martens find it hard to get through the thorny branches. So nests and young birds are well protected.
90584.m: Thorns protect the bird nests in the hawthorn.

90585.q: What are the fruits of the blackthorn called?
90585.e: The blackthorn is also called the sloe bush. Its small, round fruits are called sloes.
90585.m: The fruits of the blackthorn are called sloes.

90586.e: Ripe sloes are bluish black. They have a pale, waxy coating.

90587.q: What is special about the blackthorn in spring?
a: It flowers before its leaves come out
90587.e: In March and April the blackthorn is full of white flowers. The leaves only grow afterwards.
90587.m: The blackthorn flowers before its leaves come.

90588.q: What do sloes taste like if you pick them early in autumn?
90588.e: Sloes are very sour and make your mouth pucker. That is why people hardly ever eat them raw.

90589.q: When do sloes become milder in taste?
90589.e: Frost makes the fruits softer and less bitter. That is why people often pick them late.

90590.q: Why is the sloe bush also called blackthorn?
a: Because it only flowers at night
Because it grows in the shade
90590.e: The twigs and bark of the shrub are very dark. It also has sharp thorns.

90591.q: How does the blackthorn like to spread?
90591.e: New shoots grow from the roots. Over time this creates a dense thicket.
90591.m: The blackthorn spreads with root suckers.

90592.q: Which fruit is the sloe related to?
90592.e: The sloe is a wild plum. It is related to damsons and plums.
90592.m: The sloe is related to the plum.

90593.q: In which month does the dog rose usually flower?
90593.e: The dog rose flowers in early summer, mainly in June. After that the fruits form.
90593.m: The dog rose flowers in June.

90594.q: What colour are the flowers of the dog rose usually?
90594.e: The flowers of the dog rose are usually pale pink to white. They have a light scent.
90594.m: The dog rose usually has light pink flowers.

90595.q: How many petals does a dog rose flower have?
90595.e: Wild roses like the dog rose have simple flowers with five petals.
90595.m: The dog rose has five petals.

90596.q: What can you make from the dried fruits of the dog rose?
90596.e: The fruits are dried and used to make tea. The tea is red and slightly sour.
90596.m: Tea is made from the fruits of the dog rose.

90597.q: Which vitamin is found in large amounts in the fruits of the dog rose?
90597.e: The fruits of the dog rose contain lots of vitamin C. They often have more of it than lemons.
90597.m: Dog rose fruits contain lots of vitamin C.

90598.q: In German the dog rose is also called “hedge rose”. Why?
a: Because it often grows in hedges
Because it is used to make tea
Because it only grows in gardens
90598.e: The dog rose often grows in hedges. That is why it is also called hedge rose in German.
90598.m: The dog rose often grows in hedges.

90599.q: What does the dog rose have on its shoots?
90599.e: The dog rose has curved prickles. With them it holds on to other plants.
90599.m: The dog rose has curved prickles.

90600.q: What kind of rose is the dog rose?
90600.e: The dog rose grows wild in hedges and at the edges of woods. It is the most common wild rose where we live.
90600.m: The dog rose is a wild rose.

90601.e: Ripe blackberries are shiny black. Only then do they taste sweet.

90602.q: What colour is a blackberry shortly before it is ripe?
90602.e: Blackberries are green at first, then red and finally black. Red blackberries are still sour.
90602.m: Unripe blackberries are green at first and then red.

90603.e: Blackberries ripen in late summer. You can often find them until well into autumn.
90603.m: Blackberries are picked in late summer.

90604.q: Which berry is the blackberry closely related to?
90604.e: The blackberry and the raspberry belong to the same plant genus. Both have fruits made of lots of little balls.
90604.m: The blackberry is related to the raspberry.

90605.q: What is a single blackberry made of?
90605.e: A blackberry is an aggregate fruit. Each little ball contains a tiny pip.
90605.m: A blackberry is made of lots of little balls.

a: As a mushroom on the ground
90606.e: Blackberries form long, prickly shoots. They quickly grow into a dense tangle.

90607.q: What colour are the flowers of the bramble?
90607.e: The bramble flowers white or pale pink in summer. The berries grow from the flowers.
90607.m: The bramble flowers white to pink.

90608.q: Which part of the bramble is often used to make tea?
90608.e: Young bramble leaves are dried. A mild tea is made from them.
90608.m: Tea is made from bramble leaves.

90609.q: Which forest animal likes to eat bramble leaves in winter?
90609.e: Bramble leaves often stay green into the winter. Roe deer find food in them when little else is growing.
90609.m: Roe deer like to eat bramble leaves in winter.

90610.q: What colour are the berries of privet?
90610.e: In autumn privet has shiny black berries. They often hang on into the winter.

90611.e: Privet berries are poisonous for people. You should never eat them.

90612.q: What colour are the flowers of privet?
90612.e: Privet flowers in early summer with small white flowers. They grow together in clusters.

90613.q: What do privet flowers smell like?
90613.e: The flowers have a strong, sweetish scent. It attracts lots of insects.
90613.m: Privet flowers have a strong scent.

90614.q: What is privet often planted for in gardens?
90614.e: Privet copes very well with being cut. That is why it is a popular hedge plant.
90614.m: Privet is a popular garden hedge.

90615.q: What happens to many privet leaves in winter?
a: They stay green for a long time
They fall off as early as July
90615.e: Privet often keeps its leaves well into the winter. In mild winters it stays almost completely green.
90615.m: Privet often stays green for a long time in winter.

90616.q: A big green caterpillar likes to eat privet leaves. What does it turn into later?
90616.e: The caterpillar of the privet hawk-moth eats privet leaves. Later it becomes a pupa, and a big moth hatches from it.
90616.m: The caterpillar turns into a moth.

90617.q: Who eats privet berries in winter?
90617.e: The berries are poisonous for people. But thrushes and other birds eat them in winter.
90617.m: Birds eat privet berries in winter.

90618.q: What colour are the fruits of the spindle tree?
90618.e: In autumn the fruits of the spindle tree glow pink to purplish red. You can see them from far away.
90618.m: The fruits of the spindle tree are pink.

90619.q: What colour is the covering around the seeds of the spindle tree?
90619.e: When the fruit splits open, you can see the seeds. They sit inside an orange coat.
90619.m: The seeds of the spindle tree have an orange coat.

90620.q: What is true of the fruits of the spindle tree?
90620.e: All parts of the spindle tree are poisonous, especially the seeds. You must never eat the colourful fruits.
90620.m: The spindle tree is very poisonous.

90621.q: In German the spindle tree is called “priest's little hat”. What does the shape of its fruit remind people of?
90621.e: The fruit looks like an old kind of cap worn by Catholic priests. In the past priests were also called “Pfaffen” in German.
90621.m: The fruit of the spindle tree looks like a priest's cap.

90622.q: Who likes to eat the seeds of the spindle tree without getting ill?
90622.e: The spindle tree is poisonous for people and many animals. But birds such as the robin like to eat the seeds. That is why it is also called robin's bread in German.
90622.m: Birds eat the seeds of the spindle tree.

90623.q: What kind of plant is the spindle tree?
90623.e: The spindle tree is a shrub. It often grows at the edges of woods and in hedges.
90623.m: The spindle tree is a shrub.

90624.q: What colour do many leaves of the spindle tree turn in autumn?
90624.e: In autumn many leaves turn bright red. Together with the fruits, the shrub is very colourful.
90624.m: The spindle tree has red leaves in autumn.

90625.q: What was the wood of the spindle tree used for in the past?
90625.e: The hard, fine wood was good for making hand spindles. That is why the shrub is called the spindle tree.
90625.m: Spindles were made from spindle wood.

90626.q: What colour are the flowers of the cornelian cherry?
90626.e: The cornelian cherry has golden yellow flowers. The small flowers grow in clusters on the bare twigs.

90627.q: When does the cornelian cherry flower?
a: As early as February and March
90627.e: The cornelian cherry is one of the first shrubs to flower. The flowers come before the leaves.
90627.m: The cornelian cherry flowers very early in the year.

90628.q: What colour are the ripe fruits of the cornelian cherry?
90628.e: The fruits are oval and shiny red. They look a little like small cherries.
90628.m: The fruits of the cornelian cherry are red.

90629.q: Can you eat the fruits of the cornelian cherry?
90629.e: The fruits are edible and taste sourish. When fully ripe they are sweeter, and people make jam from them.
90629.m: The fruits of the cornelian cherry are edible.

90630.q: What else is the cornelian cherry called in German-speaking Switzerland?
90630.e: In German-speaking Switzerland the cornelian cherry is also called Tierlibaum. In Austria it is called Dirndlstrauch.
90630.m: In Switzerland the cornelian cherry is also called Tierlibaum.

90631.q: What is the wood of the cornelian cherry like?
90631.e: The wood of the cornelian cherry is very hard and heavy. It is hard to split.
90631.m: The cornelian cherry has very hard wood.

90632.q: Why is the cornelian cherry important for bees?
a: It flowers when there is still little food
It has water in its flowers
It builds honeycombs for the bees
90632.e: In early spring hardly anything is flowering yet. The cornelian cherry is then one of the first food plants for bees.
90632.m: The cornelian cherry is bee food early in the year.

90633.q: Is the cornelian cherry a real cherry?
a: No, its fruits only look similar
Yes, it is a sour cherry
Yes, it is a wild sweet cherry
Yes, it is a small dwarf cherry
90633.e: The cornelian cherry is not a real cherry. Its red fruits only look a bit like cherries.
90633.m: The cornelian cherry is not a real cherry.

90634.q: What colour are the twigs of the common dogwood often in winter?
90634.e: In winter, when there are no leaves, the twigs often glow red. They are especially bright on the sunny side.
90634.m: The common dogwood has red twigs in winter.

90635.q: What colour are the flowers of the common dogwood?
90635.e: The common dogwood flowers in early summer. Lots of small white flowers grow in flat clusters.

90636.q: What colour are the fruits of the common dogwood?
90636.e: In autumn the shrub has small, bluish black fruits. Birds like to eat them.
90636.m: The fruits of the common dogwood are bluish black.

90637.q: Should you eat the fruits of the common dogwood raw?
90637.e: The raw fruits taste bitter and do not agree with people. It is better to leave them for the birds.
90637.m: You do not eat the fruits of the common dogwood raw.

90638.q: What do you see if you carefully pull a leaf of the common dogwood apart?
90638.e: When you pull it apart, the two halves of the leaf stay joined by fine white threads. This is a good way to recognise dogwood.
90638.m: Dogwood leaves have fine threads in their veins.

90639.q: The German name of the dogwood, “Hartriegel”, contains the word for “hard”. What does it refer to?
90639.e: The shrub has very hard wood. In the past, tool handles, for example, were made from it.

90640.q: How do the veins run on a leaf of the common dogwood?
a: In curves towards the tip of the leaf
Like a star from the stalk
Not at all, it has none
90640.e: The side veins curve forward towards the tip of the leaf. This is a good way to recognise it.

90641.q: Where does the common dogwood like to grow?
a: At the edges of woods and in hedges
In the middle of the water
90641.e: The common dogwood is a common shrub at the edges of woods and in hedges. It likes sun and partial shade.
90641.m: The common dogwood likes to grow in hedges.

90642.q: What does the hedgehog have on its back?
90642.e: The hedgehog's back is covered with sharp spines. They protect it from enemies.
90642.m: The hedgehog has spines on its back.

90643.q: About how many spines does an adult hedgehog have?
90643.e: An adult hedgehog has about 6,000 to 8,000 spines. They are hollow and light.

90644.q: When is the hedgehog mainly out and about?
a: Only in the rain during the day
90644.e: The hedgehog is a nocturnal animal. During the day it sleeps hidden in leaves or in the hedge.
90644.m: The hedgehog looks for food at night.

90645.q: What does a hedgehog mainly eat?
90645.e: The hedgehog eats beetles, caterpillars, earthworms and slugs. It finds them with its good nose.
90645.m: The hedgehog eats beetles and worms.

90646.q: Where does a hedgehog often sleep through the winter?
90646.e: The hedgehog builds its winter nest from dry leaves and grass. It is often under a hedge or a pile of branches.
90646.m: The hedgehog spends the winter in a nest of leaves.

90647.q: Why is a hedge good for the hedgehog?
90647.e: The hedgehog can hide in the hedge. Lots of beetles and worms also live under the shrubs.
90647.m: The hedgehog finds shelter and food in the hedge.

90648.e: The red-backed shrike is a songbird, a bit bigger than a sparrow. It likes to live in thorny hedges.
90648.m: The red-backed shrike is a bird.

90649.q: What does the red-backed shrike do with its prey?
a: It buries it in the ground
It hides it in the water
It puts it in its nest under leaves
90649.e: The red-backed shrike spikes insects and other prey on thorns. In the past people believed it caught nine animals first, which is why its German name means nine-killer. In English shrikes are also called butcher birds.
90649.m: The red-backed shrike spikes its prey on thorns.

90650.q: Why does the red-backed shrike spike its prey?
a: It makes a store of food
It dries it for the nest
90650.e: In bad weather there are few insects. Then the shrike eats from its spiked stores.
90650.m: The red-backed shrike makes food stores.

90651.q: What does the male red-backed shrike have on its face?
90651.e: The male has a black stripe across its eyes. It looks like a mask.
90651.m: The male red-backed shrike has a black mask.

90652.q: Where does the red-backed shrike spend the winter?
90652.e: The red-backed shrike is a migrating bird. In autumn it flies all the way to southern Africa.
90652.m: The red-backed shrike spends the winter in Africa.

90653.q: When does the red-backed shrike come back to us in spring?
90653.e: The red-backed shrike comes back late, usually at the beginning of May. By then there are enough big insects.
90653.m: The red-backed shrike comes back in May.

90654.q: What does the red-backed shrike mainly eat?
90654.e: It mainly hunts beetles, bumblebees and grasshoppers. Sometimes it also catches a mouse.
90654.m: The red-backed shrike mainly eats big insects.

90655.q: Where does the red-backed shrike build its nest?
a: In the reeds by the water
90655.e: It likes to build its nest in blackthorn, roses or brambles. The thorns protect the young.
90655.m: The red-backed shrike nests in thorny shrubs.

90656.q: Roughly how much of the Earth's surface is covered by sea?
90656.e: Around 71 per cent of the Earth is covered by sea. That is why the Earth is also called the blue planet.
90656.m: More than two thirds of the Earth is sea.

90657.q: What in the sea produces about half the oxygen we breathe?
90657.e: Tiny algae in the sea make oxygen just like plants. They are called phytoplankton.
90657.m: Tiny algae in the sea make a lot of oxygen.

90658.q: What is it like in the deep sea?
90658.e: Sunlight does not reach down into the deep sea. The water there is only a few degrees warm.
90658.m: The deep sea is dark and cold.

90659.q: What is the deepest place in the oceans called?
90659.e: The Mariana Trench lies in the Pacific. That is where the sea is deepest.
90659.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in the sea.

90660.q: Roughly how deep is the Mariana Trench?
90660.e: At its deepest point, the trench is almost 11,000 metres deep. That is about 11 kilometres.
90660.m: The Mariana Trench is about 11 kilometres deep.

90661.q: What are hot springs on the deep seabed that pour out dark water called?
90661.e: On the seabed there are springs that pour out very hot, dark water. They are called black smokers, and special animals live around them.
90661.m: Black smokers are hot springs in the deep sea.

90662.q: What is especially great in the deep sea?
90662.e: There is a huge amount of water above the deep sea. It presses with enormous force on everything down there.
90662.m: In the deep sea, the water presses very hard.

90663.q: Which Swiss man was one of the first to dive to the deepest point in the sea in 1960?
90663.e: In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench with the American Don Walsh. No one had ever managed that before.
90663.m: Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960.

90664.q: Do we already know all the animals of the deep sea?
a: Yes, there are no animals there
90664.e: The deep sea is hard to explore. Researchers keep discovering new animal species there.
90664.m: There are still many unknown animals in the deep sea.

90665.q: Which large whale dives very deep to hunt squid?
90665.e: The sperm whale dives more than 1000 metres deep. There it hunts squid.
90665.m: The sperm whale hunts squid in the deep sea.

90666.q: Where is the largest coral reef in the world?
90666.e: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of Australia. It is so big that it can be seen from space.
90666.m: The largest coral reef is off Australia.

90667.q: In which water do coral reefs grow best?
90667.e: Reef corals need warm, clear and fairly shallow sea water. That is why they are found mainly in the tropics.
90667.m: Coral reefs grow in warm seas.

90668.q: What happens to corals when the sea gets too warm?
90668.e: When the water is too warm, corals lose their colourful algae. Then they turn white, which is called coral bleaching.
90668.m: Water that is too warm makes corals bleach.

90669.q: Which orange and white fish lives in the reef among sea anemones?
90669.e: The clownfish lives among the tentacles of sea anemones. A layer of slime protects it from their stings.
90669.m: The clownfish lives in sea anemones.

90670.q: How fast does a coral reef grow?
90670.e: Many corals grow only a few millimetres to centimetres a year. A large reef takes thousands of years.

90671.q: What lives inside corals and helps feed them?
90671.e: Tiny algae live inside the corals. They make food from sunlight and give the corals their colours.
90671.m: Tiny algae help feed the corals.

90672.q: Why are coral reefs also called the rainforests of the sea?
a: A great many animal species live there
90672.e: A great many different animals live in coral reefs. That is similar to the rainforest on land.
90672.m: A great many animal species live in a coral reef.

90673.e: A submarine is a boat that travels under the sea. It can dive and move along underwater.

90674.q: What does a submarine let into its tanks in order to dive?
90674.e: When water flows into the tanks, the submarine becomes heavier. Then it sinks down.
90674.m: With water in its tanks, the submarine dives.

90675.q: How does a submarine get back to the surface?
a: Air pushes the water out of the tanks
It waits for a big wave
A ship pulls it up on a rope
90675.e: Compressed air pushes the water out of the tanks. The submarine becomes lighter and rises.
90675.m: Air in the tanks makes the submarine rise.

90676.q: What do you use to look above the water from a submerged submarine?
90676.e: A periscope sticks out of the water and uses mirrors to show what is happening above.
90676.m: You look out of a submarine through a periscope.

90677.q: What was the name of the submersible that dived to the deepest point in 1960?
90677.e: The submersible Trieste was designed by Auguste Piccard. In 1960 it reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
90677.m: The Trieste dived to the deepest point in 1960.

90678.q: In which Swiss lake did a tourist submarine operate from 1964?
90678.e: At the 1964 national exhibition in Lausanne, the submarine “Auguste Piccard” took visitors into Lake Geneva. It was the world's first passenger submarine.
90678.m: A tourist submarine operated in Lake Geneva in 1964.

90679.q: What do research submersibles use to collect samples from the seabed?
90679.e: Research submersibles have a robotic arm. With it they carefully pick up stones and animals.
90679.m: Submersibles collect samples with a robotic arm.

90680.q: What does a diver usually breathe from their tank?
90680.e: A diving tank usually contains completely normal air. It is tightly compressed so that a lot fits in.

90681.q: What does a diver wear on their feet?
90681.e: With flippers you move much faster underwater. They look like duck feet.
90681.m: Divers wear flippers on their feet.

90682.q: Why does a diver wear a mask over their eyes?
a: So they do not get cold
90682.e: Without a mask everything looks blurry underwater. With air in front of your eyes, you can see clearly.
90682.m: With a diving mask you can see clearly underwater.

90683.q: What is a neoprene wetsuit for?
90683.e: Water cools the body down quickly. A neoprene suit keeps the diver warm.

90684.q: What is an important rule in diving?
90684.e: Divers always go into the water with a buddy. That way they can help each other.

90685.q: Why must a diver come up slowly?
90685.e: If you come up too fast, bubbles form in the blood. That can make you ill.

90686.q: Which Frenchman became famous for films about the underwater world?
90686.e: Jacques-Yves Cousteau explored the oceans and made many films. He also helped develop modern diving equipment.
90686.m: Jacques-Yves Cousteau showed the underwater world in films.

90687.e: You cannot speak underwater. That is why divers use agreed hand signals.
90687.m: Divers talk underwater with hand signals.

90688.q: Roughly how long can a blue whale grow?
90688.e: Large blue whales grow up to about 30 metres long. That is as long as two or three buses in a row.
90688.m: A blue whale grows up to about 30 metres long.

90689.q: What does a blue whale have in its mouth instead of teeth?
90689.e: Baleen is made of long horny plates like a comb. The whale uses it to sieve its food out of the water.
90689.m: The blue whale has baleen instead of teeth.

90690.q: What does a young blue whale drink?
90690.e: The baby whale drinks its mother's rich, fatty milk. It grows very fast on it.
90690.m: A young blue whale drinks milk.

90691.q: How do blue whales communicate over long distances?
90691.e: Blue whales are among the loudest animals in the world. Their deep calls can be heard very far away in the sea.
90691.m: Blue whales call with loud, deep sounds.

90692.q: What colour is a blue whale?
90692.e: The blue whale is bluish grey with pale spots. Underwater it often looks truly blue.
90692.m: The blue whale is bluish grey.

90693.q: What does an octopus have on its arms?
90693.e: There are many suckers on its arms. The octopus uses them to hold on to prey and to feel and taste.
90693.m: Octopuses have suckers on their arms.

90694.q: What does an octopus squirt out when in danger?
90694.e: The octopus releases a dark cloud of ink. Behind it, it can quickly escape.
90694.m: Octopuses escape behind a cloud of ink.

90695.q: How does an octopus camouflage itself?
90695.e: Octopuses can change colour and pattern in a flash. That way they look like stones or sand.
90695.m: Octopuses camouflage themselves by changing colour.

90696.q: What can an octopus learn to do, for example?
a: Open a jar with a lid
90696.e: Octopuses are thought to be very clever. In experiments they have learned to open screw-top jars.

90697.q: Why can an octopus fit through very narrow gaps?
90697.e: An octopus's body is soft and has no skeleton. So it can make itself very thin.

90698.q: What does an octopus use to break up its prey?
90698.e: In the middle, between its arms, the octopus has a hard beak. With it, it can even crack crabs and mussels.

90699.q: What are jellyfish mostly made of?
90699.e: Jellyfish are about 98 per cent water. That is why they are so see-through and soft.

90700.e: The jellyfish squeezes its bell together and pushes water out. This moves it forwards.
90700.m: Jellyfish swim by squeezing their bell together.

90701.q: Which sea animal likes to eat jellyfish?
90701.e: Sea turtles like eating jellyfish. Sadly, they sometimes mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.

a: No, it has no bones and no fins
Yes, it is a small fish
Yes, it is a baby fish
90702.e: Jellyfish are neither fish nor plants. They are animals without bones, like corals and sea anemones.

90703.q: Is it OK to touch a dead jellyfish on the beach?
a: Yes, it is even as soft as cotton wool
Yes, but only with wet hands
90703.e: Even dead jellyfish can still sting. So it is better not to touch them.

90704.q: Are there jellyfish in Swiss lakes too?
a: Only in the ice in winter
90704.e: The freshwater jellyfish lives in some Swiss lakes. It grows to about 2 centimetres at most and is harmless to people.
90704.m: There are small jellyfish in Swiss lakes too.

90705.q: What can a starfish do if it loses an arm?
a: It lives without the arm for ever
It swaps it with another one
90705.e: Starfish can grow back lost arms. But it takes a long time.

90706.q: What does a starfish use to move?
90706.e: On the underside of its arms, a starfish has hundreds of tiny feet. With them it crawls slowly forwards.
90706.m: Starfish crawl on lots of tube feet.

90707.q: What does a starfish like to eat?
90707.e: The starfish pulls mussels open with its little feet. Then it eats the soft animal inside.

90708.q: Where does a starfish have simple eyes?
a: At the tips of its arms
90708.e: There is a small eye at the tip of each arm. With it, the starfish can tell light from dark.
90708.m: Starfish have eyes at the tips of their arms.

90709.q: What flows through many tubes in a starfish instead of blood?
90709.e: A starfish does not have blood like ours. Sea water flows through its body in fine tubes.
90709.m: Sea water flows through a starfish.

90710.q: What happens at the seaside at low tide?
90710.e: At low tide the sea level falls. The water draws back from the beach.
90710.m: At low tide the sea goes out.

90711.q: What happens at the seaside at high tide?
90711.e: At high tide the sea level rises. The water comes far up the beach.
90711.m: At high tide the water rises.

90712.e: The Moon pulls on the Earth's water with its gravity. This creates the tides.

90713.q: Roughly how often is there a high tide in one day?
90713.e: On most coasts there are two high tides and two low tides a day. They take turns.
90713.m: There are about two high tides a day.

90714.q: What is the seabed on the North Sea coast that lies dry at low tide called?
90714.e: At low tide you can walk around on the mudflats. Worms, mussels and crabs live there.
90714.m: At low tide the mudflats on the North Sea lie dry.

90715.q: Can you notice the tides on Lake Geneva?
90715.e: Tides are only clearly noticeable in the great oceans. In lakes like Lake Geneva, you hardly notice them.
90715.m: There are hardly any tides in Swiss lakes.

90716.q: When are the tides especially strong?
a: At full moon and new moon
90716.e: At full moon and new moon, the Sun and Moon pull in a line. Then the difference is greatest.
90716.m: The tides are strong at full moon and new moon.

90717.q: Roughly how long does it take from high tide to low tide?
90717.e: It takes just over 6 hours from high water to low water. Then the water rises again.
90717.m: It takes about 6 hours from high tide to low tide.

90718.q: What does sea water taste like?
90718.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in sea water. That is why it tastes salty.

90719.q: Can you drink sea water when you are thirsty?
a: No, it makes you even thirstier
Yes, but only in the morning
90719.e: The body needs a lot of water to get rid of the salt again. That is why sea water makes you even thirstier.
90719.m: Sea water does not quench your thirst.

90720.q: Where does most of the salt in the sea come from?
90720.e: Rain and rivers dissolve tiny amounts of salt from rocks. Over a very long time, the rivers carry it into the sea.
90720.m: The salt in the sea comes from rocks.

90721.q: Which sea in Europe is only slightly salty?
90721.e: Many rivers with fresh water flow into the Baltic Sea. That is why its water is much less salty than ocean water.
90721.m: The Baltic Sea is only slightly salty.

90722.q: In which salty body of water can you float on top without any effort?
90722.e: The Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than normal sea water. That is why you do not sink there.
90722.m: You do not sink in the Dead Sea.

90723.q: Where does the salt that is taken from the ground in Switzerland come from?
90723.e: A very long time ago, a sea covered parts of Switzerland. When it evaporated, salt was left behind in the ground.
90723.m: Swiss salt comes from an ancient sea.

90724.q: At what temperature does sea water freeze?
90724.e: Salt in water lowers the freezing point. Sea water only freezes at about minus 2 degrees.
90724.m: Sea water only freezes below 0 degrees.

90725.q: What does the anglerfish use its glow for?
90725.e: The anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head, like a fishing rod. Small fish swim towards the light and get eaten.
90725.m: The anglerfish lures prey with light.

90726.q: What is it called when living things make their own light?
90726.e: Many deep sea animals make their own light. This is called bioluminescence.
90726.m: Light made by living things is called bioluminescence.

90727.q: What is it called when the sea glows bluish in the waves at night?
90727.e: Tiny living things in the water light up when the water moves. This is called sea sparkle.
90727.m: In sea sparkle, tiny living things in the water glow.

90728.q: What makes the light in the glowing lure of many anglerfish?
90728.e: Tiny bacteria that glow live in the lure. In return, the fish gives them a place to live.
90728.m: Glowing bacteria make the anglerfish's light.

90729.q: What colour is the light of many deep sea animals usually?
90729.e: Blue light travels furthest in water. That is why many deep sea animals glow blue.
90729.m: Many deep sea animals glow blue.

90730.q: Which deep sea fish is named after a lamp?
90730.e: Lanternfish have lots of small glowing spots on their bodies. They are among the most common fish in the deep sea.
90730.m: The lanternfish has glowing spots on its body.

90731.q: Why do many deep sea fish have a huge mouth?
a: They need a lot of air
90731.e: There is little to eat in the deep sea. With a big mouth they can grab any prey, even large prey.
90731.m: Deep sea fish often have a big mouth.

90732.q: Which animal on land also makes its own light?
90732.e: Like deep sea fish, glow-worms make their own light. You can see them glowing on summer nights.
90732.m: Glow-worms make their own light too.

90733.q: According to Swiss advice, how often at most should you eat meat?
90733.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise eating meat and sausage at most 2 to 3 times a week. On the other days you can have eggs, fish or tofu, for example.
90733.m: Meat is eaten only a few times a week.

90734.q: What is at the very top of the food pyramid?
90734.e: The top is very narrow. Sweet things and salty snacks should only be eaten rarely and in small amounts.
90734.m: The top of the pyramid shows what you should eat only rarely.

90735.q: Why is the food pyramid so wide at the bottom?
a: You should eat most of that
You should eat least of that
That is where the most expensive food is
90735.e: The wider a level is, the more of it you should eat or drink. At the top the pyramid gets narrow; that is where the things you need only a little of are.
90735.m: Wide levels mean a lot, narrow levels mean a little.

90736.q: How many portions of cereals or potatoes does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90736.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise 3 portions a day from this group, for example bread, pasta, rice or potatoes.
90736.m: Three portions of cereals or potatoes a day give you energy.

90737.q: How many portions of dairy products does the Swiss food pyramid recommend per day?
90737.e: 2 to 3 portions of milk or dairy products a day are recommended. One portion is, for example, a glass of milk or a yoghurt.
90737.m: Two to three portions of dairy products a day are enough.

90738.q: Which group is directly above drinks in the food pyramid?
90738.e: Just above the drinks comes the second wide level with vegetables and fruit. So you should eat a lot of them.
90738.m: Vegetables and fruit are near the bottom of the pyramid.

90739.q: Which vegetable oil do the Swiss dietary guidelines especially recommend?
90739.e: The guidelines advise at least one tablespoon of rapeseed oil a day. Rapeseed is also grown in Switzerland.
90739.m: Rapeseed oil is a healthy cooking oil.

90740.q: How many tablespoons of vegetable oil does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90740.e: About 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil a day are recommended, for example rapeseed oil for salad. The body needs oil in small amounts.
90740.m: A little vegetable oil every day is healthy.

90741.q: How many portions of meat, fish, eggs or tofu does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90741.e: 1 portion of a protein-rich food a day is recommended. You should vary it.
90741.m: One portion of protein a day is enough.

90742.q: Which of these foods is a vegetable?
90742.e: The cucumber is a vegetable. Apples, pears and grapes are fruit.

90743.q: Which vegetable is orange and grows in the ground?
90743.e: The carrot is the orange root of the plant and grows underground. In Switzerland it is also called Rüebli.
90743.m: The carrot grows in the ground as an orange root.

90744.q: Which vegetable often makes your eyes water when you cut it?
90744.e: When you cut an onion, a substance is released that stings the eyes. That is why your eyes water.

90745.q: Which green vegetable looks like little trees?
90745.e: Broccoli has lots of small green florets on thick stalks. That is why it looks like little trees.
90745.m: Broccoli looks like a little forest.

90746.q: What colour is a ripe tomato usually?
90746.e: Ripe tomatoes are usually red. But there are also yellow and green varieties.

90747.q: What is lamb's lettuce, called Nüsslisalat in Switzerland?
a: A salad with small green leaves
90747.e: Lamb's lettuce has small dark green leaves and also grows in winter. Its Swiss name contains the word for nut, but it has nothing to do with nuts; it just tastes a little nutty.
90747.m: Lamb's lettuce is a salad with small leaves.

90748.q: Which vegetable is dark red and stains your hands when you cut it?
90748.e: Beetroot has a strong red colouring. It stains your hands and the chopping board red.

90749.q: Which vegetable is sauerkraut made from?
90749.e: Sauerkraut is made from finely shredded white cabbage that turns sour with salt. In Switzerland white cabbage is also called Kabis.
90749.m: Sauerkraut is made from white cabbage.

90750.q: Which fruit is yellow and curved?
90750.e: The banana has a yellow skin and is curved. It grows in warm countries.
90750.m: The banana is yellow and curved.

90751.q: Because of its many fruit trees, Thurgau is jokingly called “Mostindien” (“Cider India”). Which fruit grows there especially often?
90751.e: There are very many apple trees in Thurgau. A lot of apple juice and cider is made from the apples there.
90751.m: Thurgau is known for its apples.

90752.q: Which fruit is a citrus fruit?
90752.e: Like the lemon and the mandarin, the orange is a citrus fruit. It has a lot of vitamin C.
90752.m: The orange is a citrus fruit.

90753.q: Which small red fruit has a hard stone in the middle?
90753.e: The cherry is a stone fruit. In the middle there is a hard stone that you don't eat.
90753.m: The cherry has a hard stone.

90754.q: Which fruit is brown and hairy outside and green inside?
90754.e: The kiwi has a brown, hairy skin. Inside it is green with lots of tiny black seeds.
90754.m: The kiwi is brown outside and green inside.

90755.q: Which small blue berry grows on low bushes in the woods?
90755.e: Bilberries grow on low bushes, including in Swiss woods. They are also called wild blueberries.

90756.q: Why should you wash fruit before eating it?
90756.e: There can be soil, dust and sprays on the skin. You wash them off with water.
90756.m: Wash fruit before you eat it.

90757.q: When are there fresh strawberries from the fields in Switzerland?
90757.e: Swiss strawberries are mainly picked in May, June and July. None grow outdoors in winter.
90757.m: Strawberries from the fields come in early summer.

90758.q: What is wholemeal bread made from?
90758.e: For wholemeal flour, the whole grain is ground, including the outer layer and the germ. Wholemeal bread is baked from it.
90758.m: Wholemeal bread contains the whole grain.

90759.q: What does wholemeal bread have more of than white bread?
90759.e: Wholemeal bread contains a lot of fibre. It is good for digestion.
90759.m: Wholemeal bread has a lot of fibre.

90760.q: Which ancient grain is related to wheat and popular in Switzerland for making bread?
90760.e: Spelt is an ancient kind of wheat. It has been grown in Switzerland for a long time and baked into bread.
90760.m: Spelt is an ancient bread grain.

90761.q: What colour is wholemeal bread usually?
90761.e: Because the dark outer layer of the grain is ground in too, wholemeal bread is usually brown.

90762.q: Which grain is most bread in Switzerland baked from?
90762.e: In Switzerland wheat is the most important bread grain. Wheat flour is used, for example, to bake Zopf plaited bread and Weggli rolls.
90762.m: Wheat is Switzerland's most important bread grain.

90763.q: Which parts of the grain are missing from white flour?
a: The outer layer and the germ
90763.e: For white flour, only the light-coloured inside of the grain is ground. The outer layer and the germ are removed.
90763.m: White flour has no outer layer and no germ.

90764.q: Which group of the food pyramid does wholemeal bread belong to?
90764.e: Bread is made from cereal grains. It belongs to the group with cereal products and potatoes.

90765.q: According to the guidelines, how many of the daily cereal portions should be wholegrain?
90765.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise eating at least half of your cereal products as wholegrain.
90765.m: At least half of your cereals should be wholegrain.

90766.q: Which of these foods is a dairy product?
90766.e: Quark is made from milk. Rice, honey and bread don't have milk as their main ingredient.

90767.q: What is the yellowish liquid left over when cheese is made called?
90767.e: When cheese is made, the milk separates into solid curds and liquid whey. The whey is often fed to pigs or made into drinks.
90767.m: Whey is left over when cheese is made.

90768.q: Which animal does most milk in Switzerland come from?
90768.e: Almost all the milk in Switzerland comes from cows. But there is also goat's and sheep's milk.
90768.m: Most milk in Switzerland comes from cows.

90769.q: Which well-known Swiss cheese has big holes?
90769.e: Emmentaler is famous for its big round holes. It comes from the Emmental valley in the canton of Bern.

90770.q: What do you get if you whip cream for a very long time?
90770.e: First the cream becomes whipped cream. If you keep going, the fat separates and you get butter.
90770.m: Cream whipped for a long time turns into butter.

90772.q: Which Swiss cheese dish is eaten from a shared pot?
90772.e: For fondue, cheese is melted in a special pot called a caquelon. Everyone dips their bread on a fork into the shared pot.
90772.m: Fondue is eaten together from one pot.

90773.q: Where do you keep an opened carton of milk?
90773.e: Milk stays fresh for longer in the fridge. In the warmth it soon goes sour.
90773.m: Opened milk belongs in the fridge.

90774.q: What should you do after eating sweets?
90774.e: After brushing your teeth, fewer bits of sugar stay on them. That keeps your teeth healthy.
90774.m: After sweet things it is best to brush your teeth.

90775.q: Which plant is sugar made from in Switzerland?
90775.e: In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet, for example in the factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.
90775.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

90776.q: How many sweet things per day does the Swiss food pyramid recommend at most?
90776.e: Sweet things are in the narrow top. You can enjoy them, but at most one small portion a day.
90776.m: Sweet things are allowed, but only a little.

90777.q: Which sweet food do bees make?
90777.e: Bees collect nectar from flowers and turn it into honey. Honey contains a lot of sugar.
