91357.e: ImageNet was presented in 2009 and contains over 14 million labelled pictures. With it, computers learnt to recognise pictures much better.
91357.m: ImageNet provides millions of labelled pictures for training.

91358.q: What does a digital picture that a computer analyses consist of?
91358.e: Every pixel has a colour value that is stored as a number. Image recognition calculates with these numbers.
91358.m: For the computer, a picture is a large table of pixel numbers.

91359.q: Which function in a car uses image recognition with a camera?
91359.e: A camera behind the windscreen recognises signs and shows, for example, the speed limit.
91359.m: Driver assistance systems in cars read traffic signs with cameras.

91360.q: What are tests for in which you have to click on all the pictures with traffic lights?
a: To tell people apart from automatic programs
To count a city's traffic lights
91360.e: Tests like these are called CAPTCHAs. They are meant to keep out bots that, for example, want to create masses of accounts.
91360.m: A CAPTCHA checks whether a person is at the device.

91361.q: Is a song still protected when the person who wrote it has died?
a: No, it is free from the day of death
Only if it is played on the radio
Only if it is on a CD
91361.e: In Switzerland, copyright usually lasts for 70 years after the death of the author. Only after that may anyone use the work freely.
91361.m: Works stay protected for a long time even after the author has died.

91362.q: What is the Swiss law called that protects works such as music, texts and pictures?
91362.e: The Federal Act on Copyright and Related Rights, CopA for short, governs the protection of works in Switzerland.
91362.m: In Switzerland the CopA protects the rights of authors.

91363.q: What is forbidden in Switzerland when swapping music on the internet?
a: Publicly offering protected music for download
Listening to a CD you bought at home
Listening to songs on the radio
Saying the title of a song
91363.e: Anyone who makes protected works publicly available without permission breaks copyright. This applies, for example, to uploads to file-sharing sites.
91363.m: You may not simply offer other people's works publicly.

91364.q: What must you always give when quoting someone else's text?
91364.e: A quotation is allowed if it serves as an explanation and the source and, if known, the author are named.
91364.m: Anyone who quotes always names the source.

91365.q: What does it mean when a work is “in the public domain”?
a: It is no longer protected by copyright and can be used freely
It may only be shown at school
91365.e: When the protection period runs out, works enter the public domain. That is why you may freely use poems by Goethe or music by Mozart.
91365.m: Anyone may freely use works in the public domain.

91366.e: Only the actual form of a work is protected. The idea, such as writing a story about a young wizard at school, is free.
91366.m: Copyright protects how something is carried out, not the idea.

a: Passing off someone else's work as your own
Borrowing a book from the library
Listening to a song on the radio
91367.e: In plagiarism, texts, pictures or ideas of others are taken over without naming the source. At schools and universities this can have serious consequences.
91367.m: Passing off someone else's work as your own is plagiarism.

a: An organisation that offers free standard licences for sharing works
A law of the European Union
91368.e: With Creative Commons licences, authors can easily set how others may use their works.
91368.m: Creative Commons licences make sharing works easy.

91369.q: With a Creative Commons licence, who decides how others may use a work?
91369.e: Whoever created a photo, song or text chooses a Creative Commons licence themselves. With it they decide what others may do with it.
91369.m: With Creative Commons, the author decides the rules of use.

91370.q: What does the abbreviation “BY” in a Creative Commons licence require?
a: Showing the work only by day
91370.e: “BY” stands for attribution. Anyone who uses the work must say who it is by.
91370.m: BY means that you must name the author.

91371.q: What does the abbreviation “NC” mean in a Creative Commons licence?
91371.e: NC stands for “NonCommercial”. The work may not be used to earn money.
91371.m: NC only allows use without a business purpose.

91372.q: What does the abbreviation “ND” mean in a Creative Commons licence?
91372.e: ND stands for “NoDerivatives”. The work may be passed on but not changed.
91372.m: ND means that you may not change a work.

91373.q: What does the abbreviation “SA” mean in a Creative Commons licence?
91373.e: SA stands for “ShareAlike”. Anyone who changes the work must pass on the new work under the same licence.
91373.m: SA requires changed versions to have the same licence.

a: The author gives up as many rights as possible
The work may never be used
The work costs zero francs, but only once
The work is only protected for 0 days and then deleted
91374.e: With CC0 an author releases a work as far as possible, similar to the public domain. You may use it without any conditions.
91374.m: With CC0 a work is released as fully as possible.

91375.q: Which condition applies to all six main Creative Commons licences?
a: You may never change the work
You may not earn money with it
91375.e: All six main licences contain the element BY, meaning attribution. The other elements such as NC or ND are only added in some licences.
91375.m: With all main Creative Commons licences you name the author.

91376.e: The term influencer comes from “to influence”, meaning to have an effect on what others think or do.
91376.m: An influencer is someone who has an influence on others.

91377.q: Why do influencers have to label paid posts as advertising?
a: So that you can tell advertising from an honest opinion
So that the video loads faster
So that more hashtags are possible
So that the platform uses less electricity
91377.e: Hidden advertising deceives the audience. That is why paid posts must be recognisable, for example with “Ad” or “Advertisement”.
91377.m: Advertising must be recognisable as advertising.

91378.e: If you follow an account, you see its new posts in your own feed. The number of followers shows how many people it reaches.
91378.m: Followers see the posts of the accounts they follow.

91379.q: What is meant by product placement?
a: A product is built clearly visibly into a post in return for payment
A product is put on the shelf in a shop
A product is handed over to the post office
A product is counted in the warehouse
91379.e: In product placement, for example, a drinks brand appears in a video as if by chance. This is advertising too.
91379.m: Even a product shown in passing can be paid advertising.

91380.q: What are influencers called who have a rather small but loyal fan base of a few thousand followers?
91380.e: Micro-influencers reach fewer people, but often have close contact with their audience. Companies value this for advertising.
91380.m: Even small accounts can have a lot of influence.

91381.q: What is a collaboration for influencers?
a: Working with a company in return for money or free products
A shared password for two accounts
A meeting with fans in the park
91381.e: In a collaboration, an influencer presents a company's products or services and gets something in return.
91381.m: A collaboration is paid work with a company.

a: Bought or automatic accounts that fake popularity
Real fans who comment very often
91382.e: Some accounts buy followers to seem bigger. So a lot of followers does not always say anything about real popularity.
91382.m: A high follower count is not always genuine.

91383.q: When did the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia start?
91383.e: Wikipedia started on 15 January 2001, first in English. The German-language Wikipedia followed in the same year.

91384.q: In how many languages does Wikipedia exist?
91384.e: Wikipedia exists in over 300 languages, even in Romansh and Alemannic. The English edition is the largest.
91384.m: Wikipedia exists in a great many languages.

91385.q: What does the Hawaiian word “wiki” mean?
91385.e: A wiki is a website that you can edit quickly and directly in the browser. The name comes from the Hawaiian “wiki wiki” for “quick”.

91386.q: Who writes the articles in Wikipedia?
a: Volunteers from all over the world
91386.e: Anyone can help write. Thousands of volunteers improve and check each other's articles.
91386.m: Wikipedia is created by the work of many volunteers.

91387.e: The non-profit Wikimedia Foundation, based in San Francisco, runs Wikipedia's servers and technology.
91387.m: Behind Wikipedia is the non-profit Wikimedia Foundation.

91388.q: May you reuse texts from Wikipedia?
a: Yes, if you name Wikipedia as the source
Only with permission from the head teacher
91388.e: Wikipedia texts are under a free licence. You may use and change them, but you must name the source and pass them on under the same conditions.
91388.m: You may reuse Wikipedia texts if you give the source.

91389.q: What does Wikipedia require for statements in its articles?
91389.e: Statements should be checkable. That is why there are references, and original research or opinions do not belong in articles.
91389.m: Good Wikipedia articles have checkable sources.

91390.e: Wikipedia shows no advertising. It is mainly paid for by donations from private individuals.
91390.m: Wikipedia lives on donations instead of advertising.

91391.q: What does “open source” mean for software?
a: The source code is open and may be read, changed and passed on
The program only runs with the window open
The program is only available on open Sundays
91391.e: With open-source software, anyone can look at the source code. Many people often work together on programs like this.
91391.m: With open source, the source code is open to everyone.

91392.q: Who started developing the operating system kernel Linux in 1991?
91392.e: The Finnish student Linus Torvalds put Linux on the internet in 1991. Today Linux runs on many servers and as the basis of Android.
91392.m: Linux was started by Linus Torvalds.

91393.q: Which well-known web browser is developed by Mozilla as open source?
91393.e: Firefox appeared in 2004 as an open-source browser. Its source code can be viewed publicly.

91394.q: What is the source code of a program?
a: The instructions in a programming language that people can read
The price in the app store
91394.e: Programmers write source code, for example in Python or Java. From it, the program that the computer runs is created.
91394.m: Source code is the program in readable form.

91395.q: What does the licence of open-source software set out?
a: What you may do with the program and its source code
How big the screen must be
91395.e: A licence is a kind of contract. With open source it allows you to read, change and pass on the source code, often with certain conditions.
91395.m: The licence says what you may do with a piece of software.

91396.q: What is software called whose source code stays secret and belongs to the company?
91396.e: With proprietary software, only the manufacturer decides about the source code. Users only get the finished program.
91396.m: Proprietary software has secret source code.

91397.q: What is a program called that is free of charge but whose source code is not open?
91397.e: Freeware costs nothing, but you usually may not view or change the source code. So free of charge does not automatically mean open source.
91397.m: Free software is not automatically open source.

91398.q: What is a program like Git used for in open-source projects?
a: It stores all the changes to the source code
91398.e: With version control like Git, many people can work on a program at the same time. Every change is stored and can be traced.
91398.m: Git stores every change to a program.

91399.q: The Swiss Confederation publishes its own software as open source in principle. What does this mean?
a: Everyone can look at the source code
Only Federal Councillors may use the software
The software only exists on paper
91399.e: Since 2024 there has been a law in Switzerland under which the Confederation in principle makes software it has developed itself public. This lets everyone check and reuse the source code.
91399.m: The Confederation publishes its own software as open source in principle.

a: Rules for polite behaviour on the internet
A label on a network cable
91400.e: The word is made up of “net” and “etiquette”, which means rules of good manners.
91400.m: Netiquette is good manners on the internet.

91401.q: What does it usually mean in chats when someone writes only in CAPITAL LETTERS?
a: It shows that you are tired
91401.e: Capital letters stand out a lot and are understood as loud shouting. That is why you only use them sparingly.
91401.m: Whole sentences in capital letters come across as shouting.

91402.q: What is a “troll” on the internet?
a: Someone who deliberately provokes and disrupts
91402.e: Trolls write provocative comments to start arguments and get attention.
91402.m: Trolls want to start arguments with provocations.

91403.q: What is the best way to react to a troll?
91403.e: A well-known piece of advice is “Don't feed the troll”. Without a reaction, they often lose interest.
91403.m: You do not feed trolls with replies.

91404.q: What is good advice if you are annoyed by a comment and want to reply straight away?
a: Wait a moment and read the reply again before sending
Reply in capital letters straight away
Forward the comment to all your contacts
Send as many angry emojis as possible
91404.e: When you are annoyed, you quickly write something you regret later. Messages that have been sent often cannot be taken back.
91404.m: When you are annoyed, take a breath first and then write.

a: Unwanted messages that are sent out in huge numbers
91405.e: Spam is mainly advertising or fraud messages that go to a great many recipients. You should not click on any links in them.
91405.m: It is best to delete spam messages without opening them.

91406.q: Why are ironic remarks in text messages easily misunderstood?
a: Because tone of voice and facial expressions are missing
Because the letters are too small
Because phones do not store irony
91406.e: In a conversation, voice and face show how something is meant. In text these clues are missing; emojis can help a little.
91406.m: Text has no tone of voice, so write clearly and kindly.

91407.q: What is part of netiquette in a class chat?
a: Only sending messages that concern everyone
Sending dozens of stickers in the middle of the night
Handing out other people's phone numbers
91407.e: In group chats, many people read along. Considerate messages on the topic and at suitable times make the chat pleasant.
91407.m: In group chats you are considerate towards all members.

a: In the water of ponds and lakes
91408.e: Water lilies are water plants. They grow in calm ponds and lakes.
91408.m: Water lilies grow in calm water.

91409.q: What colour is the flower of the white water lily?
91409.e: The white water lily has large white flowers with a yellow centre.
91409.m: The white water lily has white flowers.

91410.q: What connects the floating water lily leaf to the rootstock at the bottom?
91410.e: The stalk of the water lily is long and bendy. If the water rises, the leaf can still float on top.
91410.m: A long stalk connects the water lily leaf to the bottom.

91411.q: Which animal likes to sit on a big water lily leaf?
91411.e: The big leaves can carry light animals. Frogs sunbathe on them and lie in wait for insects.
91411.m: Frogs like to sit on water lily leaves.

91412.q: When are the flowers of the water lily open?
91412.e: The flowers open in the morning and close again in the afternoon or evening.
91412.m: Water lilies open their flowers during the day.

91413.q: What shape is a water lily leaf?
a: Long and pointed like a needle
91413.e: The water lily leaf is almost round. In one place it has a narrow slit up to the stalk.
91413.m: A water lily leaf is round and has a slit.

91414.q: Which yellow-flowered plant with floating leaves looks like the water lily?
91414.e: The yellow water lily, also called brandy-bottle, also has leaves that float on the water. But its flowers are smaller and yellow.
91414.m: The yellow water lily is a yellow relative of the white water lily.

91415.q: What happens to water drops on a water lily leaf?
a: They make holes in the leaf
91415.e: The top of the leaf has a waxy layer. That is why drops simply roll off.
91415.m: Water rolls off the water lily leaf.

91416.q: What is a wide strip of reeds along a lake shore called?
91416.e: Reeds often grow so thickly on the shore that they lie around the lake like a belt. Many animals find shelter there.
91416.m: A reed belt is a thick strip of reeds on the shore.

a: Only as tall as a thumb
Only as tall as a lawn
91417.e: Reeds can grow about four metres tall. That is more than twice as tall as an adult.
91417.m: Reeds can grow much taller than a person.

91418.q: What is the stem of a reed like inside?
91418.e: The reed stem is hollow inside, like a little tube. In German the plant is also called “reed pipe” because of this.
91418.m: The reed stem is a hollow tube.

91419.q: What colour are reeds in winter?
91419.e: In autumn reeds become dry and light brown. The dry stems often stay standing all winter.
91419.m: In winter reeds are light brown and dry.

91420.q: What did people often use reeds for in the past?
91420.e: Thatched roofs are made from reeds. Such roofs keep out the rain and insulate well.
91420.m: You can make roofs from reeds.

91421.q: Which small bird builds its nest in the reeds?
91421.e: The reed warbler weaves its nest between several reed stems. It is well hidden there.
91421.m: The reed warbler nests in the reeds.

91422.q: Which group of plants do reeds belong to?
91422.e: Reeds are a very large grass. They belong to the true grasses, like wheat.

91423.q: What do the flower heads of reeds look like?
91423.e: In late summer there is a soft, feathery flower head at the top of the reed stem. It sways in the wind.
91423.m: Reeds have a feathery flower head at the top.

91424.q: How do reeds help the shore?
a: Their roots hold the soil in place
They scare away all the fish
91424.e: The dense network of roots holds the soil together. Reeds also slow down the waves.
91424.m: Reeds protect the shore from waves.

91425.q: What does the flower head of the bulrush look like?
91425.e: There is a thick brown head on the long stem. It looks like a sausage on a stick.
91425.m: The bulrush has a brown head on its stem.

a: In shallow water at the edge
91426.e: The bulrush likes to stand with its feet in the shallow water of ponds and ditches.
91426.m: The bulrush grows in shallow water.

91427.q: What happens to the brown head of the bulrush in winter?
a: It breaks up into white, fluffy flakes
It falls into the water like a stone
91427.e: The head is made of a huge number of seeds with fine hairs. In winter it bursts open and the fluff spills out.
91427.m: The ripe head breaks up into seed fluff.

91428.q: How are the seeds of the bulrush spread?
91428.e: Each seed has fine hairs like a tiny parachute. This lets the wind carry it far away.
91428.m: Bulrush seeds fly away on the wind.

91429.q: What do the leaves of the bulrush look like?
91429.e: The leaves are long and narrow and stand upright. They can be more than a metre long.

91430.q: What were the fluffy seed hairs of the bulrush used for in the past?
91430.e: The soft fluff from the head was used to stuff cushions and upholstery.
91430.m: Bulrush fluff was used to fill cushions.

91431.q: How tall can the common bulrush grow?
91431.e: The common bulrush usually grows one to two and a half metres tall.
91431.m: The bulrush can grow over two metres tall.

91432.q: What does the head of the bulrush feel like?
91432.e: The head is densely covered with tiny flowers and later with seeds. That is why it feels soft like velvet.
91432.m: The head of the bulrush is soft like velvet.

a: On the surface of the water
Deep on the bottom of the pond
In the air above the pond
In the soil on the bank
91433.e: Duckweed is made up of tiny plants that float freely on the water.

91434.q: How big is one little leaf of duckweed?
a: As big as a sheet of paper
91434.e: One part of common duckweed is only about the size of a pinhead to a lentil.

91436.q: Why is it dark in a pond under a thick carpet of duckweed?
a: Because the duckweed blocks out the light
Because the pond is deeper there
Because it is always night there
91436.e: A thick layer of duckweed lets hardly any light through. Plants under the water then get little light.
91436.m: Lots of duckweed makes the pond below it dark.

91437.q: What hangs down into the water under a little leaf of common duckweed?
91437.e: Under each part of common duckweed, a thin root hangs down into the water.
91437.m: Duckweed has a fine root hanging down.

a: New little leaves grow out at the side and break off
It lays eggs in the water
It flies away on the wind
91438.e: New parts grow out of an existing part. They separate and float away. This is how duckweed multiplies very quickly.
91438.m: Duckweed multiplies by growing new little leaves.

91439.q: What do you see when a lot of duckweed grows on a pond?
a: A green carpet on the water
91439.e: Duckweed multiplies a lot in summer. Then it covers the pond like a green carpet.
91439.m: Lots of duckweed forms a green carpet.

91440.q: Which plant is thought to be the smallest flowering plant in the world?
91440.e: Watermeal is only about one millimetre in size. It is a relative of duckweed.
91440.m: The smallest flowering plant is a kind of duckweed.

91441.q: Does duckweed have a long stem?
a: No, it is made almost entirely of tiny leaves
Yes, it is a metre long
Yes, it is as hard as wood
Yes, it grows down to the bottom
91441.e: Duckweed has no real stem and no real leaves. It is made of small, flat parts.
91441.m: Duckweed is made of flat little plants with no stem.

91442.q: What colour are the flowers of the marsh marigold?
91442.e: The marsh marigold has bright golden yellow flowers.
91442.m: The marsh marigold has golden yellow flowers.

91443.q: When does the marsh marigold flower?
91443.e: It flowers early in the year, from about March to May, and is one of the first flowers by the stream.
91443.m: The marsh marigold flowers in spring.

91444.q: Where does the marsh marigold grow?
a: In wet places such as stream banks
91444.e: The marsh marigold needs a lot of water. You find it by streams, ditches and in damp meadows.
91444.m: The marsh marigold loves wet ground.

91445.q: How many petals does the marsh marigold usually have?
91445.e: Its flower usually has five yellow petals. Sometimes there are a few more.
91445.m: The marsh marigold usually has five petals.

a: No, people make tea from it
No, people make salad from it
91446.e: The marsh marigold contains substances that can irritate your skin and stomach. You should not eat it.

91447.q: Which yellow meadow flower is the marsh marigold related to?
91447.e: The marsh marigold is related to the buttercup, which grows in meadows. Both have shiny yellow flowers.
91447.m: The marsh marigold is related to the buttercup.

91448.q: What do the leaves of the marsh marigold look like?
91448.e: The leaves are large, roundish to heart-shaped and have a shiny surface.
91448.m: The marsh marigold has shiny, roundish leaves.

91450.q: What colour is the flower of the yellow iris?
91450.e: As its name says, the yellow iris has bright yellow flowers.
91450.m: The yellow iris has yellow flowers.

91452.q: Where does the yellow iris grow?
a: On the bank and in shallow water
91452.e: The yellow iris is also called the yellow flag. It grows by ponds, streams and in marshes.
91452.m: The yellow iris grows on wet banks.

91453.q: When does the yellow iris flower?
91453.e: It flowers from about May to July.
91453.m: The yellow iris flowers in early summer.

a: No, people eat it as a salad
Only the flower is sweet and edible
91454.e: All parts of the plant are poisonous, especially the rootstock.
91454.m: You must not eat the yellow iris.

91456.q: How many large petals hang downwards on the yellow iris?
91456.e: The flower has three large petals that hang outwards. Smaller petals stand between them.
91456.m: On the iris, three large petals hang downwards.

91457.q: How can the seeds of the yellow iris travel?
a: They always stay in the flower
91457.e: The seeds have a layer of air and can float. This way they drift with the water to new places.
91457.m: Iris seeds travel by floating on the water.

91458.e: Waterweed is an underwater plant. Its stems grow completely in the water of ponds and streams.

91459.q: Where does Canadian waterweed originally come from?
91459.e: As its name says, it comes from North America, for example from Canada. It was brought to Europe by accident.
91459.m: Canadian waterweed comes from North America.

a: Under water in ponds and lakes
91461.e: Canadian waterweed is a water plant from North America. It grows submerged in still and slow-flowing waters and can form dense stands.

91462.q: What rises in tiny bubbles when waterweed is in sunlight?
91462.e: Using light, the plant makes food and gives off oxygen as it does so. You can see this as tiny bubbles.
91462.m: Waterweed gives off oxygen in the light.

91463.q: Where else do people like to keep waterweed?
a: In a flowerpot on the balcony
91463.e: Waterweed grows easily and quickly. That is why it is a popular aquarium plant.
91463.m: Waterweed is a popular aquarium plant.

91464.q: How does waterweed mainly multiply in Europe?
91464.e: A piece that has broken off can drift away and grow new roots. This creates a new plant.
91464.m: A new plant grows from a piece of waterweed.

91465.e: The stems and little leaves of waterweed are dark green.

91466.e: Algae live mainly in water: in ponds, lakes, streams and in the sea.

91467.q: What colour are most algae in a pond?
91467.e: Many algae in ponds are green because, like plants, they contain the green pigment chlorophyll.

91468.q: What do algae need to grow?
91468.e: Like plants, algae use sunlight to make their food.

91469.q: What are algae called that grow in the water like long green hairs?
91469.e: Filamentous algae form long green threads. Sometimes they look like green cotton wool in the pond.
91469.m: Filamentous algae are long like hair.

91470.q: Why does pond water sometimes turn completely green in summer?
a: Because huge numbers of tiny algae live in it
Because leaves are lying in it
91470.e: When it is warm and there is lots of light, tiny algae multiply quickly. Then they colour the whole water green.
91470.m: Lots of tiny algae turn the water green.

91471.q: Which pond animals like to scrape algae off stones and plants?
91471.e: Water snails have a rough tongue. They use it to scrape off algae.

91472.q: Where do the largest algae grow?
91472.e: In the sea there is seaweed that can grow many metres long.
91472.m: The largest algae live in the sea.

91473.q: What can happen if a pond has too many algae?
a: The fish get too little air
The pond freezes over in summer
91473.e: When lots of algae die, they use up the oxygen in the water as they rot. Then the fish do not have enough air to breathe.
91473.m: Too many algae harm the pond.

a: The edge where the stream and the land meet
The deepest point in the stream
91474.e: The bank is the strip of land right next to the water. Many plants and animals live there.
91474.m: At the bank, water and land meet.

91475.q: Which trees like to grow on stream banks?
91475.e: Willows and alders like wet ground. You often see them along streams.
91475.m: Willows like to grow by the water.

91476.q: Which plant with stinging hairs on its leaves often grows on stream banks?
91476.e: Stinging nettles like damp, nutrient-rich soil. Their stinging hairs sting your skin.
91476.m: Stinging nettles easily sting your skin.

91477.q: Which blue and orange bird hunts small fish by the stream?
91477.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch and dives into the water at lightning speed to catch fish.
91477.m: The kingfisher is a colourful fish hunter by the stream.

91478.q: Which animal fells trees on the bank and builds dams?
91478.e: The beaver gnaws trees down with its strong teeth. In Switzerland it now lives again by many streams and rivers.
91478.m: The beaver is a builder by the water.

91479.q: Which long-legged bird often stands still in shallow water and catches fish?
91479.e: The grey heron waits very calmly. Then it strikes like lightning with its pointed beak.
91479.m: The grey heron fishes with patience.

91480.q: What should never be left on a stream bank?
91480.e: Rubbish harms animals and plants and pollutes the water. You always take it away with you.
91480.m: Take your rubbish home from the stream.

91481.q: Which bird can dive into a stream and walk along the bottom?
91481.e: The dipper dives in fast-flowing streams and looks for insect larvae under water.
91481.m: The dipper walks under water along the stream bed.

91482.q: Where do dragonflies lay their eggs?
91482.e: Dragonflies lay their eggs in the water or in plants by the water.
91482.m: Dragonflies need water for their eggs.

91483.q: What is a young dragonfly called?
91483.e: A larva hatches from the egg. It looks completely different from the adult dragonfly.

91484.q: Where does a dragonfly larva live?
91484.e: Dragonfly larvae live in water, often for several months or even years.

91485.e: Dragonflies are hunters. They catch small insects in flight.
91485.m: Dragonflies hunt mosquitoes and other insects.

91486.q: What is special about a dragonfly's eyes?
91486.e: The eyes take up almost the whole head. They are made of many thousands of tiny single eyes.

a: Yes, it stings like a wasp
91487.e: Dragonflies are harmless to people. They have no sting.
91487.m: Dragonflies are harmless and do not sting.

91488.q: What does a dragonfly larva do when it has finished growing?
a: It climbs out of the water up a stalk
It digs itself into the soil
91488.e: The larva climbs up a plant stem. Then its skin splits open and the dragonfly comes out.
91488.m: The dragonfly emerges on a stalk above the water.

91489.q: What is left on the stalk after the dragonfly has come out?
91489.e: The empty case of the larva stays hanging on the stem. You can often find them by ponds.
91489.m: The empty larval skin stays on the stalk.

a: A young frog or a young toad
91490.e: Tadpoles are the larvae of frogs and toads. They look completely different from the adult animals.
91490.m: A tadpole becomes a frog or a toad.

91491.q: What does a young tadpole breathe with?
91491.e: Young tadpoles breathe with gills, like fish. Later they grow lungs.

91492.q: What does a young tadpole swim with?
91492.e: At first the tadpole has no legs yet. It swims with its paddle-like tail.
91492.m: The tadpole paddles with its tail.

91493.q: Which legs grow first on a frog tadpole?
a: All four at the same time
91493.e: The back legs grow first. Later the front legs appear as well.
91493.m: Tadpoles get their back legs first.

91494.q: What happens to the tadpole's tail when it turns into a frog?
a: It falls off in one piece and grows back
91494.e: The body slowly breaks down the tail. In the end, the little frog has no tail any more.

91495.e: Tadpoles use their mouths to scrape off algae and soft bits of plants.

91496.e: Tadpoles can only live in water. They only go onto land once they are little frogs.

91497.q: What is the change from tadpole to frog called?
91497.e: During metamorphosis the whole body changes. A water animal becomes an animal that also lives on land.
91497.m: The tadpole transforms into a frog.

a: A frog's nest made of twigs
91498.e: Female frogs lay lots of eggs in the water. These eggs are called spawn.
91498.m: Frogspawn is the eggs of frogs.

a: Red balls with a hard shell
91499.e: Each egg has a dark centre in a clear, slimy coating. The coating protects the egg.
91499.m: Frogspawn is slimy with black dots.

91500.q: How does the common frog lay its spawn?
a: In a nest in a tree
91500.e: The common frog lays its eggs in large clumps of spawn. Toads, on the other hand, lay long strings of spawn.
91500.m: Frogs lay clumps of spawn, toads lay strings of spawn.

91501.q: When can you find frogspawn in Switzerland?
91501.e: Many frogs spawn in early spring, from about February to April.

91502.q: In Switzerland, are you allowed to take frogspawn home from a pond?
a: No, frogs and toads are protected
Yes, as much as you like
Yes, if you have a jar
91502.e: All amphibians are protected in Switzerland. You leave the spawn in the pond and watch it there.

91503.e: After a few days to weeks, little tadpoles hatch from the eggs.

91504.q: Where do frogs most like to lay their spawn?
a: In still water such as ponds
91504.e: In the calm, shallow water of ponds the spawn is not washed away and is warmed by the sun.

91505.q: How many eggs can a female common frog lay at one time?
91505.e: A common frog often lays well over a thousand eggs. Many of them are eaten, which is why so many are needed.
91505.m: Frogs lay a great many eggs.

91506.q: Why do helpers put up small fences along roads in spring?
a: So that toads are not run over on their way to the breeding pond
So that cows do not run away
So that snow stays on the ground
91506.e: In spring, toads and frogs travel to their ponds. Helpers collect them at the fences and carry them safely across the road.
91506.m: Amphibian fences save toads on their way to the pond.

91507.q: What does a glacier form from?
91507.e: Over many years, snow stays on the ground and is pressed together by new snow. In this way it slowly turns to ice.
91507.m: A glacier forms from snow that turns to ice over years.

91508.q: What does a glacier do slowly but steadily?
91508.e: The ice is so heavy that it moves very slowly down the valley. You cannot see it, but you can measure it.
91508.m: A glacier flows very slowly down the mountain.

91509.q: What is the front, lower part of a glacier called?
91509.e: The lower end of a glacier often looks like a long tongue. That is why it is called the glacier tongue.
91509.m: The lower end of a glacier is called the glacier tongue.

91510.q: What do glaciers store in large amounts?
91510.e: Glaciers are made of frozen fresh water. When they melt, the water flows into streams and rivers.
91510.m: Glaciers are huge stores of fresh water.

91511.q: In which mountain range are most of Switzerland's glaciers?
91511.e: The Alps are high and cold enough for glaciers. There are no glaciers in the Jura or on the Plateau.
91511.m: Switzerland's glaciers are in the Alps.

91512.q: What is the grainy old snow that later becomes glacier ice called?
91512.e: Firn is snow that has survived at least one summer. It gets denser and denser and finally turns to ice.
91512.m: Over time, old grainy firn turns into glacier ice.

91513.q: Roughly how many glaciers are there in Switzerland?
91513.e: The Swiss glacier inventory counts around 1400 glaciers. But many of them are very small.
91513.m: There are around 1400 glaciers in Switzerland.

91514.q: On which continent is most of the Earth's ice?
91514.e: Antarctica at the South Pole is almost completely covered by a huge ice sheet. Most of the Earth's ice is there.
91514.m: Most of the Earth's ice is in Antarctica.

91515.q: Roughly how long is the Great Aletsch Glacier?
91515.e: The Aletsch Glacier is more than 20 kilometres long. That is about as far as you can walk in five hours.
91515.m: The Aletsch Glacier is over 20 kilometres long.

91517.q: Which special protected area has the Aletsch Glacier belonged to since 2001?
91517.e: Since 2001, the Jungfrau Aletsch area has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was the first natural World Heritage Site in the Alps.
91517.m: The Aletsch Glacier is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

91518.q: What is special about the Great Aletsch Glacier?
a: It is the largest glacier in the Alps
It is the highest mountain in Switzerland
It is the largest lake in Switzerland
It is the longest river in Switzerland
91518.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps.
91518.m: The Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

91519.q: What is the Great Aletsch Glacier made of?
91519.e: The Aletsch Glacier is a huge river of ice. It formed from snow that turned to ice over many years.
91519.m: The Aletsch Glacier is a great river of ice.

91520.q: Roughly how thick is the ice of the Aletsch Glacier at its thickest point?
91520.e: At its thickest point, the ice is more than 900 metres thick. That is taller than three Eiffel Towers stacked on top of each other.
91520.m: The ice of the Aletsch Glacier is almost a kilometre thick.

a: A deep crack in the ice
91521.e: Crevasses can be many metres deep. Some are so wide that a person can fall in.
91521.m: A crevasse is a deep crack in the ice.

91522.e: Fresh snow can cover a crevasse completely so that you cannot see it any more. Anyone who steps on it can break through and fall.
91522.m: Crevasses are dangerous because snow can hide them.

91523.q: What do mountaineers use to secure each other on a glacier?
91523.e: On a glacier, mountaineers tie themselves together. If someone falls into a crevasse, the others hold them on the rope.
91523.m: On a glacier you walk roped together.

91524.q: What is a thin layer of snow that covers a crevasse called?
91524.e: A snow bridge lies over a crevasse and looks like solid ground. But it can collapse under a person.
91524.m: A snow bridge can hide a crevasse.

91525.q: Who should you cross a glacier with if you have no experience?
91525.e: Mountain guides know the dangers on the glacier and where the crevasses are. Without experience, you should never go onto a glacier alone.
91525.m: It is best to cross a glacier with a mountain guide.

91526.q: What do mountaineers wear under their boots so they do not slip on glacier ice?
91526.e: Crampons have sharp metal spikes. They bite into the ice and give you grip.
91526.m: With crampons you do not slip on the glacier.

91527.q: What is the large crevasse at the upper edge of a glacier called?
91527.e: The bergschrund separates the moving glacier ice from the ice that sticks to the rock. It is often hard to cross.
91527.m: The bergschrund lies at the very top of the glacier.

91528.q: Why does a glacier get cracks?
a: The ice flows over rocks and breaks
The sun does not shine enough
Too much snow falls at once
91528.e: When the ice flows over a rock step or round a bend, it gets stretched. Because ice does not give enough, it breaks open.
91528.m: Crevasses form where the ice is stretched.

91529.q: Why is the meltwater of a glacier also called glacier milk?
91529.e: The water is full of tiny grains of rock. That is why it looks cloudy and milky.
91529.m: Glacier milk is cloudy meltwater that looks like milk.

91530.e: The glacier grinds down the rock into a fine powder. This rock flour floats in the water.
91530.m: Rock flour makes glacier water cloudy.

91531.q: When does the most glacier milk flow out of a glacier?
91531.e: When it is warm, a lot of ice melts. That is why glacier streams carry the most water on summer afternoons.
91531.m: The most glacier milk flows in summer.

91532.q: What colour are mountain lakes often when glacier milk flows into them?
91532.e: The tiny grains of rock in the water scatter the light. That is why many mountain lakes shine turquoise blue or greenish.
91532.m: Glacier milk often turns mountain lakes turquoise.

91533.q: What is the stream that flows out of a glacier called?
91533.e: The meltwater comes out at the end of the glacier tongue. It collects in a cold glacier stream.
91533.m: A cold glacier stream flows out of a glacier.

91534.q: What does glacier milk feel like when you put your hand in it?
91534.e: The water comes straight from the melting ice. So it is only just above zero degrees.

91535.q: What happens to the fine grains in glacier milk when they flow into a large lake?
a: They slowly sink to the bottom
91535.e: In the calm lake water, the fine grains slowly sink. Over time, a layer of mud forms on the lake bed.
91535.m: The fine grains slowly sink to the bottom of the lake.

91536.q: Which Swiss river carries glacier milk from Valais into Lake Geneva?
91536.e: The Rhône collects the meltwater of many glaciers in Valais. It flows cloudy into Lake Geneva and comes out again as a clear river.
91536.m: The Rhône brings glacier water into Lake Geneva.

91537.q: What was different in Switzerland during the last Ice Age compared with today?
a: Glaciers covered almost the whole country
91537.e: In the last Ice Age, the glaciers reached far out of the Alps. Only a few areas stayed free of ice.
91537.m: In the Ice Age, almost all of Switzerland lay under ice.

91538.q: Which large animal with long fur lived in the Ice Age?
91538.e: The woolly mammoth had thick fur and lived in the cold. Mammoth bones and teeth have been found in Switzerland too.
91538.m: The mammoth was an Ice Age animal.

91539.q: Roughly when did the last Ice Age end?
91539.e: About 12,000 years ago it became much warmer. The great glaciers drew back into the Alps.
91539.m: The last Ice Age ended about 12,000 years ago.

91540.q: Which rhinoceros with thick fur lived in the Ice Age?
91540.e: The woolly rhinoceros had thick fur and was adapted to the cold. Today it is extinct.
91540.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in the Ice Age.

91541.q: What carved out many Swiss lakes such as Lake Zurich?
91541.e: The huge glaciers scoured valleys deep into the land. When the ice melted, the hollows filled with water.

91542.q: Which animals did people often hunt in the Ice Age?
91542.e: Reindeer also lived in what is now Switzerland back then. They gave people meat, fur and bones for tools.

91543.q: What shape are valleys that a glacier has carved out?
91543.e: Glaciers grind the valley sides wide. This creates a trough valley shaped like a U.
91543.m: Glacial valleys are shaped like a U.

91544.q: Roughly how thick was the ice in Valais during the Ice Age?
91544.e: In the Rhône valley there was a layer of ice well over a thousand metres thick. Only the highest peaks stuck out.
91544.m: In the Ice Age there was over a thousand metres of ice in Valais.

91545.q: What is the moraine along the side of a glacier called?
91545.e: At the edge of the glacier, rubble falls from the mountainsides. It forms long ridges on the left and right, the lateral moraines.
91545.m: Lateral moraines lie along the sides of the glacier.

91546.q: What is the moraine in front of the glacier tongue called?
91546.e: The glacier pushes rubble in front of it like a bulldozer. At its furthest point a ridge is left behind, the terminal moraine.
91546.m: The terminal moraine lies in front of the end of the glacier.

91547.q: What often forms when two glaciers flow together?
91547.e: The rubble at the edges of the two glaciers joins to form a dark stripe in the middle of the ice. You can see it clearly on the Aletsch Glacier.
91547.m: A medial moraine is a stripe of rubble in the middle of the glacier.

91548.q: How can you tell how big a glacier used to be?
a: From the colour of the sky
From the length of the road
91548.e: Old moraine ridges often lie far in front of today's glacier. Ice used to lie there.
91548.m: Old moraines show how big a glacier used to be.

91549.q: What lies all jumbled up in a moraine?
91549.e: A glacier does not sort its material. That is why big boulders, gravel and sand are all mixed up in a moraine.
91549.m: Big and small stones lie jumbled together in a moraine.

91550.q: What can a moraine lying across a valley hold back?
91550.e: A moraine can lie across a valley like a dam made of rubble. Water collects behind it and forms a lake.
91550.m: A moraine can hold back a lake like a dam.

91551.q: What is a moraine that lies underneath a glacier called?
91551.e: Under the ice, rock is ground up and dragged along. This layer on the bottom is called ground moraine.
91551.m: The ground moraine lies underneath the glacier.

91552.q: How can you often recognise a glacial erratic?
a: It does not match the rock around it
91552.e: An erratic comes from a different area, often from the Alps. That is why it is made of a different rock from the ground it lies on.
91552.m: An erratic is made of a different rock from its surroundings.

91553.q: Where in Switzerland are many glacial erratics found?
91553.e: In the Ice Age, the glaciers reached as far as the Plateau. There they left behind many boulders from the Alps.
91553.m: Many erratics from the Alps lie on the Plateau.

91554.q: In old tales, who was said to have hurled the large erratic boulders through the air?
91554.e: In the past, people did not know how the huge boulders got into the landscape. So they told each other that giants had thrown them.
91554.m: In old legends, giants were said to have thrown the erratics.

91555.q: Why were many erratic boulders broken up in the past?
a: People needed the stone for building
People looked for gold inside them
People wanted to get salt from them
91555.e: Granite erratics were a good building material. That is why many were broken up for houses, bridges and fountains.
91555.m: Many erratics used to be turned into building material.

91556.q: What do erratic boulders show researchers?
a: How far the glaciers used to reach
91556.e: You can find out which valley an erratic comes from. That way you can work out the route and size of the old glaciers.
91556.m: Erratics show how far the glaciers used to reach.

91557.q: Why are the glaciers in Switzerland getting smaller?
91557.e: Temperatures on Earth are rising. So in summer more ice melts than is added by snow in winter.
91557.m: The glaciers are melting because it is getting warmer.

91558.q: What is the warming of the Earth that makes glaciers melt called?
91558.e: The Earth has been getting warmer for over a hundred years. This is called climate change, and glaciers react especially strongly to it.
91558.m: Climate change makes the glaciers melt.

91559.q: What is often left behind when a glacier melts a lot?
91559.e: Where the ice disappears, a hollow in the rock is often left. Meltwater collects in it and a glacial lake forms.
91559.m: New lakes often form where glaciers melt.

91560.q: What are parts of some glaciers covered with in summer so that they melt more slowly?
91560.e: White sheets reflect the sunlight. That way the ice underneath stays cooler and melts less.
91560.m: White sheets protect some glaciers from the sun.

91562.q: What is suddenly uncovered where a glacier disappears?
91562.e: Under the ice, bare rock with stones and rubble appears. Only after many years do mosses and plants grow there.
91562.m: Where a glacier disappears, bare rock is left behind.

91563.q: How do researchers know whether a glacier is getting shorter?
a: They measure every year where the tongue ends
They count the crevasses every year
They measure how cold the ice is
They count the days with snow
91563.e: Every year researchers measure where the glacier tongue ends. That way they see how many metres the glacier has retreated.
91563.m: Researchers measure the length of glaciers every year.

91564.q: What is missing in hot summers when there are no glaciers any more?
91564.e: Glaciers release a lot of meltwater, especially in dry summers. Without them, some streams then carry less water.
91564.m: Without glaciers, streams lack water in summer.

91565.q: Which big river rises at the Rhône Glacier?
91565.e: The Rhône begins at the tongue of the Rhône Glacier. It then flows through the whole of Valais.
91565.m: The Rhône begins at the Rhône Glacier.

91566.q: Which pass is the Rhône Glacier near?
91566.e: The Furka Pass road runs very close to the Rhône Glacier. From there you can reach it on foot.
91566.m: The Rhône Glacier is at the Furka Pass.

91567.q: How far did the Rhône Glacier reach around 1856?
a: Only to the top of the pass
91567.e: Around 1856 the Rhône Glacier was at its largest and reached down to the valley floor. Today it ends much further up the mountain.
91567.m: Around 1856 the Rhône Glacier reached the valley floor.

91568.q: Roughly how long is the Rhône Glacier?
91568.e: The Rhône Glacier is just under eight kilometres long. But it gets shorter every year.
91568.m: The Rhône Glacier is just under eight kilometres long.

91569.q: What has formed in front of the tongue of the Rhône Glacier since about 2006?
91569.e: Because the glacier is retreating, meltwater collects in a hollow. In this way a lake has formed in front of the tongue.
91569.m: Today there is a glacial lake in front of the Rhône Glacier.

91570.q: What is the small place in the valley below the Rhône Glacier called?
91570.e: Gletsch lies in Valais at the foot of the Furka Pass road and the Grimsel Pass road. The name comes from the German word for the nearby glacier.
91570.m: The village of Gletsch lies below the Rhône Glacier.

91571.q: What do people cover part of the Rhône Glacier with in summer?
91571.e: The white sheets reflect the sunlight. That way the ice underneath melts more slowly.
91571.m: White sheets protect the ice of the Rhône Glacier.

91572.q: What can you marvel at in the Glacier Garden in Lucerne?
91572.e: In the Glacier Garden you can see round, deep holes in the rock. These glacier potholes date from the Ice Age.
91572.m: You can see glacier potholes in the Glacier Garden in Lucerne.

91573.q: How did a glacier pothole form?
a: Water whirled stones round in circles
91573.e: Meltwater plunged down underneath the glacier. It spun stones round in circles, which ground the hole into the rock like a drill.
91573.m: Whirling stones ground out the glacier potholes.

91574.q: What can you see in the Glacier Garden in Lucerne?
a: Glacier potholes from the Ice Age
91574.e: In the Glacier Garden you can see glacier potholes that meltwater drilled into the rock during the Ice Age. They were discovered in 1872.
91574.m: The Glacier Garden shows traces of the Ice Age.

91575.q: What did the discoverer of the Glacier Garden actually want to build?
91575.e: While digging for a wine cellar, the glacier potholes came to light. Instead of a cellar, a museum was created.
91575.m: The Glacier Garden was discovered while building a wine cellar.

91576.q: What fun maze is there in the Glacier Garden in Lucerne?
91576.e: The Alhambra mirror maze dates from 1896. Inside, you see yourself again and again in lots of mirrors.
91576.m: There is a mirror maze in the Glacier Garden.

91577.q: Which famous monument is right next to the Glacier Garden?
91577.e: The Lion Monument shows a dying lion carved into the rock. It is only a few steps from the Glacier Garden.
91577.m: The Lion Monument is next to the Glacier Garden.

91578.q: Roughly how old are the glacier potholes in Lucerne?
91578.e: The glacier potholes formed towards the end of the last Ice Age. That was about 20,000 years ago.
91578.m: The glacier potholes in Lucerne are about 20,000 years old.

a: A tunnel or cave in the ice
91579.e: An ice grotto is a hollow space in glacier ice. Some are formed by meltwater, others are dug out by people.
91579.m: An ice grotto is a cave in the ice.

91580.q: Why does the ice in an ice grotto glow blue?
91580.e: Thick ice absorbs the red parts of light. What is left is mainly blue light.
91580.m: Thick ice glows blue because it absorbs red light.

91581.q: Where is there an ice palace in the glacier at over 3400 metres?
91581.e: On the Jungfraujoch, passages and halls have been cut into the glacier ice. There are also figures made of ice there.
91581.m: There is an ice palace on the Jungfraujoch.

91582.q: Why does the ice grotto in the Rhône Glacier have to be dug again every year?
a: The grotto is walled up every winter
91582.e: The glacier moves and melts in summer. That is why the tunnel changes shape and has to be hollowed out again every year.
91582.m: The ice grotto in the Rhône Glacier is dug again every year.

91583.q: What should you wear in an ice grotto?
91583.e: It is very cold in an ice grotto, even in summer. So a warm jacket is important.
91583.m: You need a warm jacket in an ice grotto.

91584.q: Roughly how warm is it in an ice grotto?
91584.e: In an ice grotto you are surrounded by ice. That is why the temperature stays around zero degrees.
91584.m: It is around zero degrees in an ice grotto.

91585.q: What often drips from the ceiling of an ice grotto in summer?
91585.e: When it is warm outside, the ice melts a little. Then meltwater drips from the ceiling.
91585.m: In summer, meltwater drips in the ice grotto.

91586.q: What digs natural caves into a glacier in summer?
91586.e: Meltwater flows under and through the glacier and eats tunnels into the ice. This is how natural glacier caves form.
91586.m: Meltwater can eat caves into a glacier.

91587.q: What is the famous glacier mummy from the Alps called?
91587.e: Ötzi is a Stone Age man who was found in the ice. His name comes from the Ötztal Alps.
91587.m: The best-known glacier mummy is called Ötzi.

91588.q: On the border between which countries was Ötzi found?
91588.e: Ötzi lay in the Ötztal Alps, very close to the border between Italy and Austria. The place where he was found is just on the Italian side.
91588.m: Ötzi was found on the border between Italy and Austria.

91589.e: Erika and Helmut Simon were out walking in the mountains. They saw a body in the ice and reported the find.

91592.q: Which hunting weapon did Ötzi have with him?
91592.e: Ötzi carried a long bow made of yew wood and a quiver of arrows. However, the bow had not been completely carved yet.
91592.m: Ötzi had a bow and arrows with him.

91594.q: Why was Ötzi's body preserved for so long?
a: He lay in the sand by a river
91594.e: Cold and ice protected the body as if it were in a freezer. That is why it is still preserved after thousands of years.

91595.q: What happens to a glacier when a lot of snow falls in winter and little melts in summer?
91595.e: If more snow is added than melts away, the glacier gains ice. Then it gets thicker and can get longer.
91595.m: A glacier grows when more snow falls than melts.

91596.q: What has been happening to the Aletsch Glacier for many years?
a: It is getting longer and longer
It is staying exactly the same
It is turning into a lake
91596.e: Because it is getting warmer, a lot of ice melts every year. So the Aletsch Glacier gets shorter and thinner every year.
91596.m: The Aletsch Glacier gets shorter every year.

91597.q: Which large bear lived in the Ice Age and is now extinct?
91597.e: The cave bear was bigger than a brown bear. Its bones have been found in many caves, including in Switzerland.
91597.m: The cave bear lived in the Ice Age.

91598.q: What grows on old moraines after many years?
91598.e: First mosses and small plants grow on the rubble. After many years there are meadows and even forest.
91598.m: Over time, meadows and forests grow on old moraines.

a: On low bushes on the ground
91599.e: Oranges grow on evergreen orange trees. These trees need a warm climate.
91599.m: Oranges grow on trees in warm countries.

91600.q: What are the separate pieces you can split a peeled orange into called?
91600.e: Inside, an orange is made up of many segments. Each segment is wrapped in a thin skin.
91600.m: You can split an orange into segments.

91601.q: What is the vitamin C in an orange good for?
91601.e: Vitamin C helps the body fight off illness. It is also important for skin and gums.
91601.m: Vitamin C strengthens the body's defences.

91602.q: Which is healthier: eating a whole orange or just drinking its juice?
91602.e: The whole fruit contains fibre, which fills you up and is good for digestion. Juice contains a lot of sugar but hardly any fibre.
91602.m: A whole orange is healthier than orange juice.

91603.q: Which countries do many oranges in Switzerland come from?
91603.e: Switzerland is too cold for orange trees. That is why many oranges come from Spain and other Mediterranean countries.
91603.m: Many oranges come from warm countries like Spain.

91604.q: In which season are oranges from Europe in season?
91604.e: Oranges from the Mediterranean are mainly picked in winter. Then they are fresh and cheap.
91604.m: Oranges are in season in winter.

91605.q: What colour are the flowers of the orange tree?
91605.e: The orange tree has white flowers with a strong scent. The fruit later grows from the flowers.
91605.m: The orange tree has white flowers.

91606.q: Why should you drink freshly squeezed orange juice soon?
a: Vitamin C is lost over time
91606.e: Vitamin C is sensitive to air, light and heat. That is why fresh juice contains the most.
91606.m: Fresh juice is best drunk straight away.

91607.q: What can happen if someone eats a huge number of carrots?
91607.e: The orange colouring can build up in the skin. This is harmless and goes away again if you eat fewer carrots.
91607.m: Lots and lots of carrots can turn the skin slightly orange.

91608.e: The colouring carotene makes the carrot orange. It even takes its name from the carrot.

91609.q: Which vitamin does the body make from the colouring in carrots?
91609.e: The body makes vitamin A from the beta-carotene in carrots. That is why beta-carotene is also called provitamin A.
91609.m: The body makes vitamin A from carrots.

91610.q: Which parts of the body is vitamin A especially important for?
91610.e: The eyes need vitamin A to see well, especially in low light. It is also important for the skin.
91610.m: Vitamin A is important for the eyes.

91611.q: What should you add to cooked carrots so the body takes in the vitamin better?
91611.e: The vitamin from carrots dissolves in fat. With a little oil or butter the body can take it in better.
91611.m: Carrots with a little oil or butter give the body more vitamin.

91613.q: What colour were many carrots in the past, before orange ones were bred?
91613.e: In the past carrots were often purple or yellow. The orange carrots that are usual today were only bred later.
91613.m: In the past many carrots were purple or yellow.

91614.q: Which animal loves nibbling carrots in stories?
91614.e: In picture books and cartoons, hares and rabbits love eating carrots. But rabbits mainly eat hay and grass.
91614.m: In stories, hares love nibbling carrots.

91615.q: What does the skin of a green kiwi look like?
91615.e: The skin of a green kiwi is brown and covered in fine hairs. It feels a little furry.
91615.m: A kiwi has a brown, hairy skin.

91616.q: What colour is the flesh of an ordinary kiwi?
91616.e: The flesh of the usual kiwi is bright green. But there are also yellow varieties.
91616.m: The flesh of a kiwi is usually green.

91617.q: What does a kiwi have compared with an orange?
91617.e: A green kiwi contains much more vitamin C than an orange of the same weight. Just one kiwi covers a large part of what you need in a day.
91617.m: A kiwi has even more vitamin C than an orange.

91618.q: What is an easy way to eat a kiwi?
a: Cut it in half and scoop it out
91618.e: You cut the kiwi through the middle. Then you can scoop out the flesh with a spoon.
91618.m: You can cut a kiwi in half and scoop it out.

91619.q: Which animal is the kiwi fruit named after?
91619.e: The kiwi is a bird that only lives in New Zealand. The fruit got its name when New Zealand started selling it to other countries.
91619.m: The kiwi fruit is named after a bird from New Zealand.

91620.q: Which country does the kiwi fruit originally come from?
91620.e: The kiwi first grew wild in China. It became well known when it was grown in New Zealand.
91620.m: The kiwi fruit originally comes from China.

91621.q: How can you tell that a kiwi is ripe?
a: It gives a little when pressed gently
91621.e: A ripe kiwi is slightly soft when you press it gently. Hard kiwis are still sour.
91621.m: A ripe kiwi gives a little when pressed gently.

91622.q: How does the kiwi plant grow?
91622.e: The kiwi grows on a climbing plant, rather like grapevines. It climbs up frames.
91622.m: The kiwi grows on a climbing plant.

91623.q: Which pepper has the most vitamin C?
91623.e: Red peppers contain an especially large amount of vitamin C. Green peppers contain much less.
91623.m: Red peppers contain an especially large amount of vitamin C.

91624.q: What is a green pepper often?
91624.e: Many green peppers are picked before they are ripe. If you leave them on the plant longer, they turn yellow or red.
91624.m: Green peppers are often still unripe.

91626.q: How should you eat peppers so that as much vitamin C as possible is kept?
91626.e: Heat destroys some of the vitamin C. Raw, for example as vegetable sticks for a snack, most of it is kept.
91626.m: Raw peppers have the most vitamin C.

91627.q: Do ordinary sweet peppers burn your mouth?
91627.e: Ordinary sweet peppers are mild and slightly sweet. Chillies, on the other hand, are hot.

a: A stone like in a cherry
91628.e: A pepper is hollow inside. In the middle there are lots of small, pale seeds.
91628.m: A pepper is hollow inside and has lots of small seeds.

91629.q: Which continent does the pepper originally come from?
91629.e: The pepper comes from Central and South America. Sailors brought it to Europe over 500 years ago.

91630.q: Which plant family does the pepper belong to?
91630.e: The pepper belongs to the nightshade family. Tomatoes and potatoes belong to this family too.
91630.m: Like the tomato, the pepper belongs to the nightshade family.

91631.q: Which part of broccoli do we actually eat?
91631.e: The green parts at the top of broccoli are lots of small flower buds that are still closed. If you leave it to grow, it flowers yellow.
91631.m: With broccoli we eat flower buds.

91632.q: Which vegetable is broccoli closely related to?
91632.e: Broccoli and cauliflower are both kinds of cabbage. They come from the same wild cabbage.

91633.q: How should you cook broccoli so that lots of vitamins are kept?
a: Deep-fry it for a long time
91633.e: Steaming briefly protects the vitamins. With long boiling, many vitamins go into the water or are destroyed.
91633.m: Steam broccoli briefly so the vitamins stay.

91634.q: What are the small, tree-like parts of broccoli called?
91634.e: A head of broccoli can be split into small florets. They look like little trees.
91634.m: Broccoli is made up of lots of florets.

91635.e: Broccoli contains lots of vitamins and minerals. They help the body stay healthy.

91636.q: Can you eat the stalk of broccoli too?
91636.e: The stalk is edible and tastes mild. You peel off the tough outer skin and cook it along with the rest.
91636.m: You can eat broccoli stalks too.

91637.e: Fresh broccoli is deep green and firm. If it turns yellow, it is old and beginning to flower.

91638.q: Which country does the name broccoli come from?
91638.e: The word comes from Italian and means little sprouts. Broccoli has been grown in Italy for a long time.
91638.m: The name broccoli comes from Italian.

91639.q: Where are lots of the vitamins in an apple?
91639.e: Lots of vitamins are in the skin and just underneath it. That is why apples are best eaten with their skin.
91639.m: Apples are best eaten with their skin.

91640.q: What is the most popular fruit in Switzerland?
91640.e: People in Switzerland eat more apples than any other fruit. Many apples are grown in the country itself.
91640.m: The apple is Switzerland's most popular fruit.

91641.q: What should you do before eating an apple with its skin?
91641.e: There can be dirt and traces of sprays on the skin. Washing it with water makes it cleaner.
91641.m: Wash an apple before eating it.

91642.q: Which canton is known for its many apple trees and is jokingly called “Mostindien” (“Cider India”)?
91642.e: There are very many fruit trees in Thurgau, especially apple trees. A lot of apple juice and cider is made from the apples.
91642.m: Thurgau is known for its apples.

91643.q: Why does a cut apple turn brown?
91643.e: When air reaches the flesh, it turns brown. A few drops of lemon juice slow this down.
91643.m: A cut apple turns brown in the air.

91644.e: Süssmost is a Swiss word for apple juice. It has not fermented, so it contains no alcohol.

91645.q: Which English saying says that apples are healthy?
a: An apple a day keeps the doctor away
91645.e: The saying means that eating an apple every day keeps you healthy. It is meant to show that fruit is good for you.
91645.m: A well-known saying praises the apple as healthy food.

91646.q: When are most apples picked in Switzerland?
91646.e: Most apples are ripe in September and October. After that they are kept fresh for a long time in cold stores.
91646.m: Most apples are picked in autumn.

91647.q: Which part of the spinach plant do we eat?
91647.e: With spinach you eat the green leaves. Young leaves can even be eaten raw in a salad.
91647.m: With spinach we eat the leaves.

91648.q: Which cartoon character becomes very strong after eating spinach?
91648.e: Popeye is a sailor from an old comic. When he eats spinach, he gets huge muscles.
91648.m: In the comic, Popeye gets strong from spinach.

91649.q: Which mineral did people long believe spinach contained especially large amounts of?
91649.e: For a long time people said spinach contained an extremely large amount of iron. But the figure was given too high. Spinach is still healthy, because it provides vitamins such as folic acid.
91649.m: Spinach is healthy but contains less iron than was long thought.

91650.q: What happens to spinach when it is cooked?
a: It gets as hard as wood
91650.e: Fresh spinach contains a lot of water. When cooked, a big heap of leaves shrinks to a small pile.
91650.m: Spinach shrinks a lot when cooked.

91651.e: Spinach leaves are dark green. The colour comes from chlorophyll, which all green plants have.

91652.q: In which season does spinach grow especially well in Switzerland?
91652.e: Spinach likes cool weather and grows quickly. That is why in Switzerland it is mainly picked in spring and autumn.
91652.m: Spinach grows well in spring and autumn.

91653.q: Which vegetable is spinach related to?
91653.e: Spinach and chard belong to the same plant family. With both you mainly eat the leaves.

91654.q: What is cooked, finely chopped spinach in a white, creamy sauce called?
91654.e: Creamed spinach is finely chopped spinach with cream. It is often eaten with potatoes and a fried egg.
91654.m: Finely chopped spinach with cream is called creamed spinach.

a: A bush in a Swiss forest
91655.e: Bananas grow in bunches on a large plant. It looks like a tree, but it is a giant plant with no wood.
91655.m: Bananas grow on a large banana plant.

91656.q: What is in a banana that is good for the body?
91656.e: Bananas contain vitamins and minerals. The body needs them to stay healthy.

91657.q: Which mineral is found in large amounts in bananas?
91657.e: Bananas are known for containing a lot of potassium. The body needs potassium for the muscles and the heart.
91657.m: Bananas contain a lot of potassium.

91658.q: How can you recognise a very ripe banana?
91658.e: A ripe banana is yellow and gets brown spots over time. Then it is especially sweet.
91658.m: Brown spots show a very ripe banana.

91659.e: Bananas need lots of warmth and rain. They grow, for example, in South and Central America.
91659.m: Bananas grow in warm tropical countries.

91660.q: Why do many athletes like eating bananas?
91660.e: Bananas contain a lot of sugar and starch. This gives the body energy quickly.

91661.q: What colour is an unripe banana?
91661.e: Bananas are picked green and ripen on the long journey to Europe. Only then do they turn yellow.

91662.q: What is a group of bananas that are joined together called?
91662.e: A group of bananas is called a hand, and a single banana a finger. This fits, because they look like fingers on a hand.
91662.m: Several bananas joined together are called a hand.

91663.q: Which plant family does the strawberry belong to?
91663.e: The strawberry belongs to the rose family. Apples, cherries and raspberries belong to this family too.
91663.m: The strawberry is related to the rose.

91664.q: Where are the tiny seeds on a strawberry?
a: On the outside of the fruit
91664.e: The tiny yellow dots sit on the outside of the strawberry. They are the real fruits, little nuts.
91664.m: On a strawberry the seeds are on the outside.

91665.q: When should you pull the little green leaves off a strawberry?
91665.e: If you only pull off the green part after washing, no water gets into the fruit. That way the taste and vitamins are kept better.
91665.m: Wash strawberries before removing the green part.

91666.q: What is found in large amounts in a handful of fresh strawberries?
91666.e: Strawberries contain about as much vitamin C as oranges. Just one bowl of strawberries covers a large part of what you need in a day.
91666.m: Strawberries contain a lot of vitamin C.

91667.q: How does the strawberry plant grow?
a: As a climbing plant on walls
91667.e: The strawberry plant stays small and grows close to the ground. That is why you have to bend down to pick them.
91667.m: Strawberries grow close to the ground.

91668.q: What are the small strawberries that grow wild in the woods called?
91668.e: Wild strawberries are much smaller than garden strawberries. But they have a very strong flavour.
91668.m: Small wild strawberries grow in the woods.

91669.q: What are the long shoots called that a strawberry plant uses to form new plants?
91669.e: The strawberry sends out long runners across the ground. Where they put down roots, a new plant grows.

91670.q: What should you do with strawberries you are not eating straight away?
91670.e: Strawberries are delicate and go off quickly. In the fridge they last one or two days longer.

91671.q: Which vitamin is found in especially large amounts in oily fish such as salmon and herring?
91671.e: Oily fish such as salmon and herring are among the few foods with a lot of vitamin D. Fruit and vegetables contain almost none.
91671.m: Oily fish contains a lot of vitamin D.

91672.q: Which healthy fats do oily sea fish contain?
91672.e: Fish such as salmon and mackerel contain omega-3 fatty acids. They are good for the heart and brain.
91672.m: Oily fish provides healthy omega-3 fats.

91673.q: What does the body need vitamin D for?
91673.e: Vitamin D helps the body build calcium into the bones. That makes bones and teeth strong.
91673.m: Vitamin D makes bones and teeth strong.

91674.q: Which vitamin is found almost only in food from animals, for example in fish?
91674.e: Vitamin B12 is found in fish, meat, eggs and milk. Plants contain almost none.
91674.m: Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal foods.

91675.q: Which fish is caught in many Swiss lakes?
91675.e: Perch, called Egli in Switzerland, is a well-known fish from Swiss lakes. Perch fillets are very popular in Switzerland.
91675.m: Perch is a fish from Swiss lakes.

91676.q: How often a week is fish often recommended as part of a healthy diet?
91676.e: Experts often recommend eating fish once or twice a week. That way the body gets valuable fats and vitamins.
91676.m: Fish once or twice a week is healthy.

91677.q: What do you need to be especially careful about when eating fish?
91677.e: Fish have fine bones. You should eat slowly so that you don't swallow any.
91677.m: Watch out for bones when eating fish.

91678.q: Which fish is pink and often oily?
91678.e: Salmon has pink to orange flesh. It is one of the oily fish.

91679.q: Where are most of the vitamins in an egg?
91679.e: The yellow yolk contains most of the egg's vitamins. The egg white contains only a few vitamins.
91679.m: Most of an egg's vitamins are in the yolk.

91681.q: How many eggs can a hen lay in a day at most?
91681.e: A hen needs about a day to make an egg. That is why it lays at most one egg a day.
91681.m: A hen lays at most one egg a day.

91682.q: What does an egg give the body a lot of?
91682.e: An egg contains valuable protein. The body needs it for the muscles and for growing.
91682.m: An egg provides a lot of protein.

91683.q: Why should you cook or fry eggs well before eating them?
a: To give them more vitamin C
91683.e: There can be germs such as salmonella on and in raw eggs. Heating them well kills these germs.

91684.q: Roughly how long do you boil a hard-boiled egg?
91684.e: A hard-boiled egg needs about ten minutes in boiling water. A soft-boiled egg is ready after about five minutes.
91684.m: A hard-boiled egg takes about ten minutes.

91685.q: How can you test whether a raw egg is still fresh?
a: Throw it up in the air
91685.e: A fresh egg sinks in water and lies flat. An old egg stands up or floats, because its air pocket is bigger.
91685.m: A fresh egg sinks to the bottom in water.

91686.q: Which vitamin is found in especially large amounts in hazelnuts and almonds?
91686.e: Nuts and almonds are rich in vitamin E. It protects the body's cells.
91686.m: Nuts contain a lot of vitamin E.

91688.q: Which nut grows on bushes in Swiss woods too?
91688.e: Hazel bushes grow at the edges of woods and in hedges in Switzerland. Their nuts sit in a green husk.

91689.q: Why should you only eat a small handful of nuts a day?
a: They have a lot of energy
91689.e: Nuts are healthy, but they contain a lot of fat and so a lot of energy. A handful a day is a good amount.
91689.m: A handful of nuts a day is enough.

91690.q: Why shouldn't small children eat whole nuts?
91690.e: Whole nuts are hard and small. Toddlers can easily get them into their windpipe and choke.
91690.m: Small children shouldn't eat whole nuts.

91691.q: Why do some children have to avoid nuts completely?
91691.e: Some people are allergic to nuts. Even small amounts can harm them.
91691.m: With a nut allergy you must avoid nuts.

91692.q: What do you use to open a hard walnut?
91692.e: The shell of a walnut is hard. A nutcracker presses it open so you can get to the kernel.
91692.m: You open hard nuts with a nutcracker.

91693.q: When are hazelnuts and walnuts ripe in Switzerland?
91693.e: Hazelnuts and walnuts ripen in September and October. Then they often fall down by themselves.
91693.m: Hazelnuts and walnuts are ripe in autumn.

91694.q: Can you eat the skin of a kiwi?
a: Yes, it is edible when washed
91694.e: The skin of a kiwi is edible if you wash it well. Many people still peel kiwis because the hairs tickle.

91695.q: Why don't bananas belong in the fridge?
a: Their skin turns brown in the cold
91695.e: Bananas come from warm countries and don't like the cold. In the fridge their skin soon turns brown or even black.
91695.m: Don't keep bananas in the fridge.

91696.q: Which substance, which in Switzerland is also added to table salt, do sea fish provide?
91696.e: Sea fish contain a lot of iodine. Because the soil in Switzerland has little iodine, iodine has been added to table salt since 1922.

91697.q: When is broccoli harvested in the fields in Switzerland?
91697.e: Swiss broccoli is available from about June to October. In winter it mostly comes from countries further south.
91697.m: Swiss broccoli is harvested from summer to autumn.

91698.q: How fast is light compared with a racing car?
91698.e: Light is the fastest thing there is. It travels about 300,000 kilometres in one second.

91699.q: About how many times could light zoom round the whole Earth in one second?
91699.e: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres in one second. The way round the Earth is about 40,000 kilometres long, so that is enough for just over 7 laps.
91699.m: In one second, light zooms about 7 times round the Earth.

91700.q: Why can you see a ball in the room?
a: Light from the ball reaches your eyes
Your eyes shine light on the ball
91700.e: Light falls on the ball and is bounced back by it. This light reaches your eyes, and that is why you see it.
91700.m: We see things when their light reaches our eyes.

91701.q: What do you need for a rainbow to appear?
91701.e: In the raindrops, sunlight is split into its colours. That is why you need sun and rain at the same time.
91701.m: A rainbow needs sun and rain.

91702.q: What is hidden in white sunlight?
a: All the colours of the rainbow
91702.e: White light is a mixture of many colours. A rainbow or a prism shows these colours.
91702.m: White light contains all the colours of the rainbow.

91703.q: Why does a bike have a red reflector at the back?
a: So that drivers can see it in the dark
So that the chain doesn't rust
91703.e: The reflector bounces back the light from car headlights. That way the bike can be seen from far away in the dark.
91703.m: Reflectors make a bike visible in the dark.

91704.q: Which clothing can be seen best in the dark when a car's lights shine on it?
91704.e: High-visibility vests have strips that strongly reflect the headlights. Dark clothes swallow almost all of the light.
91704.m: Bright high-visibility vests keep you safe in the dark.

91705.q: What colour is your shadow on the ground?
91705.e: A shadow is a place that gets less light. That is why it is dark, whatever colour your clothes are.

91706.q: On which side of you is your shadow?
a: On the side away from the light
Always on the side of the lamp
91706.e: You block the light. That is why the shadow forms on the side facing away from the light source.
91706.m: Your shadow is always opposite the light.

91707.q: Two lamps shine on you from different sides. How many shadows do you have?
91707.e: Each lamp makes its own shadow. So with two lamps there are two shadows.
91707.m: Each lamp makes its own shadow.

91708.q: What does the shadow of an object show?
91708.e: A shadow only shows the shape at the edge, that is, the outline. You cannot see colours and patterns in a shadow.
91708.m: A shadow only shows the outline.

91709.q: Why does a tree's shadow move during the day?
a: The sun is in a different place all the time
91709.e: The sun seems to move across the sky from east to west. That is why the shadow points in a different direction too.
91709.m: The shadow moves as the sun moves.

91710.q: Whose shadow falls on the Earth during a solar eclipse?
91710.e: During a solar eclipse, the Moon moves in front of the Sun. Its shadow then falls on part of the Earth.
91710.m: During a solar eclipse, the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

91711.q: Whose shadow falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse?
91711.e: During a lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow makes the Moon dark and often reddish.
91711.m: During a lunar eclipse, the Moon is in the Earth's shadow.

91712.q: How long are shadows early in the morning?
a: Exactly as long as at midday
91712.e: In the morning the sun is low in the sky. Then the light falls at a slant and the shadows become long.
91712.m: In the morning, shadows are long.

91713.q: Why do you have no shadow in a dark tunnel without a lamp?
91713.e: Without light, no shadow can form. A shadow always needs a light source.

91714.q: What casts the shadow on a sundial?
91714.e: A sundial has a rod that casts a shadow. The shadow falls on the numbers and so shows the time.
91714.m: The rod of the sundial casts the shadow.

91715.q: Where do you often find a sundial in Switzerland?
a: On the walls of houses and churches
91715.e: Many old houses and churches have a painted sundial on a sunny wall. It is called a wall sundial.
91715.m: Sundials are often on sunny house walls.

91716.q: In which direction does the shadow turn on a flat sundial where we live?
