91716.e: Where we live, the shadow on a flat sundial moves just like the hands of a clock. That is probably why clock hands turn in this direction too.
91716.m: The shadow on a sundial turns like a clock hand.

91717.q: What do you need to build a simple sundial in the garden yourself?
91717.e: You push a stick into the ground. Every hour you put a stone at the end of the shadow, and you have a clock.
91717.m: A stick in the ground can be a sundial.

91718.q: In spring the clocks go forward one hour. What do you do with a sundial then?
a: You put it forward one hour
You put it in the shade
91718.e: A sundial always shows the time by the sun. You can't change it, so in summer it shows a time one hour different from your watch.
91718.m: You can't change a sundial to summer time.

91719.q: What does a sundial show when thick clouds are in front of the sun?
a: Nothing, because there is no shadow
91719.e: A sundial needs sunlight so that the rod casts a shadow. Without a shadow you can't read the time.

91720.q: What kind of bulb do most new torches have?
91720.e: Modern torches have LED bulbs. They are bright and use little electricity.

91721.q: What is the shiny cone behind the bulb of a torch for?
91721.e: The shiny cone reflects the light forwards like a mirror. That way the torch shines a long way.
91721.m: A shiny cone directs the light forwards.

91722.q: How can a wind-up torch shine without a battery?
a: You put it in the fridge
91722.e: When you turn the handle, electricity is made inside. This electricity makes the lamp shine.
91722.m: A wind-up torch makes its own electricity.

91723.q: How do you flash the distress signal SOS with a torch?
91723.e: SOS is a well-known distress signal. You flash three times short, three times long and three times short again.
91723.m: SOS means three short, three long, three short.

91724.q: Why should you switch off a torch after using it?
a: So that the battery doesn't run flat
91724.e: A lamp that is switched on uses electricity all the time. If you switch it off, you save the battery.

91725.q: Why should you never shine a torch into someone's eyes?
a: It dazzles and can harm the eyes
91725.e: Bright light straight into the eyes dazzles strongly. Afterwards you can't see well for a while.
91725.m: Never shine a light into someone's eyes.

91726.q: Which device that many adults carry can also be used as a torch?
91726.e: Many mobile phones have a bright light next to the camera. You can switch it on as a torch.
91726.m: A mobile phone can also be a torch.

91727.q: Apart from the figures, what do you need for a shadow theatre?
a: A lamp and a white sheet
91727.e: The lamp shines from behind onto a light-coloured sheet. The figures in between cast their shadows onto the sheet.
91727.m: A shadow theatre needs light and a screen.

91728.q: Where does the audience sit at a shadow theatre?
a: On the other side of the sheet
91728.e: The players are behind the sheet with the lamp and the figures. On the other side, the audience only sees the shadows.
91728.m: At a shadow theatre, the audience only sees the shadows.

91729.q: Which animal can you easily make as a hand shadow with two fingers as ears?
91729.e: If you stretch two fingers upwards, in the shadow they look like long ears. That makes a rabbit.
91729.m: Two fingers as ears make a shadow rabbit.

91730.q: What is good for making figures for a shadow theatre?
91730.e: Cardboard doesn't let light through. That is why cardboard figures cast a clear shadow.

91731.q: Why is it best to perform a shadow theatre in a darkened room?
a: So that you can see the shadows clearly
So that the figures don't get cold
So that the lamp lasts longer
So that the audience falls asleep
91731.e: If the room is bright, light also falls on the shadows. Then they look pale. In the dark, they stand out clearly against the bright sheet.
91731.m: In a dark room, shadows are clearest.

91732.q: How can you get coloured patches in a shadow theatre?
91732.e: Coloured light shines through coloured film. That makes colourful spots on the sheet.
91732.m: Coloured film makes colourful spots in a shadow theatre.

91733.q: What colour should the sheet for a shadow theatre be?
91733.e: On a white sheet you can see the dark shadows best. On a dark sheet they would be hard to make out.
91733.m: Shadows show up best on a white sheet.

91734.q: What do you often use to move the arms of a figure in a shadow theatre?
91734.e: The figures have moving parts. With thin sticks the players can move them behind the sheet.
91734.m: Shadow figures are moved with sticks.

91735.q: About how long do a day and a night last together?
91735.e: In about 24 hours the Earth turns once around itself. That is how long a day and a night last together.
91735.m: Day and night together last about 24 hours.

91736.q: In which season are the days longest where we live?
91736.e: In summer the sun stays in the sky for a long time. Around 21 June is the longest day of the year.
91736.m: In summer, the days are longest.

91737.q: In which month is the shortest day of the year where we live?
91737.e: Around 21 December the sun rises late and sets early. That is the shortest day of the year.
91737.m: The shortest day is in December.

91738.q: What is it called when, far in the north, the sun shines even at midnight in summer?
91738.e: In countries far in the north, the sun doesn't set at all in summer. This is called the midnight sun.
91738.m: Far in the north there is the midnight sun in summer.

91739.q: Which animal is mainly awake at night?
91739.e: Owls hunt at night. During the day they sleep in hiding.
91739.m: The owl is an animal of the night.

91740.q: When it is midday here in Switzerland, what is it on the other side of the Earth?
a: Early morning of the day before
91740.e: The other side of the Earth is then facing away from the sun. It is night there.
91740.m: When it is day here, it is night on the other side of the Earth.

91741.q: What are the two days of the year when day and night are about the same length called?
91741.e: In March and September, day and night are about the same length. These days are called the equinoxes.
91741.m: In March and September, day and night are about the same length.

a: Something that gives off its own light
91742.e: A light source makes light itself. Examples are the sun, a candle or a lamp.
91742.m: A light source gives off light by itself.

91743.q: Which of these is a light source?
91743.e: The flame of a candle makes light itself. Mirrors, glass and paper only reflect light or let it through.
91743.m: A candle flame is a light source.

91744.q: Which light source can you see in a thunderstorm?
91744.e: Lightning is a huge electric spark. It shines so brightly that everything is bright for a moment.
91744.m: Lightning is a bright light source.

91745.q: Which light source is made by people, that is, artificial?
91745.e: The light bulb was invented by people. The sun, stars and lightning are natural light sources.
91745.m: A light bulb is an artificial light source.

91746.q: Which light sources can you see twinkling in the sky on a clear night?
91746.e: Stars are huge, hot balls that give off their own light. They are so far away that they look like tiny dots.
91746.m: Stars are light sources in the night sky.

91747.q: What comes out of a volcano and glows red and orange?
91747.e: Lava is melted rock and is very hot. Because it is so hot, it glows and shines.

91748.q: How did people in the Stone Age make light at night?
91748.e: In the Stone Age there was no electricity yet. People made light with a fire or with flaming torches.
91748.m: Long ago, people made light with fire.

91749.q: Is a bike reflector a light source?
a: Yes, but only during the day
91749.e: A reflector only shines when light hits it. It bounces this light back but makes none itself.
91749.m: A reflector is not a light source.

91750.q: What kind of animal is a glow-worm?
91750.e: Glow-worms are called that, but they are not worms. They belong to the beetles.

91751.q: When is the best time to see glow-worms shining in Switzerland?
91751.e: Glow-worms shine mainly in June and July. You can see them on warm nights at the edges of woods and in meadows.
91751.m: Glow-worms shine on warm summer nights.

91752.q: What does the light of a glow-worm feel like?
91752.e: Glow-worms make a cold light. Almost no energy is lost as heat.

91753.q: On which part of its body does a glow-worm shine?
91753.e: The light organ is at the back of the body, on the abdomen. That is where the light is made.
91753.m: A glow-worm shines on its abdomen.

91754.q: What colour is the light of glow-worms where we live?
91754.e: Our glow-worms shine yellowish to greenish. You can see it well on dark nights.

91755.q: What do glow-worm larvae like to eat?
91755.e: Glow-worm larvae hunt snails. That is why they are useful in the garden.

91756.q: What disturbs glow-worms so that there are fewer of them?
a: Lots of artificial light at night
91756.e: Street lamps and brightly lit gardens outshine the glow of the glow-worms. Then they can no longer find each other well.
91756.m: Too much light at night harms glow-worms.

a: So that they can find each other
So that they can eat better
91757.e: With their light, glow-worms show each other where they are. That way they find each other at night.
91757.m: Glow-worms shine to find each other.

91758.e: The light of the lighthouse warns ships about rocks and coasts. That way they find their way safely into the harbour.
91758.m: A lighthouse shows ships the way.

a: In the middle of a forest
91759.e: Lighthouses stand by the sea, on coasts and at harbour entrances. That is where ships need help at night.

91760.q: When is the light of a lighthouse most important?
91760.e: At night, sailors can't see the coast. Then the light shows them where land is.

91761.q: How do sailors know at night which lighthouse it is?
91761.e: Every lighthouse has its own flashing pattern, called its character. That way sailors know where they are.
91761.m: Every lighthouse flashes in its own way.

91762.q: What was the job of the person who looked after the light in a lighthouse in the past called?
91762.e: In the past, a lighthouse keeper lived by the tower. He made sure the light was burning every night.
91762.m: In the past, a lighthouse keeper looked after the light.

91763.q: Why are many lighthouses striped red and white?
a: So that they can be seen well during the day
So that birds land on them
91763.e: The eye-catching stripes can be seen from far away during the day. That way the tower works as a sign even without its light.
91763.m: The stripes make a lighthouse easy to see during the day.

91764.q: In which ancient city stood the famous lighthouse that was one of the Seven Wonders of the World?
91764.e: The Lighthouse of Alexandria in Egypt was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It no longer stands today.
91764.m: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was a Wonder of the World.

91765.q: On which lake on the Swiss border is there a well-known lighthouse in the harbour of Lindau?
91765.e: Lindau lies on Lake Constance, right next to Switzerland. Its lighthouse stands at the harbour entrance.
91765.m: There are lighthouses on Lake Constance too.

91766.q: Why does the light of many lighthouses shine first in one direction, then in another?
a: The light turns round in a circle
91766.e: At the top of the tower, the light turns round in a circle with large lenses. That way it shines in all directions across the sea, one after another.
91766.m: The light in a lighthouse turns round in a circle.

91767.q: Why can't you see anything in a completely dark room?
91767.e: We can only see when light reaches our eyes. Without light we can't see anything at all.
91767.m: Without light we can't see anything.

91768.q: What does the black part in the middle of your eye, the pupil, do in the dark?
91768.e: In the dark, the pupil gets bigger. That way more light can get into the eye.
91768.m: In the dark, the pupil gets bigger.

91769.q: What happens when you are in dim light for a while?
a: Your eyes get used to it and you see more
Your eyes get tired and close
91769.e: The eyes slowly adjust to the little light there is. After a few minutes you can see much more than at the beginning.
91769.m: The eyes slowly get used to the dark.

91770.q: Why can you hardly see colours at dusk?
a: In low light the eyes see almost only grey
91770.e: In low light, the eyes mainly use cells that can't see colours. That is why everything looks grey.
91770.m: In low light we can hardly see colours.

91771.q: How does a bat find its way in the dark?
91771.e: Bats make very high-pitched calls. From the echo they can hear where obstacles and insects are.
91771.m: Bats find their way using echoes.

91772.q: Why can you only see a few stars at night in a big city?
a: The many lamps make the sky bright
The houses hide all the stars
There is always fog in cities
91772.e: Street lamps and lit-up buildings brighten the night sky. This is called light pollution.
91772.m: Lots of light in the city hides the stars.

91773.q: Can a cat see anything in complete darkness?
a: No, it needs a little light
91773.e: Cats see much better than we do in low light. But in complete darkness without any light, they can't see anything either.
91773.m: Cats also need a little light to see.

91774.q: Why do a cat's eyes shine when a car's lights fall on them in the dark?
a: A layer in the eye reflects the light
The cat makes its own light
The eyes are made of glass
91774.e: At the back of a cat's eye there is a mirror-like layer. It reflects the headlights, which is why the eyes seem to shine.

91775.q: What do you call a material that you can see through clearly?
91775.e: Light passes through a transparent material almost freely. You can see clearly what is behind it.
91775.m: You can see through transparent things.

91776.q: Which material lets no light through?
91776.e: Wood is opaque. Light can't get through, which is why a board casts a dark shadow.

91777.q: What do you call baking paper, which lets some light through but which you can't see through clearly?
91777.e: Translucent things let some light through. But you can only see blurrily what is behind them.

91778.q: Why do bathrooms often have a window made of frosted glass?
a: It lets light in, but you can't see through it
91778.e: Frosted glass is translucent. Light gets into the bathroom, but nobody can look in from outside.
91778.m: Frosted glass lets light through, but not people's looks.

91779.q: Which of these things is opaque?
91779.e: Kitchen foil lets no light through. Clear bottles, glasses and spectacles, on the other hand, are transparent.

91780.q: Why can you see the stones at the bottom of a clear mountain lake?
a: The water gives off its own light
91780.e: Clear water lets light through. So you can see right to the bottom.

91781.q: What does a thick curtain at the window do with the morning light?
91781.e: A thick curtain is opaque. It keeps the light out, which is why the room stays dark.
91781.m: A thick curtain keeps the light out.

91782.q: What happens to clear water when you stir in lots of milk?
a: It goes cloudy and you can't see through it
91782.e: The milk spreads through the water and blocks the light. The water becomes cloudy and opaque.

91783.q: When is moonlight at its brightest at night?
91783.e: At full moon we see the whole lit-up side of the Moon. That is why it is brightest then.
91783.m: Moonlight is brightest at full moon.

91784.q: What is it called when you can't see the Moon in the sky at all?
91784.e: At new moon, the lit-up side of the Moon faces away from us. That is why we can't see it.
91784.m: At new moon you can't see the Moon.

91785.q: Is moonlight brighter or weaker than sunlight?
91785.e: The Moon only reflects a small part of the sunlight. That is why moonlight is much weaker than sunlight.
91785.m: Moonlight is much weaker than sunlight.

91786.q: Can you have a shadow on a bright night with a full moon?
91786.e: The light of the full moon is strong enough for a faint shadow. You can see it outdoors away from lamps.
91786.m: Moonlight can make a shadow too.

91788.q: Can you get sunburnt in moonlight?
a: No, the light is too weak
91788.e: Moonlight is far too weak to burn your skin. You only get sunburn from the sun.

91789.q: Which side of the Moon do we always see from Earth?
91789.e: The Moon turns around itself exactly as fast as it goes round the Earth. That is why it always shows us the same side.
91789.m: We always see the same side of the Moon.

91790.q: Which element does a red giant later fuse into carbon in its core?
91790.e: When the core of a red giant gets hot enough, a new kind of nuclear fusion starts there. Helium fuses into carbon.
91790.m: In red giants, helium fuses into carbon.

91791.q: Why does a red giant shine reddish?
a: Its surface is cooler than the Sun’s
It is surrounded by red dust
91791.e: The colour of a star depends on the temperature of its surface. A red giant is cooler on the outside than the Sun and therefore shines reddish.
91791.m: Red giants are relatively cool on the outside.

91792.q: Which fuel runs low in the core of a star before it becomes a red giant?
91792.e: Stars like the Sun fuse hydrogen into helium in their core. When the hydrogen in the core runs low, the giant phase begins.
91792.m: A star becomes a red giant when the hydrogen in its core runs low.

91793.q: Which planets will the Sun very probably swallow as a red giant?
91793.e: The Sun will expand so much that the inner planets Mercury and Venus will disappear inside it. Whether the Earth will also be swallowed is uncertain.
91793.m: As a red giant, the Sun will swallow Mercury and Venus.

91794.q: Why does a red giant give off more light in total than the Sun, even though it is cooler?
91794.e: Each square metre gives off less light, but the surface is enormous. So in total the star gives off much more light.
91794.m: Because of its enormous surface, a red giant shines very brightly.

91795.q: At what stage in the life of a Sun-like star does the red giant phase happen?
a: Towards the end of its life
In the middle of its life
It was always a red giant
91795.e: A star spends most of its time quietly on what is called the main sequence. Only late on, when the fuel in its core runs low, does it swell up.
91795.m: The giant phase comes late in a star’s life.

91796.q: What is special about the red giant Mira in the constellation Cetus (the Whale)?
a: It always stands still in the north
91796.e: Mira pulsates and changes its brightness over about eleven months. Sometimes you can see it with the naked eye, sometimes only through a telescope.
91796.m: Mira is a pulsating red giant.

91797.q: How does the diameter of the Sun change when it becomes a red giant?
a: It becomes several hundred times larger
It shrinks to the size of the Earth
91797.e: As a red giant, the Sun will become several hundred times larger than it is today. Its edge will then reach about as far as the Earth’s present orbit.
91797.m: A red giant is many times larger than today’s Sun.

91798.q: What will be left as a small, hot remnant at the end of our Sun’s life?
91798.e: After the giant phase, only the hot, dense core of the Sun will be left. This small remnant is called a white dwarf.
91798.m: In the end, the Sun will become a white dwarf.

91799.q: Roughly how big is a white dwarf?
a: About as big as the Earth
About as big as the Sun
About as big as a house
91799.e: A white dwarf has about the mass of the Sun, but is only about as big as the Earth. So it is packed extremely densely.
91799.m: A white dwarf is about as big as the Earth.

91800.q: Roughly how heavy would a one-cubic-centimetre cube of white dwarf material be?
91800.e: White dwarfs have an average density of about one tonne per cubic centimetre. A piece the size of a sugar cube would be as heavy as a car.
91800.m: White dwarf material is unimaginably dense.
